Before Watching the Video: Deciding whether this is going to make me a better C++ programmer, or make me somehow hate it more than i already do... (I'm a game developer, it's inescapable)

- A lot of the reason why it's still dominant in the game industry is the requirement to be able to very strictly control memory. A lot of UB in C++ is a hard crash on game consoles, in particular out of memory. Not that this isn't possible in Rust and Zig, just that it (mostly) precludes being able to make AAA games using a garbage-collected language.

- It also gave me some 300-700 page books that I probably need to read.

Ultimately, I don't hate C++ more, I just hate it more personally. I think this will ultimately make me better at writing it, inasmuch as that's a goal I should still have.

author: @lonkwuzhere4433
text:
I feel like basically all of these issues come from how C++ is trying to be "backward compatible" with C. Basically all the issues (weird fucked up int types, headers, include guarding vs #pragma once, the #define keyword, const_cast vs static_cast vs reinterpret_cast vs C-style cast, etc..) come directly from C or are re-implementations of C behaviour that realistically doesn't belong in a higher level language. Lots of these features make sense in C, only because C is so simple. With all these extra rules and exceptions to said rules it's boarder-line unusable. It's like it can't decide what it wants to be, and now were stuck with nearly 50 years worth of tech debt.

I started with C++ and Python but after picking up C a couple years ago it's been my go to language for the simple fact that I can look at a line of code and generally tell what it's doing. You don't have to worry about side effects generally in a well-written C codebase simply because everything is so explicit. Funnily enough, C actually handles OOP better than C++ does in some cases. With the newer style of struct initialization, you can't access member variables until after the struct is initialized, meaning you can't access the struct in a partially initialized state. This is unlike how C++ constructors work, where the "this" pointer is literally just a pointer to uninitialized memory, and you can't control or guarantee the order of initialization of variables in the constructor. With how includes work in C, you can get away with just including source files in other source files to avoid writing definitions in a header all together. This allows you to do the kind of implementation hiding C++ just fails to, and makes you treat header files like an actual interface. You *can* do this in C++ too, but you'd basically be writing C code masquerading as C++. Even then, you'd have a very difficult time using it with templates and other such features of the language without massive amounts of boilerplate code, not to mention the linker problems that will come up in most IDEs from doing things this way.

author: @jfolz
text:
Re: Age of Rust libraries.

In any other language that I know, when looking for a library to use, I first check when it was last updated. An abandoned library is a time bomb. With Rust it's the opposite. A library with a well-defined scope is simply done at some point. Importantly, breaking changes in new editions do not break old code. An app written in Rust 2024 can use any library written in Rust 2015 without issue. Metadata instructs the compiler which edition of the language to use for each code unit. And naturally, someone made a library that lets you switch editions inside the same file XD

text_clean: I don't see anybody trying to defend C++ (probably someone did this, but I couldn't find it), so here I go. I stopped watching the video halfway, at the end of this comment you will understand why. - I would say that the number of initializations is a bit inflated here. For example, "int x=int(10)" does two things: converts 10 to int (which does nothing, since 10 is already an int) and initialize x as 10. You can even argue that is three things: convert 10 to int, create a variable x and write 10 to x. You can call it another way of initialisation, but you can also say that you can initialize with "int x=10;" and "int x=10+0-0/69;", creating an inifinite number of initializations. Also writing "auto x=(1,0);" is pure evil, I don't think anybody does that (unless they want to troll readers of the code). The return value of comma operator is probably a bad design decision, but it's not initialization issue. - I don't get the hype around std::print fuction. The printf function was here for decades and print doesn't look like a big upgrade. Maybe I'm wrong, maybe it works better for printing classes or something. But it looks like some C++ programmers deliberately refuse to use functions that are from C. - Random numbers - fully agree. Again, in C++ you can use rand() (which is from C), but mt19937 is "more random". - "int i = (int) myFloat;" works in C++ as well, you can use static_cast to have more safety in some scenarios (usually pointers), but you don't have to. - Instead of "MyClass* obj=new MyClass();" you can simply use "MyClass obj();" and in 80%-95% of cases (depending on your style of writing code) this works as well. - I agree that working with multiple files in C++ is hard. - I agree that interfaces in Java are better than in C++. But in Java, it is much harder to avoid them. Let's say that there are 2 classes: Triangle and Rectangle. I want a function that calculates total area in a list of triangles or rectangles. If both Triangle and Rectangle have a area() function, then in C++ all you need to do is to write something like this: template<class T> double totalArea(vector<T>& shapes){ double sum=0; for(auto shape:shapes){ sum+=shape.area(); } return sum; } while in Java you need to write interface for Shape and explicitly write that Triangle and Rectangle implements Shape to do a similar thing. Alternatively, you can do some ugly type checking inside the totalArea function. - vector is a tuple of n numbers, where n is a dimension of a space. The only problem is that vectors can be added or multiplied by a number and C++ doesn't support that (i.e. you can't write 5*x to get a vector where every number is 5 times bigger). You can think of a vector as an object with magnitude and direction, but when you want to write it down, you usually use its coordinates. So after all, vector is not a terrible name choice. - "Set and map are not what you think they are" - I mean, why should I think that set is hashset? In Java, Set is an interface, so it may be either HashSet or TreeSet. In Python, set is a hashset, but I think the main reason is that in Python standard library there is no treeset. Many languages has their naming conventions, and blaming C++ has its own make no sense, especially that C++ is older most of the other languages shown for comparison. - The problem with modern C++ is that many people thinks that newer is better. Let's imagine that we use this idea in mathematics. Then we shouldn't use Pythagorean theorem, since law of cosines is newer and more general. We shouldn't use Riemann integral, since Lebesgue integral is more general. Actually, we shouldn't use Lebesgue integral either, since Bochner integral is even more general. The problem with this approach is that newer things are better in the sense that they are more general, but they usually are also harder to learn and harder to use. I'm pretty sure the "C-style C++" name comes from a usual C++ programmer who rarely always use the "modernerest" approach as was tired of hearing that his code is outdated. - "If you like C++, then you don't know it well enough" - aah, the ancient reverse skill issue. xD - I've realized that I never had a problem with returning a pointer to a locally created object because whenever I want to return an object big enough that using a pointer would be a good idea, I use out-parameter technique (i.e. one of the parameters is used as output). - I don't think that const has anything to do with speed. It can be used to increase code safety (in similar way to making a class member private). Some people (including me) thinks that it's usually not worth a hassle, since the safety benefit is marginal and putting const in one place often forces you to put it in another. - "Many flags have cryptic names that aren't self-explanatory" - Once I had a problem with Java, and I found that the solution is to add -XX:-OmitStackTraceInFastThrow flag. What does the flag do? It ensures that stacktraces are NOT omitted in some cases. Maybe this flag name wasn't cryptic, but is very misleading and I think that is even worse. - Fully agree, CMake is scary. - Again, fully agree, using anything else than a standard library is usually a nightmare. - "The debugger often takes you deep into the internals of the standard library instead of pointing to a clear failure in your own source code" - I mean, that's the idea why whenever an error occurs, a stacktrace is shown. If you know that some code is correct, you jump out on the stacktrace until you reach your own code. - Implicit suggestion that vector.end and vector.back should be switched is a terrible idea. First of all, in English back sometimes means last, like the back page of a newspaper means the last page, while endpapers of a book is used to protect the actual content of the book. So the natural order is begin, front, middle/inside/main, back, end. Also, if you would like to switch back with end, then for consistency you should also switch begin and front. - "vector<bool> is slower because bools are packed together." Is it, really? Because I've never noticed a significant difference in speed between vector<char> and vector<bool>. But maybe it's because it was never a critical part of my code. - using if(map[key]) in C++ as existence check only makes sense if you don't use 0 as values (and value can be converted to bool). Also, if(map[key]) doesn't work either in Python (where using a nonexistent key gives you a KeyError) or Java (where it simply wouldn't compile). I think the only reason if(map[key]) was given as an example was that it kinda does what the author wanted, but not quite. - "The ergonomics of hashmaps in Java and Python are way better" I would argue the opposite. If I use hashmap as a counter, than all I have to do is map[key]++; In Python I have to do if key in map: map[key]+=1 else: map[key]=1 while in Java if(map.containsKey(key)) map.put(key,map.get(key)+1); else map.put(key,1); And yes, in Python there is a Counter class, but I like the C++'s simplicity. - instead of if(map.find(key)!=map.end()) you can use if(map.count(key)) - let's be honest, please tell me WTF is this code if not a pure ragebait. if(map.find(1)!=map.end()){ map[1]=1000; } else{ map[1]=1000; }

author: @ayushgupta7580
text:
Finally, a video that gives solid reason as to why C++ is a horrible language. I have been wusing C++ for the past 3 years and every time, and I always see some new problems. While the online discourse always ends with C++ supremacists that, "you don't know this thing, or that thing, that you are stupid and cannot appreciate the holy-grail that C++ is". You listed all my complaints ( and many more that I didn't faced yet )

In fact, the industry is using C++ by restricting some ( or sometimes, a lot of features ). I work in a networking company, while on paper we use C++, what we actually use is a wrapper on C++ instead. A recent video by LaurieWired also discussed about JSF standard that does this as well. Coming back to my company, basically, we write code in that wrapper and that generates the C++ code instead which is used later. Thankfully, I didn't have to go through the pain of setting up the project and handling linker errors. Obviously, I tried reading the generated C++ code and found that it uses their own custom C++ library their. And then I tried understanding that and I realised, this is complicated. Then, I watched Cherno's playlist ( it is the best C++ playlist on youtube, so many resources online are just information dump without any explaination as to why we need those things ) only to realise, I still don't know enough. Then, I tried watching cppcon videos and it all bounced over my head.

After that, I tried making my own C++ projects, tried creating Splitwise application (just backend) in C++. That is when I realised that testing also sucks in this. Then, I thought how should I structure my project. Now, I know my project is really small, so it didn't matter much, but I was just shocked that there is no concensus for this either. I wrote the logic but after that, I didn't have enough strength to write tests as well. At that point, I seriously started doubting my capability as a programmer. Writing code in python is so simple, but I thought, that python abstracts everything and it is slower ( so I don't know what is happening under the hood ) so I never considered creating projects in python. I always felt C is more easy but it is so small that you will need to write every data structure for yourself. If anyone is doing leetcode in C, just give me your github. 

This video convinced me why so many low-level developers glaze Rust so much. And I am convinced that you really need Go or Python for most software engineering tasks ( yeah, mainly web development ) Maybe Rust when you require memory-safety. I am pretty much convinced that if you are professional C++ developer, most probably, it's not like you choose that language, the industry choose that language for you. So, if you have mastered it, great. But it doesn't mean you need to convince the rest of the programmers to master it as well. We can do the same thing with other languages with far less effort. 

The most important things is that you get the job done, nobody actually cares how you did, but only if you did it. So, no need to make things painful for yourself and pick what suits your need.

text:
Here’s a practical list of commercial companies that publicly show significant C++ use, grouped across different industries. I focused on official engineering pages, product docs, and SDK/API documentation, so this is a conservative list rather than an exhaustive one.

Finance / market data — Bloomberg
Bloomberg says “C++ is central” to how it works, and ties that to its real-time market-data systems and thousands of applications for clients.
Web browsers / internet — Google (Chrome / Chromium)
Google lists Chrome as a flagship product, and Chromium maintains an official C++ style guide plus a Modern C++ use in Chromium policy, which is strong evidence of substantial production C++ in the browser stack.
Web browsers / internet — Mozilla (Firefox)
Mozilla’s Firefox source docs include a page explicitly titled “Using C++ in Mozilla code”, and its source-tree docs reference multiple C++ interfaces and components inside Firefox.
Gaming / game engines — Epic Games
Unreal Engine’s official docs center on programming with C++, and Epic’s coding standard states Unreal is built to be portable across many C++ compilers.
Consumer internet / social media — Meta
Meta says it uses many programming languages internally and has engineering posts discussing its large amount of existing C++ code and C++-specific tooling/workflows.
Databases / data infrastructure — MongoDB
MongoDB’s official language pages state that MongoDB is written in C++, and the company maintains an official MongoDB C++ driver.
AI / GPU computing / semiconductors — NVIDIA
NVIDIA publishes the official CUDA C++ Programming Guide, including C++ language extensions and support details, which is strong evidence that C++ is a core development surface for its accelerated-computing ecosystem.
Automotive / industrial software — Bosch
Bosch says C++ is a cornerstone of much of its work, especially in safety-critical and performance-demanding applications, and says C++ underpins critical systems in multiple Bosch divisions.
GIS / mapping / geospatial — Esri
Esri maintains an official ArcGIS Maps SDK for Qt C++ API Reference and positions it for building cross-platform mapping apps with routing, geocoding, and spatial analysis.
Creative software / imaging — Adobe
Adobe’s Photoshop developer docs advertise a C++ SDK and a C++ Plugin SDK, which shows meaningful C++ use in its commercial creative-software ecosystem.
Broadcast / video production — Blackmagic Design
Blackmagic Design publishes SDKs for Desktop Video and Blackmagic RAW, and explicitly says its developer tooling is intended for building custom solutions and even commercial products.
3D animation / VFX / digital content creation — Autodesk
Autodesk’s Maya developer docs and API pages document a full C++ API, showing C++ as an important part of its commercial 3D/VFX software platform.

A simple takeaway: C++ is still strongest where performance, latency, hardware access, portability, or long-lived native codebases matter most—finance, browsers, engines, databases, GPU computing, automotive, GIS, and pro creative tools.

NASA, CERN, etc. So just shut up and go learn some C++

author: @国松慶喜
text:
I have spent many years working with C++ and have faced numerous challenges along the way, but thanks to that experience, I can now use it without any issues. I leverage techniques like metaprogramming and can write highly abstracted, readable code with zero overhead, all while maintaining a full grasp of the language's implicit behaviors.

C++ is the ultimate language—provided that every team member possesses this same level of mastery. However, the most critical issue is that it’s unlikely my colleagues will ever reach this level of proficiency. The fundamental problem with C++ lies in its steep learning curve and high cognitive load. If C++ were a strictly licensed language—where a professional certification body issued licenses and developers were restricted to coding within rules tailored to their certified level—we would all be much better off.

text:
If you think C++ was the worst programming language of all time, you certainly have never seen COBOL.

This was very entertaining, but the conclusions are all wrong. 
C++ is not dying, it's dead. It is incomprehensible and unusable for new programmers AND old programmers competent in other languages. ANSI C, C99 and C style in C++ might survive going forward, but C++ is effectively buried. 
D, Zig, C3 and Odin are C alternatives. Go is also a reasonable alternative in most situations. 
Rust will fail miserably because the church of type safety is wrong about bugs. It fixes C++ issues, but C++ should have never been used. It was an ugly hack job on top of C, from the start. 
I find it amusing that the same masochistic programmers that tormented themselves for decades with C++ would obviously enjoy being tormented by another horrible language, so they pick Rust. Good luck with it! But don't expect pity, because you're doing it to yourselves and actively making the whole software industry worse.

Anyone who has basic knowledge about the concept of vector in mathematics would think they are immutable by default and do not change in its size. I'm really sad that Rust took this nonsensical legacy of C++ which was just a result of pure laziness of the original STL authors. They could have taken better names like DynArray or ArrayList, as Java did.

author: @TranscendentBen
text:
1:15:04 I saw this 'problem' circa 1986 when first learning C. All the how-to-C books showed programs starting with prototypes of all functions used at the start of the source file, then the body of main() and finally the bodies of the functions. I had already learned Pascal years earlier which traditionally has each function body defined before usage, then main at the bottom of the file. I eventually figured out you could do the same with C, put main at the end and you'd only need prototypes for external or recursive functions. I was quite annoyed at the textbooks claiming to teach C.

Having learned assembly back then, I understood that this was to help the compiler build the symbol table by defining something before it's used, to reduce the number of passes and make assembly/compilation faster. Nowadays computers are (orders of magnitude) faster but we have other ways of slowing down compilation (you already mentioned having whole libraries in include files - I've use BOOST, it's quite effective at slowing compilation).

author: @GRAHAMAUS
text: I spent 12 years starting in the 90s writing a large complex app in C++. It wasn't quite the bloated monster it has become, and being noobs with it led to us ignoring some of its more esoteric features anyway, for better or worse. I dread to think how anyone can master it from scratch nowadays, every new version just seems to make it more problematic in some way or ways. I moved to using Objective-C in the 2000s and have now written a hell of a lot more code in that than I ever did in C++. It still inherits some of C's problems but it is just so much more productive than C++ it was a breath of fresh air (and of course a large part of that were its frameworks on Mac/iOS derived from OpenStep). It made me realise just how much of the actual code I wrote in C++ was simply keeping the language happy. You don't get many people defending Objective-C these days and of course it's got its own flaws, but when you look at the history of C++ and Obj-C, it's surprising and disappointing that C++ was the one to gain so much traction, when the other is just so much better. For the Obj-C haters, think of it this way: if Obj-C is objectively better than C++ (see what I did there?), it shows you just how bad C++ really is! This is a timely and necessary video, I'll be bookmarking it.

author: @kyker71
text:
When I first saw this video, I was so amazed and galvanized I wanted to comment it… but my comment started to span almost several pages. What truly hit me is how accurate what you’re saying is, but most of all how perfectly on point it is with what I had to go through these last few years. I have projects which require C++ for API bindings, and I went through almost all of the hoops you mentioned.

Here is an example.

I made researches on many build systems for C++: because I am a lazy guy with a ton of projects, I needed something modern, simple and powerful.

I ended up using xmake, but even with that I had to write a TypeScript wrapper (my projects are Node.js based) around it, to more easily automate some parts. Why xmake and not CMake? Well: it uses Lua with a sensible API, not a crappy DSL which does not make sense, it has better support for compilation database generation since it handles it itself, and even good support for C++ modules. However, xmake has a bug when mixing C++ modules and compilation database. Bummer.

So, to keep IDE support, I tried wrapping CMake… turned out it’s not much better: in Visual Studio Code, the CMake Tools extension acts only as a configuration provider for the main C++ extension, but it gives very basic information, which includes nothing about C++ modules. Frustration is rising.

Long story short, I ended up writing my own build system, with C++ modules support, compilation database support, and it worked quite nicely… Of course I kept things simple for my simple use cases, but it was not that hard for God’s sake! Getting even more frustrated seeing the other build systems be so crappy then, and seeing CMake be the de facto standard while being so horrible to use.

However I did all of that while knowing that vscode does not yet support C++ modules properly anyways: as mentioned the CMake Tools are lacking, and the core C++ extension uses the EDG compiler for the language server, which has yet to implement correct C++ modules support. So, I sort of prepared for the future, when vscode is a viable option. But in the meantime?

I could use CLion, where funnily the team explains that, to support C++ modules, they had to implement their own logic layer on top of CLang’s. But that means I lose the integrated DX of vscode… And that I have to start paying for an IDE I would be reluctant to use. Seriously, is there a solution?

Well I could go back to simple headers… But the thing is, headers are a nightmare to me, for several reasons. But the main one is that C++ modules allowed me to actually write C++ as in C# or else: I could define and declare at the same time, and the C++ module compilation process would extract the interface part and the implementation part into two separate binaries, naturally achieving what I wanted, instead of having to duplicate information between a declaration and a definition in the source code. And the fact that modules would not leak the “using namespace” statements, I would finally be able to simplify those horrible lines of code. So no, no headers.

So in the end: 

- no good build system
- no good IDE
- one good thing that could solve some issues comes from C++ itself: modules. But after more than 5 years, still not supported.

And that’s the thing here: all the frustration I built with episodes like this one over the years is expressed through this video, and it’s healing to watch it.

I wish each topic which frustrates it as much (and there are so many) would see a video like this pop up. I could start making a list, but that’s how my initial draft started to span pages. And this comment is already long enough ^^

author: @Ralphpotato
text:
A few things about Rust especially since you mentioned it at the end:
- the compiler and cargo aren’t “standardized” in the way that C and C++ are standardized. Cargo and rustc are essentially the de facto implementations but the exact behavior is subject to change.
- regarding rust’s bounds checking, you can use things like get_unchecked to avoid bounds checking, which is exactly the type of explicit “opt in” behavior that you outline a lot in this video. There are lots of various “do_unchecked” operations in rust that are not the default but available anyway just for these purposes.
- additionally, legitimately 90% of the time it’s more idiomatic to use iterators in cases where you’d use a bounds checked access in a loop, and if the compiler can prove that the access is safe it can do some optimizations that C++ cannot. You can’t rely on this for performance but in general iterators are truly zero cost abstractions in rust
- more on the iterator stuff, natural functional programming patterns like map and filter are also lazy and zero cost, unlike in languages like JavaScript where a full temporary object is created for each map, filter, etc that you do. Even though you pointed out JavaScript has having more ergonomic ways to iterate through lists at some points, I consider it a minor footgun that a lot of times the most ergonomic patterns in JS are not the best/performant. I think rust generally follows the ergonomic/idiomatic -> generally good way to solve that problem pretty well.
- I think it’s also important to mention that rust gets a lot of the benefits of what people reach for OOP design for, like encapsulation and member functions, without the headache of inheritance. With rust, as long as you implement the traits on a struct required by a function call, you can pass this struct to that function. You’re basically saying that, “this struct implements all the features you say you require”. This is basically enforcing composition over inheritance at the language level, which I feel like most people are onboard with
- rust also is one of the very, very few languages with syntax support for lifetimes/lifetime annotations. People get really confused by lifetimes especially since they usually only come up when doing generics, but lifetimes exist in literally every language. It’s just much worse to deal with in C/C++ since you have to manage these lifetimes completely implicitly. In rust, almost all lifetimes can be elided by the compiler, and you only need to annotate them in more advanced cases, and the compiler can then prove ownership rules
- rust also has really good test support, docs, and doctests. You can literally just write valid code into the doc comments above functions, which is usually used for libraries to show examples in their docs. When these libraries run their test suite for releases, these tests actually run so you both verify the examples are valid and the user can see a fully working example. So many code examples in other languages, either in docs or people’s random blogs, don’t actually run and might as well be JavaScript flavored pseudocode. The acceleration you get when using a halfway decent rust library that includes these doctests so you have a base to start with is invaluable.
- cargo is by far the best build + programming package manager I’ve ever used. C/C++ are nightmares like the video mentioned, but javascript’s package.json is also awful, pip + having to use virtual envs is awful (uv is much better and guess what’s it’s written in rust), go is _ok_ but leaves a lot to be desired for a relatively modern language and is a source of complaints. Cargo isn’t perfect but it makes setting up anything from a trivial new project to at least medium, production products pretty simple. I’m sure huge projects may still have to wrestle with things. 

The general takeaway for Rust is that while it has its own problems and complaints (like Stroustrup’s quote), if you become adept at Rust, the mental overhead of keeping track of things like ownership, undefined behavior, all the various semantics, etc largely go away. You can confidently trust the compiler and rust-analyzer to take care of the foot guns for you and you can focus almost entirely on actual program logic. I made this comment on Reddit, and BurntSushi, a far more experienced Rust dev who wrote the rust Regex package and ripgrep, replied that this is his experience too.

author: @melihcelik9797
text:
I opened this video expecting an AI slop, doing text-to-speech about new C++26 changes and forum topics about that. I was under the impression that no human being is going to make a 2 hour long voiceover for a programming language.
I was thinking maybe watch for a minute or two and just close the video. But it turns out this was an amazing video. 
I am not a C++ developer myself. I sometimes maintain and add some features to old "modern" C++ code but I mainly do Kotlin and C (weird combo I know). I deliberately avoid C++ in every chance I get. I just borderline disobey direct orders from management about C++ and do it in C. I dont care, the language is just too complex for me. And I don't want to be mistaken, I am fine with new cool features but in C++ almost no-one in the same project uses the same subset of the language. The C++ maintaining I told about, the project is about 15 years old, it is technically C++11, but reading and understanding it is just impossible because some developers in the past did it like "C style C++" and some smartass came around and used std free functions with lambdas (a side rant about lambda functions in C++: the syntax is just ugly I want to take my eyes out when I see one), some other developer years later tought "yeah I will use meta programming with impossible to understand templates" and some time later someone came around with extensive inheritence that makes no sense etc. And years later I come around, fairly new fo C++ (I was a C dev for a while before that), I didn't know most of the features and trying to understand the code was just impossible and I went back to square one, "C style C++"
Whenever we need a new application or want to recreate a part of a big application as a small application I either use C, or Python, depending on the size and performance requirements. If that project is mostly I/O bound, then I am using Python, otherwise C with GLib. Feature wise, not as many features exist in C, but I still prefer creating my own vtable for inheritence or modularity rather than using C++ and risking some other person 2 years later will try some fancy feature of C++26 and make it impossible the maintain for rest of us, thus restarting the cycle. 
Recently I was exploring Android POS devices and Kotlin was a fresh breath of air. I never liked Java with long function chains that looks ugly and unnecessary capsulations were just unnecessary for me. Kotlin fixed these issues, plus it mostly fixes the NullPointer problem, plus it has a great async programming interface so you dont have to deal with threads and monitors or locks. Really cool language and Composable UI is also really cool. I sometimes develop in house programs like custom file format editors, encryption tools, file generation automations and I used React + Electron combo with some of them and I must tell you Kotlin with Composable UI is just as good or better in some cases, really cool technology. 
And since this was a POS device, I still needed to access the PCD reader of said device, low level, and use and EMV kernel, which is also low level. There are native modules in the android project, whil Android Studio defaults to C++ with these I still develop most of them outside of Android Studio with plain old C, and plug them in with couple of wrapper methods in C++ or Kotlin.

TL;DR, I dont like C++ and I enjoyed this 2 hour long rant about C++. Normally there would be no way I watch something this long about a language that I dont like, but here we are. You my friend, gained a subscriber

text:
Bit arrays do NOT come with a "great perfomance cost" when compared to boolean arrays!!!!! On the contrary!!!!!

In x86 assembly, loading a bool and branching based on it requires 2 instructions before the branch, loading, then testing for 0.
Loading a byte with bits representing booleans also takes 2 instructions before the branch, loading the byte and executing "bt" (bit-test), with one operand being the index within the word.
There is zero shifting and masking involved, and even if it were, it would be like 2 cycles. On the other hand, when iterating over all bools, new bytes have to be read, while one read from the bitset holds 8 packed reads and in reality, we load 64bit words at a time, with the benefits of leading/trailing zero count ("find first true/false" and friends) and population count ("count all trues/falses" and friends) instructions available and testing the entire word for != 0 or == 0. All of this also gets auto vectorized to operate on 128 vs 16, 256 vs 32 and 512 vs 64 booleans at once, respectively.
That also applies to setting, zeroing and flipping bits, with the respective "bts", "btr" and "bitcoin" - i mean "btc" instructions, while also allowing you to read the previos value all in one instruction. Bruh.

Actually, i said shifting and masking wasn't involved... I lied. To get the byte from the index you want you have to divide by 8 (one shift by 3 lol) and take the remainder when dividing by 8 (AND-ing with 7) to get to the bitindex within the byte. Such overhead. Please learn about out-of-order-execution, instruction-level-parallelism and superscalar CPUs to see how CPUs hide the latency for 2-cycle dependency chains pretty much entirely, especially when those things can be done in parallel to memory reads (100s of cycles) or even L1 cache reads (~3 cycles). Bruh.

Considering the fact the ULTIMATE BOTTLENECK for computer performance is MEMORY BANDWIDTH and not computational capability (the "Von Neumann Bottleneck"), it is actually a tell in terms of the programmer not knowing anything about performance when they use true, actual boolean arrays. That's not even close to justified even when using them for SIMD, since SIMD lanes have varying bit-widths and converting a bitfield to the appropriate SIMD mask can be done in 2 (most times) to 5 instructions (only for 64 bit booleans), 1 instruction with AVX512 and sometimes even 1 instruction without AVX512. And for the other way around, the "movmsk" instructions actually convert SIMD boolean masks directly to bifields and are literally the most efficient way to move _anything_ from SIMD registers to general purpose registers (no, extracting a scalar value costs ~3 cycles because of them being entirely different register files). Bruh.

It's fine not to know these things. But if you don't, consider not making these kinds of stupid, uninformed and misleading statements that affect others negatively.
I agree that implementing std::vector<bool> as a bitset is terrible design (even if the reasoning is sound) because C++ is supposed to give you full control and even do 80 IQ things like using boolean arrays.

Great video otherwise, mostly.

text: After coding in C++ for a couple of decades, nowadays I find myself reaching for Zig instead (when ever that's an option). It lets me do almost anything I could do in C++ but in a saner way, and it also offers some nice features that C++ doesn't offer yet. Zig's comptime and metaprogramming is wonderful and reflection is clean and trivial and unlike C++, building isn't an awful, awful abomination. Zig isn't perfect, of course, e.g. not having operator overloading (which I agree are often abused) makes stuff like linear algebra a bit unpleasant and the language hasn't gotten to a stable release milestone yet, so each compiler update is likely to incur some pain points for your codebase, but in general it really is a truly wonderful low level language that I personally find much more interesting and pleasant to use than Rust.

C++17, C++20 are good releases, and there are some very good quality libraries around.

Of course, I wish the committee would just cut the bulls**t and make a very breaking C++29 or C++32. A lot of things can be fixed, and I think that there should be a breaking point where some features have to disappear from the language. But some additions are also absolutely nuts. That being said, I will probably still use C++ in the forseeable future, and I don't regret the time spent learning how everything works in order to make very small things in my favorite language. In the end, the control I have when I do C++ is amazing, and it's the one thing that makes me come back to it every single time.

text:
C++ was my first language in my "Intro to Programming" course at university. It was quite painful to learn. There were so many other things that hurt so much. Certain coding preferences were pushed on us that, later on, I learned encouraged a lot of bad practices. This is back in the late 2000's, so we learned C++03.

1. Some TAs actually took points away on homework assignments if you did not use `using namespace std;` everywhere.
2. We were told to always use std::endl and never do something like `cout << '\n'` because "reasons". No actual reasons were given.
3. The way we were taught OOP principles was completely broken. Proper polymorphism patterns, memory usage best-practices, C vs C++, etc., were glossed over. A lot of the time, we were told that we would "figure it out" over time. Almost like we were expected to learn through osmosis.

It also didn't help that right after we completed our "Intro to Programming" and "Intro to Data Structures and Algorithms" courses, the very next course in the curriculum was a "Systems Programming in C" course. So... you suffer learning C++, then are asked to throw all that out and learn C while the professor assumes you already know C because it's "basically C++". As it turned out for your sophomore me at the time... C++ was not in fact "just C with classes".

text:
just one thing I noticed: I think the section about the ABI and the lack of a package manager is a bit unfair, in my opinion. Comparing this to languages like C#, Python, and similar ones overlooks an important difference: all of those languages (with the exception of Rust) rely on some form of intermediate layer, such as a JIT compiler or an interpreter. That abstraction makes it much easier to build a package manager, since you don’t have to deal directly with OS and architecture-specific details at compile time.

Rust, while also not using an intermediate layer, is very restrictive in how software can be deployed. For example, distributing libraries in binary form is essentially not supported. If you attempt to do so, you lose the borrow checker guarantees at the API border and end up in an unsafe C-like situation - similar to how C++ makes use of the stable C ABI, as mentioned in the video. What also makes it way easier to manage packages.

Given these constraints, I think the comparison deserves a bit more nuance.

author: @lunaticwastaken
text:
I use CLion for all my C++ Development, and it is just mindboggling to see how like 99% of the issues of the "IDE Problems" section are actually specific to Visual Studio.

In CLion:
- Errors can be copied just fine.
- New Projects default to CMake with C++20.
- Formatting can be entirely customized (Either via clangformat, editorconfig, or even the built-in IntelliJ Formatter)
- Renaming really anything automatically finds and updates ALL occurrences in the Project.
- Code Snippets (Here called Live templates) work just fine.
- Namespace comments are afaik dependend on the Formatter, i think e.g clangformat does this by default, not sure if Visual Studio can use it natively.
- Inlay hints do show the full type when hovered.
- Renaming files (e.g from "hpp" to ".h") will lead to everything being auto updated (To be fair, i use globbing in my CMake Configs for retrieving src files)
- Headers are always auto-included when selecting an option in the autocompletion popup.
- For the new structs feature, the autocomplete popup shows a "designated-initialization" option at the top, that will do exactly that, auto-fill all the fields in the right order.

So yea, i'd like to say i'm surprised that Visual Studio is a piece of garbage, but i am not. I fail to understand why anyone would use it willingly in 2025 (almost 2026).

But yea, otherwise, anything language-specific in the Video was pretty accurate.

text:
I agree with a lot of your points.  But on namespaces, you should use nested namespaces, BUT use fully qualified names.  I do wish the language just required you to use fully qualified names.  And aliases are fine.  It's better to have a descriptive name for things, and then use aliases.  aliasing static_cast as sc seems fine to me.  A lot of custom casts can exist in a project, and aliases aren't hard to look up.

For UI libs in C++, I'd actually just use a game engine or game library framework and develop a UI in that.  It's a little annoying to set up, and some engines can add some bloat, but compared to web dev based UI I think it's far nicer.  And it's better than Qt or WxWidgets or ImGui imo.

At 1:05:10 the code shown is complicated far more by the overuse of lambdas here in my opinion.  I would expect that, as is true in many cases, those functions probably don't need to be lambdas and should just be broken down into separate named functions.

I do like Zig's approach to meta programming.  Zig and Odin have both been very interesting to me.

I 100% agree with the IDE issues section, though I'd hardly say that's unique to C++.

I actually had to use std::launder recently with std::construct_at because our unit test framework decided to overload the new keyword.  That was indeed quite annoying, and I've now learned when I would ever need std::launder.  Answer: when someone else has broken the normal semantics with operator overload and you still need to respect lifetime constraints for memory that you use, but aren't actually responsible for initializing at construction in nice cases where you manually handle initialization separately because your compiler doesn't properly hand the linker property you need for normal NVM access support otherwise.

On the diamond problem, note that this is actually not really a problem at all if you are careful.  What IS a problem is chaining the diamond pattern more than 4+ times as while this is perfectly valid according to the standard it blows up your compiler with it simply failing to resolve symbols and scopes correctly.  Guess how I learned that one?  That was a nightmare of debugging to isolate as a compiler bug just trying to extend a feature with an additional layer of another diamond inheritance pattern(seemed to make sense as it was the convention up until that point in the project and was working fine, and so it seemed reasonable to try to me consistent rather than swapping to a composition based solution initially)

I have been doing c++ for a decade now, and I still have not created a triangle from scratch in vulkan, haha.  I guess that means my time to triangle is pretty bad :P  (Really though, I like to be a level of abstraction higher using stuff like raylib and sdl)

All this said though, I still love C++.  As much as I hate it, I also love it.  It is my favorite language.  But maybe someday Zig or Odin will entice me instead.  I doubt rust will ever be my language of choice as I hate the syntax.  Especially as to create some data structures with certain algorithms, which are entirely safe, you still need to disable the borrow checker and write unsafe code.  I've never really cared for Go, but that may just be because the project I was looking at was a mess.  I don't really like python.  C# is actually really nice, but I don't like the memory model it uses to a point where it's prohibitive for a lot of the things I'd want to do, unless I throw everything in unsafe blocks... but then I may as well just write in C again.  

I do think I'll take another look at Zig after this.  It looks a lot more mature now just from the macro snippet shown.  I like that.

I do also have a lot of hope for something similar to cpp2 with cppfront.  It still makes a few mistakes I wish it didn't, but I think it's a lot closer to what I'd want in a language than how rust or garbage collected languages go about solving it.

author: @rperez02
text:
While I agree with almost all the points in the video, I disagree with the fearmongering used in an attempt to strengthen the argument, and the most important part is sadly at the end of the +2h long video: there's no good, full substitute for C++ at the moment, and it's arguably the most critical programming language there is today. The design issues of the language that make its barrier of entry so high has actually come full circle to be a godsend, because we DON'T need more underqualified people starting projects in C++ over other, more adequate languages.

C++ actually perfectly fulfills its current purpose: To be a massive, uncompromising language that offers literally everything you AND anyone else might want, and doesn't care about looking pretty while doing it. It's not meant to be easy, it's not meant to be any good for greenfield projects, it's not meant to be safe, it's not meant to be the best tool for any particular job, hell, it's not even meant to be the fastest. The design sucks because the design goal isn't not to suck, it's to exist and to keep existing for as long as possible (what the video refers to, in my opinion inaccurately, as "backwards compatibility"). It's the epitome of utilitarianism, and that's the whole point.

author: @mariusg8824
text:
These two hours don't even touch issues like that testing technology for C++ is abysmally bad. Unit testing apparently plays a niche role, all test runners I have seen have significant flaws and/or are outdated.

I have seen multiple big projects that chose C++ as language for the reason alone that they use one or two C++ libraries, therefore C++ code bleeds into every corner of the project.
You don't have to do that! There is a way to stop the infection. If you need a C++ library, write a small adapter that bridges C++ with the language of your choice. C# does this very elegantly with CLI, but basically all languages know some way to create a typesafe bridge that goes back and forth. For example, most languages under Windows know memory streams, and you can use that to serialize and deserialize objects, so you can call C++ methods and get back rich objects from your language of choice. Dependending on how wide the API gets this can become tedious, in many cases you just need a few functions from a C++ library. This way you can profit from high performance low-level implementations and still write your business logic and UI in a high level language. Don't be afraid to use two different programming languages in the same project, if you can limit the use of C++ this way.

author: @AusSkiller
text:
I love C++, but I'm a game developer and I need the "problems" of C++ to make games better, I agree with almost all of what was said but you give me a language that smooths out all the edges and I'll only love it for about 30 minutes, then I'll try to do something, spend a day working out how to do it, find out it is either impossible or performs terribly, and immediately go back to C++ where it lets me do the "bad" things that allow games to run well (or even just acceptably). As much as I love working in C++ it is clearly not a language for all (or even many) use cases. If I'm not working on a game then I'll usually prefer something like C# which makes development faster and easier but still performs reasonably for most cases, but as nice as other languages are to use for the common case I often get frustrated with how hard it can be to get it to do what I need for very specific cases because I'm used to the performance of C++ and 100ms is a completely unacceptable amount of time to do almost anything bar actual physical limitations like drive performance.
I wouldn't recommend using C++ outside of a few niches mentioned in this video, but I do recommend learning it because it will give you a better understanding of what the other languages are doing under the hood and make it easier to switch between languages. It will also make you more aware of the issues those other languages have that is usually hidden from you like leaking memory because you have circular refs, or understanding the performance benefits of things like storing objects in contiguous memory.

author: @Bolpat
text: I don’t think Rust is actually a prime competitor for C++. It has a slightly different domain, and attracts a vastly different kind of person. The people enamored with C++ don’t like things like the borrow checker. Zig is probably what comes closer to appealing to this kind of person. C++ devs don’t like the silent copies or choice of defaults. Zig’s philosophy to getting your UB-free (code memory safe etc.) is testing. It gives you excellent tools to test your code. Rust is basically saying: “Prove to me you’re not double-freeing.” Zig is basically saying: “You’re going to test your app anyways, so use this testing-purpose allocator that will tell you if you’re double-freeing.” You need to be somewhat mathematical leaning to like proving something to the compiler. I don’t know Rust well, but my sense is, if a code path exists that could double-free, it’s an error, even if the code path is never taken (let’s say two frees, each behind an "if", such that they’re never both true), but for non-obvious reasons. Zig will just roll with it. Testing shows it simply doesn’t happen, and so _you_ (not the compiler) decide to ship the product. I’ve had chats with Rust enthusiasts and asked them: What do you do if you realize you didn’t implement some requirement correctly, you have maybe a day or two, and to implement it, you need to modify some value that’s passed by const? After a few attempts, you know you have to fudge it, there’s not enough time to do it properly by reworking the layout of stuff. My sense is, a language that doesn’t allow fudging around is DOA in the actual industry.

What I don't like about Rust is, for one, the huge build cache. Take Tauri and Wails (go), make two Hello World apps, Wails project folder will be... about as much as your node_modules, Tauri is that plus ~3.5GB. I'm sick of the "storage is cheap" argument. I'm already sick of 300MB node_modules, don't want to have ~3.5GB projects. And this is not exclusive to Tauri. With Rust, it builds the libraries from scratch when you compile so it's generating a cache in the project folder with all those libraries' build artifacts.

I'm not against Rust building libraries from scratch but if it builds a remote library, it should only cache its build output (because you aren't going to be changing library code so you don't need all the build artifacts) and put it in a global space (and postfix it with version) so if you have many projects using the same library (and same version) then it'll not take space every time. Like that's how .NET does it.

author: @richardzhao143
text:
C++ has turned into a mess, and Windows bears at least half the blame. In the UNIX tradition, writing low-level software in C has always been the best practice.
* The OS package managers are naturally C package managers - if you need dependencies, just apt install xxx-dev.
* Object-oriented systems shouldn't be the default; they should naturally evolve when the software needs object abstraction. For example, in the Linux kernel, file systems and device drivers naturally suit object management, so object design is used moderately. But C++ encourages you to design with classes by default - when you have a hammer, everything looks like a nail, so code naturally becomes a mess.
* The closed-source development model of big companies is the real root of all this evil. Colleagues in the same team can communicate anytime, so it doesn't matter if the language is complex or the code hides a lot of information - you can just oncall colleagues when you don't understand something. Teams need KPIs, so there's a natural demand for complex new features to put in PPTs, and different needs from various companies eventually end up in C++ committees.
* In contrast, well-known open-source software like the Linux kernel, git, nginx, cpython... have tens of thousands of collaborative developers worldwide, yet they're all managed in an orderly way with clear and understandable code. Because of asynchronous communication and reviews, simplicity and unambiguity in language and code are important - you can't just ask someone anytime. Similarly, open-source software has higher requirements for documentation quality.
* Currently, the only scenario I can think of where C++ should still be used for new projects is high-performance computing in the AI era (with languages like CUDA), because templates are indeed needed to reduce code duplication - but it should be limited to “C with templates”. For other scenarios, if it's low-level software, use C or Rust; if it's application development, any mainstream garbage-collected language is better.

Most of the things you complain about show lack of understanding of the memory layout of a program. casting, static keyword, interfaces, inline stuff, integer size, pointers... Overall you want a higher level programming language to do what you want at that point, and that's perfectly fine. But let people who want (or need) to handle their memory do their own thing. This thing is C++, and it's as complicated as managing the memory yourself... Overall C++  just lets you do more stuff than most languages. Starting programming with C++ is not a good idea, it's something you learn because you need it, ideally with a few programming languages in your hand, preferably including a bit of C. 

Then there are other misconceptions: 
 - "include" is a preprocessing construct, it has nothing to do with C++. here you complain about the compiler and the preprocessing engine, which is the same in C, Fortran, and any language supported by your compiler. I am completely baffled why so many strawman arguments and made-up problems are in here when C++ has more than enough real problems to fill 2 hours easily.
Like, what is up with complaining about formatting rules? This applies to basically every language on this planet. Oh and a lot of people have probably already pointed this out, but const_cast is not "considered bad practice" its actual undefined behavior and the compiler is allowed to delete all related code that interacts with the result of a const_cast that removed a real const. It's only use is to remove const from something that wasn't originally const but was referred to by a const variable somewhere else. The only reason this actually works in practice is because way too much code does this expecting it to work and compilers can not break the world over an issue like that. And this also explains why mutable const makes sense. author: @SkigBiggler
text:
I think the core problem that causes so much grief is that for some reason C++ is still aspiring to be like C. Closely mapped to basic assembly constructions. Except all the features added on are completely at odds with that. This is why you get stuff like vectors [] operator having no bounds checking, because in C, the [] operator is just an offset from pointer pointed to, and is compiled as such, but in C++ the [] operator isn’t mapped like this for non-primitive types, it can be overloaded. 

It’s such a weird hybrid of approaches. The raw close to hardware stuff from C mixed with attempts at the more abstracted approaches of first managed languages like Java and C#, and now compiled languages like Rust and Zig.

C++ evolved over time to meet a variety of needs, most of the quirks come from backwards compatibility. text:
Surely static_cast is necessary because - _unlike_ Java, C# etc, there are actually different ways to cast to another type. In languages that don't allow raw pointers, casting actually transforms a value to another value in a different location in memory. 

But C++ allows you to simply look at the same value in the memory as if it were of a different type, something you can't do in those other statically typed languages -- hence reinterpret_cast, which, while unsafe, is faster than static_cast where it is possible.

author: @H75000
text:
Haha, liked and subbed just from the thumbnail+title combo. In the famous words of Andrei Jikh: came for the C++ hate, stayed for the knowledge.

This is such an entertaining video for a Gen Xer like me! Although plenty of other languages might compete for this title, C++ is so prevalent and crucial to the industry that its shortcomings are massively magnified. I find myself struggling to disagree with the title.

I loved C and struggled to see the advantage of OOP in C++ (and Pascal) until I switched to Java in 1997 and fell in love. After that, I couldn't imagine coding without OOP.

Switched to C# in 2002, but I still have nothing but love for Java (highly elegant language), and I also still appreciate C and nostalgically love Pascal.

Also, I loved the version number suggestion in the video (doSomething2()) is so pragmatic precisely because it's inelegant - it screams "this is a patch, not a design." At least then everyone knows what they're dealing with. Instead, C++ gives you make_shared vs make_unique vs shared_ptr vs unique_ptr (don't know much about them myself, as I'm not a C++ dev, but I just learned it's a problem), where the naming conventions are inconsistent, and you need tribal knowledge to understand why things are named the way they are.

It's like they're allergic to admitting "we got it wrong the first time, here's version 2." So they invent a new name that sounds different enough to be "better" but doesn't actually clarify what's deprecated or why. And then 5 years later, there's another way to do the same thing with yet another naming convention.

I'm legit vicariously feeling helpless and frustrated on behalf of C++ developers. Imagine having to constantly check "wait, which era of C++ am I supposed to use for this?" Every new standard adds features but doesn't really remove the confusion, it just layers on top.

author: @rotschke
text:
I've started programming in C++ around 2 years ago. And to me it was better than Java, which was the only programming language I used before. I've learned a little bit of Python and some Rust later and yet my opinion, that C++ is good, remains unchanged for the following:

* C++ features destructors, which were amazing, because in Java I had to manually destroy and discard objects. In C++ I simply delete it or automaticly, when it's in stack, which is pretty simple and as self-explanatory as the constructors. The reason why Java didn't implement destructors was because of its garbage collector. I really like that idea and makes stuff for me easier.
* No package manager, that can mess around with my project. I've used Python's pip for a project with my fellow students and I remember we had problems with accidentally using the wrong versions of libraries. That took us some time to fix that. We're programming in Rust now and we didn't use cargo yet - at least not directly - so we didn't have problems with that.
* I'm no longer using an IDE for C++. I've tried a few IDEs like Code::Blocks, but soon uninstalled them, because they were too old or too hard to configure. MSVC wasn't a choice, because it was kind of too heavy and I was a little concerned about its licensing LOL. Right now I'm using a simple text editor for keyword and syntax highlighting, a Makefile for building on Linux and Batchscripts for compiling on Windows (both with MinGW and MSVC's compiler).
* C++ doesn't force me to either program everything in functions only (C-like) or classes only (Java-like). I've been taught in college, that in Java you have to instantiate objects, EVEN THOUGH YOU NEED ONLY ONE AT A TIME. Then I have to pass a reference to others and so on and care about sharing the pointer. And the garbage collector frees the memory, when you're done. Making variables or classes static was discouraged. I hated that philosophy, because it didn't make any sense to me. In C it's kind of narrow: You only have structs and functions, no classes = no OOP. C++ allows to balance it the way you like to.
* It's the only programming language I know about, that has the least restrictions. There's no rule on which naming convention (camelCase, snake_case, SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE, ...) to use, how to use macros, handle exceptions and other shit. I think this is also why I like this programming language so much: It allows you to be creative.

There are probably more reasons, why I like C++, but I don't know them straight out of my mind.

The flaws you've pointed out though made me think for a bit, but honestly it doesn't bother me anymore, because I'm used to it. For instance I've already accepted, that the std::vector is called that way, to be fair however, it's hard to find an appropriate name for it. You wouldn't call it a dynamic array, because arrays aren't dynamic. Ironicly Rust copied the name for the same purpose, but I don't think they were stupid. It's probably because of "human-brain-backwards compatibility". We programmers are used to that name so much, they just copied it.

Needless to say C++'s weakness is memory safety. I don't disagree. But Rust's verbosity about memory safety is kind of too much for me (don't ask me why). And my fellow students try to convince me to use Rust instead of C++, because they're obsessed with its modern spirit, safety and woke femboydom. Speaking of gayness, it's disgusting, that most communities of all programming languages try to tie them to that pride-shit, that has nothing to do with programming at all.

Btw, I haven't used many programming languages. HTML, CSS, Java and C++ were the only ones I've ever used actively. I've used Python and Rust only for a little so far and I don't have any intention in using them for my own hobby projects.


At the moment I program a game engine in C++ myself. The only library used is STB-image for texture loading. I've discarded GLFW, because I thought to myself tieing the window manager to the renderer tightly would reduce some footprint. I programmed the window manager for Windows, X11 and later probably for Wayland either. It uses Vulkan for rendering and it took me around 3(?) months to get it working (including the window manager). I have to say I've programmed with OpenGL before, so I had some experience with rendering beforehand. I don't know how far I'll go with this project, but it's private and not for the industry. It's basicly for fun and self-teaching.

I've been re-learning and using modern C++ for my pet projects for about three years now, simply because I enjoy the challenge. And during this time, I’ve really tried to understand why, in some cases, people suggest using algorithms, yet using them often feels much more verbose or even misleading compared to just writing a for loop. Or why there’s so much complexity: with all the  virtuals, noexcept, public, private keywords; why does it have to be this way?

Even making a simple change in CMake, such as properly updating your binary output folder, feels unnecessarily complicated. Sometimes it works on Windows  and then is completely broken on Linux. Why is it so complex?

I am glad I am not alone here.

These are the kinds of questions I’ve had, and I think this video really helps to answer them.

I've now switched to C99, and I can see where many of these problems originate. But in C, the issues are expected and (somewhat) explicit, which is actually nice. In C++, they’re buried under layers of incomplete abstractions. 😉

I'm assuming you're talking about generics in Rust and not about Rust macros since macros are capable of arbitrary transformations and completely smoke anything C++ template programming can do.

And they're far easier to read and reason about, partially because their compiler error messages aren't 500 lines of cryptic angle bracket nonsense.

author: @yaksher
text:
A lot of the opening complaints seem... meh. Like, the 15 initializer syntaxes which are largely equivalent is one thing, the output streams were a neat idea but clearly lost to just having a print function, sure. But the RNG and casting complaints are basically just "it's a low level language" and the formatting complaints apply almost one to one with basically every language that isn't on the short (though increasing) list of languages to ship with a formatter.

The example with JavaScript map @50:55 is an excellent example as well. It's a function which is misused for poor performance because it eagerly spits out a new array regardless of what you want to do with it. I think, like many of the complaints, the way Rust resolves it is a far better compromise for a low level language than the stuff suggested (which is that `.map` is an iterator adaptor, which does mean that in the relatively rare case where purely doubling a vector is the thing you want, you have `vec.into_iter().map().collect()` instead of just `vec.map()` but you're rarely just doubling a vector and immediately turning it back into a vector). Method chaining as methods _on vectors/arrays_ is an antipattern. JavaScript supporting this is _bad_ and Rust and Python not supporting it is a good thing.

@1:19:20 I am genuinely baffled by people who think this is a good idea. Zero-init is fucking stupid. If you want the int to be 0, just... make it 0??? It's not hard? The obviously correct solution to variable initialization is the one taken by Rust/Zig, which is to say... all variables must be initialized, always. Rust then has the heavy "MaybeUninit" construction for cases where you want to leave the variable uninitialized which is safe but heavy and Zig has the straightforward `undefined` keyword used to explicitly opt-out of initialization, both useful in cases where you want to defer initialization for performance or perform incremental initialization for self-referential objects or whatever. Both Zig and Rust also have ways to specify default values (in Zig, this is done with default _fields,_ (which must have comptime-known values) so an empty initializer uses defaults, if they exist, or errors if they don't; in Rust this is done with the Default trait, which can run arbitrary code). 

The fact that someone who is at least passingly familiar with both Rust and Zig suggests zero-initialization as the default when C++ could trivially do the Zig thing and just require explicit initialization on a syntactic level is baffling to me.

author: @michaelwaters1358
text:
As someone who has been writing C++ professionally for over a decade, yeah this language is bad. Ironically, it can be fixed to a large degree very easily: if there was a mandated ABI and API break. C++'s main struggle is that it has grown over 4 decades without the ability to remove "mistakes". Things like initialization rules could be drastically simplified if the early stuff was removed. And this is what a significant portion of the "modernization" efforts like cppfront are trying to do.

If there was a way to compile a specific set of code under a specific "standard", then many footguns could be removed. I generally find that writing completely modern C++ with no baggage is a fine language. But legacy code is unmaintainable and worse, when learning the language, people find resources that were accurate 20 years ago but are no longer the proper way to write code. So they learn an old practice and it compounds the problem.

I am happy that I have learned C++, but learning it was definitely painful and a huge portion of that learning was dedicated effort to seek out modern resources and mentorship. I hope I can pay my knowledge forward to other people who are learning the language.

author: @germandiagogomez
text:
Even if many things are valid, there are a few that I can see he does not fully understand. He says things like layout should be hidden. If he means at the compiler level, yes. If he means hidden as in automatic pimpl that would make a pessimization mess. ODR should be better with modules. He also says there is lots of bad learning material. Yes: for every language. He obviates the need to often interface with C. When you use your shiny language, you will have directly available all that C ecosystem? Or u will need to wrap it + interact with GC, allocation and the bugs you create when wrapping it? I have been there so no need to explain to me. Also, nowadays, just turning -Wall -Wextra -Werror (or MSVC equivalent) a compiler catches lots of this stuff, like narrowing conversions, even some forms of dangling. So it is just much better in practice than it is on the paper when you sit down. C++ has also some of the most powerful IDEs and whwn you need your code to run fast in a server, believe me that it is, nowadays, probably the best option.

Many of the defects of C++ are old choices or C compatibility and certainly it is not the easiest language to master. But to finish *full projects* (interfacing with libs, for example) it is, asof today, unbeatable.

As for safety, C++26 already jas library hardening. Enable it! Your big compilers already support it today.

Header files: yes this is an old one. It could be better bc when you do not need it... you do not need it and you are forced but to do equivalent things in C#/Java you end up separating in different files anyway if you want explicit interfaces. 

I agree the lookup rules are difficult. Do not nest your namespaces beyond 2.

I still think that C++ is a very competent language and with all warnings on, it is still ok.

As for compilation times: use ccache or sccache. They are transparent and accelerate compile times by a lot. Ah, also: C++ compiles faster than Rust, even if it is slow at it. Noone ever complains about it... Greetings!

I agree with almost everything here, which is amazing considering the topic is C++ 😂

One of the disagreements:

The cast in parenthesis is a C style cast. That is where java got it from. A C style cast also works in C++.

HOWEVER, a cast is essentially a suppressed bug. It is meant to be an eye sore! That is the whole point. It is intentionally ugly!

By forcing developers to type it out, they also become easy to grep, which is nearly impossible for a java/C style cast. That is a point for C++, not against it. Defining a macro to shorten casts should probably result in capitol punishment. First for writing code that requires so many bugs to be suppressed, and second for using a macro to hide them.

Within our own code we may require a dynamic_cast once in a blue moon, but otherwise good code doesn't require casts. Of course, this all goes out the window when you are interfacing with 40 year old C code, like Win32, where there is little consistency and you have no choice but to accept what the developers of the time chose to use, rather than how the C++ standard does it today.

text_clean: : You don't need to create new data types and functions for every collection type you make in C. You just need to use macros. For example, suppose you want a function that adds a value to an array. #define array_add(_array, _value) do { \ if ((_array)->length == (_array)->capacity) \ break; \ (_array)->value[(_array)->length] = _value; \ (_array)->length++; \ } while (0) That's it. The thing is, you don't have an 'array_t' type. You just *make* one when you need it. E.g. #define array_new_from_buffer(_buffer) { \ .capacity = sizeof(_buffer) / sizeof(*(_buffer)), \ .value = (_buffer) \ } float valuebuf[10]; struct { int capacity, length; float *value; } myarray = array_new_from_buffer(valuebuf); array_add(&myarray, 3.5); array_add(&myarray, 6.7); The macros don't care what types you're using or what other data you have in your struct. This is one of those extremely powerful idioms that makes implementing generic collections in C so much less of a pain in the ass.

text:
The one true build system is 'make'. Everything else is people complicating shit to the moon because they're too lazy to learn 'make'.

In my projects, I start off by taking the suckless approach of having a singular 'Makefile' that include a 'config.mk' file. The 'config.mk' file defines a set of variables. Usually the and PACKAGE, VERSION, then package installation information like PREFIX, BINDIR, INCDIR, and LIBDIR, then tooling information like CC, LD, AR, RANLIB, and STRIP; then compiler and linker flags with CFLAGS and LDFLAGS. Those latter two will usually embed the IPATHS and LPATHS variables for preprocessor include directories (-I) and library directories (-L). When I need to link one of my projects to another that exists in a different directly, I just IPATHS += ../other project and LPATHS += ../otherproject instead of installing said project on my system.

The name of the program binary is usually stored in BIN. For libraries, the name is stored in LIB.

The source files are usually listed in a variable called SRCS. If I'm using lex and yacc (or just other languages) this variable will usually reference other source lists like CSRCS, LSRCS, and YSRCS. The OBJS variable contains a list of all of the object files to be built. Usually generated by replacing the '.c' suffix of the source files in SRCS with '.o'.     ${STRIP} $@

    ${AR} rcs $@ $^
    ${RANLIB} $@

I usually keep documentation and testsuites outside of the project, but if I am going to embed them into it, I also tend to make them be subdirectories of the include directory. E.g. ./include/check/.

The rest of the source files either sit at the root of the project file or exist in subdirectories that exist for organizational purposes. E.g. ./output/graphics/vulkan.c for the vulkan graphics backend of a game. The root directory will also usually contain a README.md and a LICENSE file.

text: RAII's name comes from the fact that it refers to the behavior of the constructor, not the behavior of the destructor. The idea is that if you construct an object (i.e. acquire a resource) then it is properly initialized into a valid and expected state and that it should not even be possible to create an object that exists in an uninitialized state. author: @nick15684
text:
I mainly write desktop applications in the field of graphics programming and game development. My most recent project is making my own 2D game engine. Needless to say, even something as seemingly ubiquitous as drawing a triangle on the screen is anything but trivial in C++ unless you use a bunch of 3rd-party libraries. GUIs in general are very convoluted to setup and maintain in C++. This is worsened by the fact that there are not many good libraries for it. Arguably the best library for developing C++ GUI applications on Windows is Microsoft Foundation Class. It's exclusive to Windows, and is from the early 90s, but it's actually very powerful, if difficult to use. It speaks volumes that to this day, Microsoft has never really made a proper successor to it. WinUI is... weird and kind of dead. It might be good for making a calendar app or something small, but that's about it. It is not equivalent to the features and power of MFC, not even close. That's why MFC it's still around and still used in a lot of applications, because Microsoft has provided no proper true alternative.

You're not making the next Adobe Illustrator, Unreal Engine, or Blender in WinUI (which is why those programs don't use those types of frameworks), although you certainly can in MFC. WinUI is basically a WinRT wrapper over Win32 as far as I can tell, which just feels kind of silly. I use MFC because it's the only frameworks other than QT that seems suited for most graphics' programs. WPF in C# exists, but it's also old at this point, and trying to interface C# with C++/Win32 is a real pain that makes you rather just use C++ for the whole thing anyway. The unfortunate reality is that if you do any graphics programming you are more or less locked into using C or C++ with very little choice. Using OpenGL, Vulkan, or DirectX requires the use of C/C++. So much so, that writing your entire application in C++ often ends up being the best choice. That's why every big game engine is written in C++. This is for performance reasons, but also because they are very tightly bound to the ability to render graphics.
