text:
I have so many problems with C++ and you beautifully put most of them to words.
For a while I thought I was alone, or that I am just stupid. Why are people not seeing these as a problem, an opportunity to get them fixed. Why are we living with these god awful hacks just to get by.
The lack of proper strings and arrays in C++ (and C) where you can check the length of the allocated buffer at runtime or compile time (not just where they are declared but when they are passed to a function, maybe several layers deep).
Passing the size separately is awful and error prone. Even Pascal/Delphi had this for decades, your code can check the capacity of the array/string, and you can even turn bounds checking ON (and OFF) in the compiler.

std::array<> and std::string<> is not it! You can't even pass std::array to a normal function so it can check the array length, because the length is part of the type signature and not a property of the value, so you need generic/template function to accept such a monstrosity. I really don't understand why does it even exists. (And of course these don't solve the problem of C missing these basic data types too!)
The awful templates in STL to work around such a huge void if basic data types missing form the core language is shameful.
Templates and meta-programing in C++ is very powerful. But with great power comes great responsibility. ... or should. But in C++ the language standard committee seem to push responsibility to the programmers, language users and not the language designers.
Just because you can prop up a barley usable language with template magic, it doesn't mean you should.

Undefined behavior is horrible. Like signed integer overflow is undefined. Why? Are we programming quantum computers with C++? If we take a real HW and execute code on the processor then on an overflow it better produce a deterministic result. I'm pretty sure the behavior is defined by the hardware engineers. So the very least it should be platform defined behavior.
Sure we might not exactly know what will happen when you over index an array, but if you know the memory layout you can now what could happen. So the behavior should be at least constrained and not completely undefined. Dragons are not going to time travel you back before the big bang just because you messed up your C++ code. (This is not a legally binding promise, don't contact me if that ends up happening ;)
My "favorite" is when the optimizer detects UB in compile time and does nothing, no error message, no warning, no generated code. Somewhere there is an UB in the code so it just refuses to generate code, because it can, the standard does not require the compiler to do anything, because the behavior is undefined, which means technically anything could happen, which include no generated code/executable. 
Don't mind that physically not anything can happen, and on a specific hardware the behavior should be quite deterministic. Comparing to unrelated pointers is UB, but if the objects they point to live in the same memory space (or even if they don't), if you can take their address (they are not in a register that doesn't have a memory address) then comparing the memory address should have only 3 possible result: less, equal, greater. Sure we don't know at compile time which, but we know it physically can't be anything other than those 3, but it's UB so in C++ it can be something else, like the compiler just omitting all the code after the comparison because it detected UB... so FU!

And a fun question: How do you read the byte from memory address 0 using C++? (for example in a micro controller, where a peripheral HW register is mapped to address 0x0000)

author: @driedurchin
text:
As an ex-professional C++ developer, here's my small points of contention. I largely agree, but feel I must advocate:
1. Many of the IDE problems are not a thing with CLion, which supports MSVC projects
2. Uninitialized variables are now initialized by default with a compiler flag, with an opt in uninitialized attribute. Too little too late, but it is in the standard now.
3. There is something to be said for the incremental compilation benefits of the .h/.cpp split. It's marginal, but worth mentioning. Rust not having dynamic linking, and per-crate TUs is a pain point.
4. Some of the "the compiler allows this" arguments are weaker than others. Yes it's important to have sane defaults, but many many people are on the level about good warnings.
5. I won't tell you how to make a video, but if affecting change was your goal, a cooler tone would be easier to forward this video to someone on the standards committee
6. To be fair, SIMD support is pretty lacking everywhere in my experience
7. RVO is not technically a compiler optimization, it's standardized.
8. Async Rust is absolutely NOT harder than other languages. Having used Python asyncio and Rust with tokio to recently write the same program twice for work (two sides of a connection) what took me 40 minutes to get working (with proper cancellation and error handling) took me 6 hours in python to get working at all, let alone handling Ctrl+C. It's harder than sync Rust, and less ergonomic, but you can get correct code wildly fast.

One thing I'd add on is that there is a book about C++14 I think that said "Use these features now, use these features carefully, and NEVER touch these features". It was about an even 3 way split of the features...

Overall, I think the biggest issue in my mind is the notions of "there should be one obvious way to do things" and "sensible defaults" are the two biggest missing philosophies in the language.

Another angle to look at it that I feel was omitted is as follows: I would assert that the single largest miss-step in the language is governance. I don't think the poor design decisions were unavoidable consequences of age. I think had the language had a governance that did a better job of soliciting feedback from real users, instead of an exclusive, high-barrier-to-entry, committee, things could have gone different.

Fantastic video overall, just thought I'd leave my thoughts.

I won't tell you how to make a video, but if affecting change was your goal, a cooler tone would be easier to forward this video to someone on the standards committee 6. To be fair, SIMD support is pretty lacking everywhere in my experience 7. RVO is not technically a compiler optimization, it's standardized. 8. Async Rust is absolutely NOT harder than other languages. Having used Python asyncio and Rust with tokio to recently write the same program twice for work (two sides of a connection) what took me 40 minutes to get working (with proper cancellation and error handling) took me 6 hours in python to get working at all, let alone handling Ctrl+C. It's harder than sync Rust, and less ergonomic, but you can get correct code wildly fast. One thing I'd add on is that there is a book about C++14 I think that said "Use these features now, use these features carefully, and NEVER touch these features". It was about an even 3 way split of the features... Overall, I think the biggest issue in my mind is the notions of "there should be one obvious way to do things" and "sensible defaults" are the two biggest missing philosophies in the language. Another angle to look at it that I feel was omitted is as follows: I would assert that the single largest miss-step in the language is governance. I don't think the poor design decisions were unavoidable consequences of age. I think had the language had a governance that did a better job of soliciting feedback from real users, instead of an exclusive, high-barrier-to-entry, committee, things could have gone different. Fantastic video overall, just thought I'd leave my thoughts.

author: @amihartz
text: I have always complained about how bad the default data types are in C/C++. It is frustrating to have code compile to entirely different behavior on different machines despite the code being the same. C/C++ is full of undefined behavior which the apologists will say "erm it's not undefined it's compiler defined behavior" which is literally the same thing. You can write code that its logical behavior is literally not defined in the C/C++ standard but will depend upon things outside of the standard. Differences in the default signage of a char for example can cause a program to compile such that it takes different conditional branches on one machine than another. I don't find the stdint header file to be a great solution because it's not universally implemented, so the moment you start using it, you will end up having to switch back and forth between the default data types if you import a library, which becomes a mess. In my opinion, a good language should compile to logically the same code across any platform. There is at least some justification for size_t to differ between platforms, but there is no reason that C/C++ can't just have default datatypes that are guaranteed to be the same width across platforms, as you said, like an i8 or i32 datatype that is built-in to the standard and not defined in a header file.

author: @Nemean
text:
I once wanted to define "spade, club, diamond & heart" and loop through them in C++. I mistakenly wanted to use enums for this. Watch this:

- There are enums and enums classes. They have almost no difference, except that enums litter your namespace, while for enum classes require the clearer CardSuit:: as prefix.
- There are also enum structs. They are the same thing as enum classes.
- Enums/Enum classes don't know how many values they define. One workaround is to define a final sentinel value "count" and use int numSuits = static_cast<int>(CardSuit::count)
- There is actually no native "for (auto suit : CardSuit{})". You have write an iterator for your CardSuit yourself that has operator*, operator++ and operator!= defined.
- Wait, don't you also have to write/define a begin and end for your iterator? Yes, but not in the iterator itself. You write those two functions somewhere outside and litter your namespace.

At this point I was thinking that maybe I should iterate in a different way than a range-based for loop. Luckily C++ has a dozen equally bad ways to do that. Let's stay with this one, because I want to mention two more funny tidbits.

- So if you now have a begin and end function randomly lying around, what do you do if you have another enum class? Can you even define begin & end for that one if the first enum class already defined them? Yes! Luckily begin & end take a dummy variable that does nothing, except that it has the type of the enum class that you want. C++ then does argument-dependent-lookup to infer what you mean.
- Did you know that the pre-increment and the post-increment operators are two different functions??? They are both overloaded with operator++, except that one takes in the object you're incrementing, and the other one also takes in that object AND a dummy integer that, again, does nothing. It's only there so that C++ can differentiate, which one you mean. Have fun remembering which definition defines which operator though :)

author: @MrPoselsky
text:
I watched all of this while working on fixing memory leak inside smart pointers, oh the irony. 
I would say 99% of your comments are correct and I've been writing c++ for living. It's horrendous language and yet, somehow, I still like it. Stockhold syndrome?

Few caveats:
You don't want virtual destructors by default because not all structs need to have vtable embedded in them. With smart pointers you don't need virtual destructors at all even with polymorphic types.
Concepts solve a lot of template error reports and simplify development a lot.
Smart pointers are not slower only because they're stored in the stack register but because they can lead to cache miss.
There's no solution to concurrency - deadlocks, spinlocks, etc.
I agree that STL is sooo unnecessarily convoluted.

I've been saying to my community and at work that a lot of cpp problems can be solved by not even bothering with OOP (which is flawed to begin with) and focus on cstyle cpp which is even more easily testable - gigachad John Carmack also advocated for cstyle cpp and he's right.

When you got to the point of std::move and it not actually moving I laughed so hard because a lot of people don't know this, my laughter stopped with algorithm.h because I didn't know that :D .

Thanks for the video, it was a treat.

author: @LordErnie
text:
I am learning the basics of learning to do my own memory management at the moment. The minor program I am following has us design a game engine in C++. Its fun, its cool, but after the minor program is finished students start putting C++ on their resume. I said it at the start and I still say it: You do not learn C++ as a language with idioms and best practices that represent the latest and greatest things, you learn about every band-aid slapped on top of an incomplete language.

What did I learn from C++? What memory actually is, what types of memory exist, different regions in memory. From this ownership naturally follows. Threads are funny, and because we work with memory in a very direct way we can just share addresses and values across threads no problem, with all consequences that follow (race conditions can hurt you and kill people, ask the therac 25). Oh yea fancy languages do all of this management work for you but it takes overhead. Yea that was it children. And I am still wondering why we did not learn Rust, Zig, or even Mojo for all I care instead of C++. Why C++? Same reason they teach Python as the first language in a software engineering mayor (start with a statically nominally typed language like Kotlin or C#, starting with dynamic structural languages is not good for a basis in programming): Its all hype train. I can say I touched cpp and hpp files, but I have not programmed in C++. I got into it and got to use smart pointers, views, concepts, all from the get-go. My group has no issues with compilers because we are running the same setup, not having to work with code bases that are not made to work with our ecosystem. That is not C++, that is a dream for most C++ developers. And what did I get in return? 4 months of C++, and I was exposed to TMP, how templates do really suck as a system in general, how incredibly stupid some behaviors are, and how shitty the language in general actually is. It is just incomplete and stdlib and stl feel like incomplete additions to the already existing skill issue which is the design of the language itself.

Learn C++? Yes because you can not get rid of the thing. Learn Rust and Zig instead if you just want to learn about working with memory? Yes. Just yes. I programmed a very minimalist mini game engine in Mojo not because I like the language (I kind of do but I prefer braces syntax over Pythonic syntax) but because I wanted to prove that you just do not need to touch C++ anymore if all you need is inter-opt. I used C++ libraries, I did not export one to be used in other C++ apps. And guess what? It ran just fine. Nuhu C++ is a form of evil that we still allow to exist. It is a root of evil, a root of bad habits, and a prime example of what happens when there is no guidance during language development. Absolute garbage language 100% would not recommend purely on its historic baggage and verbose garbage alone.

author: @RegularOriginalYT
text:
Wall of text inc for anyone who is interested. Feel free to disagree.

You point out real problems, but they are framed in a way that ignores the forces shaping C++. Most of the strange or difficult parts of the language come from two things: decades of backwards compatibility with C and a cost model where nothing happens unless the programmer explicitly requests it. Once you take those constraints seriously, the structure of C++ becomes predictable.
Templates, header-based generics, undefined behavior, limited default safety, ABI quirks and the overall size of the language are direct consequences of trying to preserve performance, determinism and interoperability across every platform for more than forty years.

Languages like Rust or Zig feel cleaner because they do not inherit these constraints. They can forbid entire categories of operations, assume a unified toolchain, ship with a single package manager and break compatibility whenever needed. C++ is difficult and messy, but not because its designers were careless. It is a systems language that still has to run kernels, games, scientific simulations, financial systems, embedded firmware and billions of lines of old code without breaking anything that already exists.

Calling it horrible overlooks the reason it remains widely used. It prioritizes control, predictability and longevity over convenience. Recognizing the complexity without assuming it implies bad design makes it easier to understand why the language looks the way it does.

If you demanded that Rust be fully ABI stable across all compilers, link against every C library ever written, preserve all of C’s semantics, never break C code, serve as a drop-in replacement for 40 years of infrastructure, keep compile-time generics with zero runtime cost and support the same memory model, Rust would start to look a lot like C++.

I actually do get somewhat annoyed when people make these comparisons. It's like complaining about a car with manual transmission making more sounds than a electric car. 
The comparison only works if you ignore everything that makes each machine what it is.

Regarding static_cast: If you don't like the typing, use a fuction-style cast: int i = int(myFloat). Or just omit the cast completely, because you get implicit conversions in most contexts. As for the other casts: You should not be doing them that often for their verbose names to become a problem. If they do, you're either working on some very special piece of code or you're doing something that probably has a better solution than all those casts.

As for that calculateForce() function: While i think its good to be explicit in such mixed-type calculations, you can omit a lot of those casts if you know how floating point conversion and integral promotion work with such expressions. But as i said: simply use a function-style cast instead of static_cast<T>(...). problem solved.

Regarding the somewhat verbose iterator-based std::sort(): You can use std::ranges:.sort() to directly sort your vector.

As for reflection: This has been voted into C++26 a few months ago and there are already implementations. True, the lack of reflection was a pain point, but not anymore.

text:
Some issues, I won't go through the entire video:
Random numbers: Why not use rand()%X instead? Yes, you can use the verbose example you gave, but that is only really needed if you want to customize the generator. I'm pretty sure Java or Python has similar customization options that would be equally verbose as your C++ example. And yes, rand() is from C, however C++ is mostly a superset of C, therefore rand() is also part of C++, same goes for printf(). If the task is merely to print a single message out, printf is more than enough and would be the more fair comparison.

New objects: Why are you comparing a normal allocation in Java with a unique_ptr in C++? unique_ptr has totally different purposes than a mere object allocation. If you use new operator, syntax-wise it's pretty much the same in Java and C++. Yes, it's less safe, but that was not the point you were making at that point.

Casts: There are many different casts because they are supposed to be used in different ways, ensuring you know what you're doing. Try emulating reinterpret_cast in Java to the same degree as what you can do in C++, it'll be a lot messier and verbose than just using it in C++.

Not saying that you are completely wrong in every point, and in several parts I agree with you, however when you want to compare languages you also have to make sure you are comparing the two languages fairly. I could turn this easily around and write verbose Java- or Python code and compare it with an equivalent one-liner in C++: "Omagawd, you need to declare an entire class in Java just to have a main function AND you need to explicitly mark it public static, that is so verbose for a simple Hello World, while in C++ you only have to write a simple global main function, clearly C++ is better".

author: @alphaflo977
text:
It’s been a year now since I have started the journey or making my own videogame from scratch, and I didn’t know C++ so I learned the language while also learning and about game development. 
I honestly fell in love with C++ because of its design and how it evolved from C++ from the start. The philosophy behind what decisions have been made for the STL while still keeping total compatibility with C is astounding when you really dive deep into it. 
If anyone had to build a language like that with total backwards compatibility with C, I can assure you that it juste couldn’t be better. Languages like Rust just don’t have that constraint and it allowed them to make fundamentally different decisions regarding hiw the language works.

text:
Technically std::remove does an unordered remove, which is the more performant way to do it, but it assumes you don't want to keep the same ordering.
It swaps the last element and the one you are removing, and changes the end of the array to be the element before the one you removed (usually it's just done by decreasing the length by one, but C++ uses begin and end, which makes things weird).
So the element is no longer within the array, and will be overwritten if the array is expanded, rather than moving every single element after it one slot forward to keep the same ordering.

author: @danielt8880
text:
Rust is the only language that actually solved the “how do we evolve without breaking everything” problem.
Everyone else either moves painfully slowly (C++, Java, Go), adds half-baked contextual keywords (C++), or just yeets backward compatibility out the window (Python 3).
Rust said “hold my borrow checker” and invented Editions.
New edition every 3 years (2015, 2018, 2021,  2024, 2027…). Each crate picks its edition in Cargo.toml. The compiler builds every crate with the exact syntax/rules and std library of its own edition. You can depend on a 2015 crate that has a function called async() and a 2024 crate that uses real async fn in the same binary. Zero conflicts. Pure magic.
When async/await became keywords in 2018, old code that used async as a variable or function name still compiles forever (guaranteed), new code can’t use async as an identifier anymore, and the ecosystem keeps moving forward with zero forced migrations.
No other language lets you drop game changing syntax while keeping an ironclad “your 10-year-old code will never break” promise.
Editions are genuinely one of the best ideas in programming language design ever. C++ should learn from that

text: Oh man. I should preface this by saying I haven't programmed in C++ in a long time. But, true story: one day my manager said, "Hey Wayne! So-and-so has left the company. You're going to be taking over his code. We need you to fix some bugs and add some new features right now!" When I went into his codebase, I literally couldn't read it. After that, I started asking, "Do things have to be this complicated?" and started doing experiments in minimizing ambiguity of code by minimizing language features used. author: @skilz8098
text:
There are 2 things about the original philosophy behind the design of the language that I don't think was mentioned maybe some parts or bits, but not the whole or complete picture. 

Sure, one of the goals of the language itself was meant to generate fast running code to a degree. Sure, the language has all of these different features about it, yet you are not bound to have to use every one of them. 

The original concept here is that you only pay for what you use, and it can be extremely efficient when done properly based on your target. Neither the language itself nor the compiler (compiler vendors, etc.) is supposed to get in your way. You the programmer aren't bound to a bunch of regulations. 

If a given known algorithm not implemented naively is supposed to run in Constant time and use Linear Space complexity, then the language itself once compiled, linked and built into useable binaries, the application or code is supposed to do just that and only use the minimal amount of system resources to achieve it. 

C++ original had the design philosophy of giving You the Programmer, Developer, the ability and freedom to Write Your Code as you See Fit. 


Has the language changed? Sure, it has grown and added many newer features, sure there are several different compilers, linkers, debuggers, IDEs, etc. built to parse it. Sure, there wasn't always a "Strict Standard" yet now they have one because of how fast and large the Language spread throughout the 80s and 90s when CPU design and systems transitioned out of the "8 - 16 bit" era into the more modern 32-bit systems and such, and this doesn't even involve differences within the architect itself such as pipeline, branch predictors, out of order execution, memory schemas (caches, cache hierarchy models, cache polices), etc. And here we still haven't even breached into the territory of multi-threading capable and multi core systems. This adds an entire new lawyer to the entire "stack-frame" pun intended.  

Hardware is always changing and changes quite fast. And to utilize that newer hardware with its newer features many compilers, interpreters etc. are bound to have to redesign almost their tool chain or set of tools for it to continuously be viable to use on that newer hardware and this doesn't even get into the middle part where you have to interface with the drivers themselves. This is typically done at the Hardware ISA to ABI level with the Platform - OS kernels and potentially some of the "compiler vendors". 

And yes, Backwards compatibility is one of the biggest things about C++ that makes it very challenging, yet that to me is one of its best features, not worse or problematic. 

Why? When it comes to the contract between hardware and software especially in terms of one where one is invested into it, and a given code base from a language runs perfectly fine on that system, but then all of a sudden (3 months later) some committee you know nothing about, people you never met, that have absolutely nothing to do with what you are doing decides: "oh we don't want or like unnamed unions because they might be unsafe". 

So now a bunch of functions, libraries, programs, applications etc. that you might have on your system that uses them, now all of a sudden break and quite working because of some snob asshole somewhere else didn't like that "feature". This is the antithesis to C++. 

The worst part is I have already recently seen this happen. Where and how? 

Oh, about a year ago, there were about 5-6 OpenGL/Vulkan Based applications that I had purchased where they all started, launched and ran perfectly fine on my system. 

Well over time and after a handful of NVidia Driver Updates for Windows 10/11 where I'm running Windows 10 Pro -x64 on a 3GHz Core 2 Quad Extreme with only 8GB DDR3 Ram with an EVGA NVidia 2GB GTX 750Ti SC graphics card... 

NVidia's newer driver sets broke every single one of those titles and prevented them from launching. 

I personally spent about 100-200 hours diving through and trying to debug them myself. Uninstalling them, reinstalling them, etc. Diving through forums, etc.

Come to find out, NVidia's latest drivers were being compile and built through MSVC's newest IDE and within their own internal development environment. They were compiling and building out their binaries for their Windows drivers and within their build environment it was configured to build under the "Assumption" that every system out there has native hardware popcnt instructions or SSE4.2 vector intrinsic instructions and there was no "branch" within their prebuilt or compiled binaries to check or test the "Target system" of its capabilities without any kind of fall back or alternative method of handling it. 

So here, these titles were crashing at startup. Was it the title itself? Nope! I checked the dev logs, bug reports, the specs, etc. Nothing there within their code base that requires the use of popcnt or SSE4.2 instructions. 

Was it coming from Windows itself? I check through the Windows Updates and other related areas. Nope, not even Microsoft at least for Windows 10 Pro x64 requires native popcnt or SSE4.2 instructions. 

I didn't have to, but did anyways, I went and double checked the Khronos group to see if their newer versions of OpenGL / Vulkan - GLSL - SPIR-V require this. Nope! OpenGL and Vulkan are supposed to be completely portable, generic.

So where was this crash coming from? Well, some of these titles were written in C++, some in C#, some in Java. They were using various different Game Engines. Some used Unity, others Unreal and even one of them was using Godot. I looked into those too. 

Now something like Unreal especially 5_x+ will use newer 4.2 instructions, popcnt, AVX, AV512 etc. if they are available and the user configures the engine to do so sure, but they don't enforce it. 

So again, where's this crash coming from? Well, it led me to the conclusion that it was coming directly from NVidia a peripheral hardware vendor and their compiled and built software for given platforms that their binaries, their drivers were ignoring target architects.

So here because I'm still using a Core 2 Quad Extreme on Windows 10 Pro, all of my OpenGL/Vulkan Titles are now bricked because some other company broke that which wasn't broke in the first place.

Well just recently back on 11/04 or 11/05 of this year 2025 with one of their newer driver updates, they officially stated: "Fixed Vulkan applications from crashing on Core 2 based systems. 

(continued...)

1:22:33 this probably is like this because in C it's very common to have the real return value be output via a pointer, whereas the function itself just returns one of its arguments (for chain calls), or returns some value which only matters for optimising future calls to the same API (like returning an array's length), or in general returns something which usually doesn't matter (a delete function returning whether or not the deleted element existed)

because an output pointer argument can't be ignored (writing NULL everywhere takes space), but the function return value can be. C++ has classes and method overloading, so none of this matters.

text:
Really long comment which I was writing on the side while watching the video so  I could add thoughts to it as they come up

Some things I wanna add:
- I WISH there was an easy way to convert a buffer into an std::vector<bool>. I had to write code where I use & with every bit on every byte of a buffer to convert it to std::vector<bool>. In debug builds, this takes really long, because it performs the actual operation and uses it's result to determine whether to insert a 0 or 1 bit.  In release mode the compiler understands that it can just memcpy my buffer. Performance matters even in debug builds because even if I have to tank a performance hit, my program should still be usable in debug mode so I can meaningfuly test it.
- std::unordered_map added contains in C++ 20
- I don't even bother with Visual Studio's UI when using the Visual Studio build system. I use VS as my editor but I edit my .vcxproj files manually in Notepad++
- Designated initializers have been a thing since C99 and it makes me sad that not every language has things like this. C++ having them is something I genuinely appreciate about it.
- A lot of cryptically named functions that were inherited from C have names like that because back when these names were invented, they had to be 6 characters or less
- std::launder exists to bypass compiler optimizations. I never used it though cause I never had a use for it.
- Due to the low level nature of C++, I'd love to be able to program with exceptions turned off. Unfortunately everything in the standard library uses them.
- One might argue that C++ does not have move semantics at all, just another reference type where programmers agreed to use it for fake move semantics
- I have a passion for low level programming and given my skillset being mainly in programming I would want to have a job in that. But I would probably do web dev so that the programming I do at work is different from the programming I do in my free time so I can more easily enjoy low level programming since it's NOT my job.
- The thing about optimizations is that you don't need to go for every last drop of performance, but if there is a 50x gain, go for it. The thing about performance is that it is the one quality about code that can be objectively measured that actually affects the user, which is why I like talking about it so much.

Some things I disagree on:
- You SHOULD learn C before learning C++. The language tries to be unique and have it's own high level concepts, but due to it's lineage to C, and it's bad design where parts of it are due to it's lineage to C, you need to learn C for C++ to make any amount of sense.
- Anyone who says that you should never resort to doing things the C way is full of shit.
- Similarly, I don't care that it's non-standard, I will use #pragma once because all 3 compilers support it
- Regarding build systems: Visual Studio, Xcode and Makefiles are the most common lowest level build systems of Windows, MacOS and Linux respectively. ("lowest level build system means that the compiler and linker are invoked directly). However, Visual Studio also ships with nmake, which can parse Makefiles and MinGW ships make. Makefiles can also be used on MacOS. There's also Ninja which is used on all three platforms. It's like make, but deliberately designed in such a way where Ninja files have to be generated by higher level build systems, with the upside of Ninja being fast. Most "higher level" build systems generate either a Makefile, a Visual Studio project, an Xcode project, or a Ninja build file.
Regarding compilers: MSVC is Windows only, Clang and GCC run on all major OSes and can compile for every major OS. Visual Studio even has first class support for Clang, which is great cause it has all my favourite compiler extensions.
- Don't use the COM interfaces way of prompting the user for a file path. Use GetOpenFileNameW to open files, GetSaveFileNameW to save files. Only use IFileDialog for opening folders (because the window you get when using the old open folder function is really clunky to use)
- You did not have to use streams for string formatting pre C++ 20. Unlike string types in other languages, std::string is not immutable -- it acts a lot like std::vector<char> so people would use that to build up strings. It even has reserve. You could also use snprintf, which is the C way of doing it.
- When it comes to making a UI, I don't think it makes sense to talk about all the shit Microsoft has been pulling and conflate that with C++ itself. If you're using builtin Windows APIs for your UI, you will have to deal with Microsoft's bullshit regardless of what language you're on. Yes C++ doesn't have a UI library and you're gonna have to bring your own. Rust and Go don't have a UI library either
- I don't get how Qt problems are related to C++ either when lots of people use Qt with other languages.
- dear imgui is absolutely suited for user facing UIs
- Errors are only as bad as you describe them when using templates. It's unfortunate really. I quite like templates but if I get a template error I don't even look at the error message, I look for the squiggly lines in Visual Studio
- Technically you can use macros to autogenerate variants of a struct for different types in C, but there is a reason people want templates.
- Discussing UX flaws with VS doesn't have much to do with C++ either but I feel you on that one´
- I NEVER use the class keyword in any scenario. If I need a class, I call it a struct, because classes are structs under the hood.
- Operator overloading is a double edged sword. You can absolutely do some insane things with it, but in my opinion it does more good than bad. For example, I'd only operate the * operator on a vector type for vector and scalar multiplications. + and - are no brainers though.
- You don't HAVE to use member initializer lists. Member initializer lists is how you tell the compiler which parameters to pass to the constructors of your members. If your members don't have constructors, there is no difference between member initializer lists and initializing your members in the constructor's body. If a member does have a constructor though but you set it's value in your constructor's body, then that member's default constructor runs before you reassign that member's value.
- Memory alignment is something you SHOULD think about when programming in a low level language.
- "never prefix your variable names with underscores" shut the fuck up
- I don't use or care about idioms. I know what I want my program to do and I just do it. Any patterns/idioms come naturally once I already know how to solve my problem.
- std::unique_ptr "looks" exactly the same as a raw pointer, because the only member inside the underlying unique_ptr class is the pointer to the data. All a unique_ptr is is something that has memory allocated that will deallocate that memory in it's destructor, which is run either when it goes out of scope, or when the other struct that it's a part of runs it's destructor
- I get why you don't want to have to check your program's assembly after compilation, but I do it because I care about performance and I want to know what my computer is actually running. This is how I know if I am getting the optimizations I am hoping for. I also do it to study behaviors of the compiler because I do reverse engineering.
- You can't tell how fast your code will be even when looking at the assembly. You can reason about how fast it should roughly be based on what operations have to be performed how many times and how many times per cycle your CPU can do them on average and how fast your CPU is, but the only definitive way to prove if your code is fast is by benchmarking it.
- I have no problem returning to C++ after taking a break from it, though I have a much easier time with reading code than other people
- Metaprogramming in Rust is actually really powerful when using proc macros. There's a great video from Logan Smith called "Comprehending Proc Macros". The title is a pun, you can figure out how.
- Use of AI generated images.

At the end of the day, the thing I find myself doing a lot of times is trying to trick the compiler into giving me an output I want where I already know what I want that output to look like. It's better than nothing, but I'm always looking for a better way to fulfill my needs.

author: @kyouko5363
text:
Regarding NeverClick 2:01:00 - I would be very interested in seeing the source code! It would be very useful as a reference to build an equivalent utility for Linux, and I have WinAPI experience so I'm fairly confident it would take around a week~ish to port, if I go that route. See, I too suffer from a form of RSI, chronic tendonitis specifically, only on my right wrist, the one that used to be dedicated to using a mouse.

I use Vim Motions to navigate my whole operating system, at least the window manager side of things, since I use a tiling window manager (i3), and the majority of the time I'm either in Alacritty (Terminal) or Firefox, both of which are completely set up for Vim Motions, down to ptipython (if you've never heard of ptipython, and use Python, thank me later, it makes ipython feel like the standard python REPL. Snappiest most feature complete Python REPL I've ever come across, has insanely good completion, automatically showing function  documentation, as well as signatures, which can be displayed a bunch of different ways, easily configured through a built-in settings menu, themable, customizable, etc, one of those things you wonder where tf its been your whole life). 

The navigational concept of NeverClick (Keyboard Hinting aka 2DJumps) is something that has deep roots in Vim. The Tridactyl browser extension I use, that brings Vim Motions into Firefox (among tons of other Vim-style :commands that let you control pretty much every other aspect of the browser, including stuff that you couldn't do at all before, very powerful extension) has around 20 different Hinting modes to target different types of UI elements and perform actions, from targeting links to open in a new tab, focusable areas, media(images, thumbnails, immediate point and download), css, plain text, anything with events (buttons),  etc, etc using that very same principle. 

This works great and all.. until I need to open a GUI application that does not have any Vim Motion support. I use tab/shift+tab if the program supports it as fallback to cycle UI elements, but some programs, I just have to grab my mouse again. Since NeverClick is OS-wide, that would solve another set of cases  where I need to go back to my mouse. The only thing left after that would be Krita / drawing or sketching programs, or certain CAD software, but I can live with that. 

Though I can already imagine all the API differences to run make the same core logic run but under X11, and what you probably used to identify UI elements with associated events/properties cycling through with tlhelp32, and how different that would have to be on X11, but I like a challenge, not to mention the educational value :)

author: @awrfs7926
text:
"C++'s verbose casts are bad"
I disagree. The C-style cast is ambiguous and relies on "secret" behavior that changes depending on which types you're casting between. You may try to convert type A to type B, and all of a sudden you realize the compiler thought you wanted to const_cast. C++-style casts show the programmer's intent very clearly. Some may reply that this still isn't good, because other languages don't require it, but that's because most languages are abstract enough to not need something like reinterpret_cast. Also, static_cast gives you compile-time checking ability, which C-style casts don't.
"Creating a global variable is difficult"
It's one line of code, using "static" if in a source file or "inline" if in a header. It becomes natural to you if you understand the compiler and how header and source files differ. Some may think that's an unreasonable expectation, but it definitely is not. And that's not just a C++ issue, it goes for C as well. Such is the tradeoff of enforcing only one pass per translation unit.
"The type sizes aren't clear and may differ between compilers"
If knowing the exact size is important you should always use the standard library's types from cstdint (int32_t, uintptr_t, etc). Or just always use them and there won't ever be confusion. Personally I like making type aliases to match Rust's type names because they're more concise (std::int32_t => i32).
"Const is confusing and also can be placed on either side"
I don't think "I cannot reassign a value to a const variable" is legitimate critique. Also, const is left-associative, meaning if there's something to the left, the const applies to that. Otherwise it applies to whatever is on the right. That is a syntax quirk that takes one minute to learn and then you know it forever.
"formatting isn't universal across all codebases"
Lol.
"Does vector.empty() *clear* the vector or does it check if the size is zero"
Lol.
"Cryptic C-like function names"
C++ standard demands that C's standard library is (at least largely) implemented. So again, that's a problem tied to C rather than C++.
"Namespaces look bad"
Lol.
Stopped there. C++ isn't perfect (far from it) but from what I watched most of it is either derived from C and therefore inevitable based on compiler specifications, or just preferable to the alternatives.

"Does vector.empty() *clear* the vector or does it check if the size is zero" Lol. "Cryptic C-like function names" C++ standard demands that C's standard library is (at least largely) implemented. So again, that's a problem tied to C rather than C++. "Namespaces look bad" Lol. Stopped there. C++ isn't perfect (far from it) but from what I watched most of it is either derived from C and therefore inevitable based on compiler specifications, or just preferable to the alternatives.

finally, someone makes this video. I'm not a C++ programmer; I'm someone who writes code in a lot of different languages depending on how I feel on any given day, and I hop between projects every 2 seconds. Whenever I have to write something in C++ (which is very, very infrequent) I'm always baffled about some language feature that makes absolutely no sense that I didn't know about before. I inevitably spend hours debugging my code because C++ is terrible. Nothing ever makes sense, and every single small thing is an infinite rabbit black hole of infinite complexity.

What annoys me the most is that the core idea of "C with extra utilities" isn't inherently bad; I personally write a lot of C and would appreciate some things to make it easier (although most things are solvable with clever use of the preprocessor). But C++ takes that good idea and distorts into a monstrous eldritch being of a programming language that serves nobody and hurts everyone.

So I end up just resorting to writing pure C and eating the lack of abstraction. and I know how garbage of a language C is, but at least I'm happy. There's enough fun things to do with the preprocessor that make writing C not actually that bad (the only annoying thing is header duplication, but vim is fast enough regarding copy/paste that it doesn't annoy me much).

author: @ScorgRus
text: 52:25 begin() and end() do not "point to an element". They point to a boundary of an element, whether that element exists (constructed) there or not. In a contiguous memory block, where the elements are placed with no gaps in between, the right boundary of element i is the left boundary of element i+1. Therefore, end() points to the right boundary of the whole array (the last element, which may not exist). The choice of left/right element matters only for dereferencing. Respectively, rbegin() and rend() point to the right and left boundaries of an array (symmetric to begin/end).

text:
Big tech companies like Apple, Google, and Microsoft make money by locking users into their ecosystems. Once you depend on their operating system or messaging platform, they can control prices, compatibility, and what apps you’re allowed to use.

Linux and most open-source software avoid this problem because no single company owns them. They’re transparent, community-driven, and not designed to trap you.

Standardized open-source protocols—like SMS, email, USB, or Wi-Fi—are essential for real competition. They let different devices, apps, and operating systems talk to each other. Without open standards, any company could create a private protocol that only works inside its own ecosystem. That instantly kills competition because no rival product could communicate with your friends, coworkers, or devices. And once a company controls the standard, it can raise prices, limit features, or block alternatives without losing users.

We’re still early in the digital age, and we can choose between a future controlled by a few corporations or one built on open, interoperable systems. If you disagree, tell me why. If you agree, try Linux.

text: I'd just like to interject for a moment. What you’re referring to as Linux, is in fact, GNU/Linux, or as I’ve recently taken to calling it, GNU plus Linux. Through a peculiar turn of events, the version of GNU which is widely used today is often called “Linux”, and many of its users are not aware that it is basically the GNU system, developed by the GNU Project. There really is a Linux, and these people are using it, but it is just a part of the system they use. Linux is the kernel: the program in the system that allocates the machine’s resources to the other programs that you run. The kernel is an essential part of an operating system, but useless by itself; it can only function in the context of a complete operating system. Linux is normally used in combination with the GNU operating system: the whole system is basically GNU with Linux added, or GNU/Linux. All the so-called “Linux” distributions are really distributions of GNU/Linux.

author: @x3haloed
text:
Such a strange video. Besides being constructed just to sell JetBrains stuff, I don't think this really really explains the differences from a developer point of view. You do go over the fact that servers primarily run on Linux, so it's important to know how to use it, but then you pretty much talk about how your development environment is cross-platform without diving into any nuance about being a developer on each platform. Very bizarre.

I'll give you the real rundown of what it's like to be a developer on all three:
1. macOS is very optimized. It's very reliable and battery efficient. But it's quirky. It has funny paradigms that you'll only encounter on a Mac, like its 5 different ways to install and uninstall software and it's unintuitive system for running unsigned code or giving applications administrative access to different feature areas of the system.
2. Linux is a developer wonderland. It's extremely flexible and customizable, but if you want to customize anything non-trivial, be prepared for a journey. It's a crazy mess of mish-mashed configuration paradigms, and sometimes you'll actually have to understand code to diagnose certain problems. The biggest reason it's used for servers is exactly the flexibility and customization. With the ability to strip out everything except exactly what's needed to host your specific service, it can be made to run extremely efficiently, reliably, and securely.
3. Windows is kind of a middle ground. It's pretty easy to pick up and use for pretty much any task, it's a very popular target for development, so you'll likely find any tool you need, and it's not as easy to break your whole OS like it is with Linux. If you only have experience with Windows, one day you will find that *you* are the weird one when it comes to line endings -- every other OS uses carriage-returns, but you use line-feeds, and while Windows is really popular, you'll have to learn how to support both. The latest versions of Windows are full of spammy services begging for your attention, and you better get ready for lousy battery life, unanticipated update reboots, and reboots that can mysteriously take half an hour for unknown reasons.

I use Mac. Since servers are Linux-based and macOS is UNIX-based, they share a common ancestor and they have an easy time running the same software and sharing similar conventions. Combine this with how reliable both the hardware and the software are, and you have a workhorse machine that's always ready to run when you have to push an emergency patch to production at midnight. The rest of the quirks I have to deal with are trivial in comparison. The upgradability thing is real, but it really all comes back to reliability. Don't tinker with your main dev box. Buy a good one, keep it clean and organized, and it will do its job for many years. Keep extra machines around for experimentation.

author: @felixjohnson3874
text:
Sorry but having had to use WSL for a month or so, its kinda shit. 

It's a tarp over a broken window; technically a 'fix' but not really. Constant freezes, many applications flat out don't don't work, filesystem consistency is... optional... and it's generally jank through and through.

Keep in mind, I say this as an arch user on wayland that primarily uses Nvidia GPUs with a multimonitor VRR set up where each monitor has a different max and set refresh rate. That is my bar for stable, and WSL (and Windows in general) doesn't have to worry about running into it, because it can't jump that high.

WSL is a patch on Windows to run a linux utility in a pinch, but it's nowhere near the reliable 'make it the spine of your workflow' foundation a lot of people act like it is. It is the rickety step ladder you use to reach your firealarm to change it's battery so it'll stop screaching at you - not the deck of your house.

I was *_very_* quickly reminded of why I left windows in the first place, and WSL was about the 572nd reminder after that.

I'd just like to interject for a moment. What you're referring to as Linux, is in fact, GNU/Linux, or as I've recently taken to calling it, GNU plus Linux. Linux is not an operating system unto itself, but rather another free component of a fully functioning GNU system made useful by the GNU corelibs, shell utilities and vital system components comprising a full OS as defined by POSIX.

author: @arctic-batcat
text:
TL;DR;       (this comment doesn't tldr the video content) 
* if you are purely interested in becoming a great software engineer at your chosen specialization your best bet is probably win+wsl+vscode environment.
* learning vim motions and getting a split keyboard might be the best thing you do for your overall developer experience during your career.

--- Environment ---

my whole career I felt like a fraud because of my "env-stack" (win11/wsl2/vscode+vim-motions) but after trying numerous linux distros over the years for extended periods of time and trying vim and emacs I have come to a conclusion that for most developers the win-wsl-vsc is probably all you would ever need to build great software. I have also realized that most of these "wars" come from people just being geeky (identity, preferences, what people believe is cool or not etc..). which is fine, I don't mean that as an insult, we all have passions and things we geek-out about, but if you are out there like myself and you are purely interested in building great software and do not care about anything but that then win-wsl-vsc is probably the best stack for you.

there are definitely more specific career paths in software engineering where it is beneficial to the actual thing you are trying to get good at to use a linux distro (like cybersecurity) or other more specialized/premium IDEs but this is a shotgun approach that you have the least chance to "get good at the wrong thing".

--- Vim Motions & Split Keyboard ---

I'd deeply recommend to anyone who writes code (and quiet honestly even edits text a lot) to learn vim motions and get a split keyboard (I personally believe kinesis adv360 is currently the best split keyboard on the market).

reasons to learn vim motions are quiet simple:
* you won't need to stretch your pinky to hit ctrl and move your entire hand to hit arrows in order to navigate text, you can do most things without having to lift your hands of the FJ resting position 
* there is plenty of motions to do common things we do as software engineers (select a code block, replace contents inside the brackets or quotes, cut/paste a block of code)

initially you will feel friction but the motions will become muscle memory over time and you definitely don't need to know them all, as with most things you will find the 80/20 rule manifest itself.

reasons to get a split keyboard:
* on most standard keyboards your thumbs are used to press only 1 key (most of the time, sometimes you press the alt key with it), on split keyboards usually thumbs are utilized to do much more than that
* in terms of ergonomics you have to kind of twist your wrists outwards to place them on the FJ resting position on standard keyboards while on a split keyboard you can angle the keyboard to achieve a more neutral position, the standard keyboard becomes even more uncomfortable the wider your shoulders are because the size of switches/keys is pretty much a constant, I find that I tend to push my shoulders forward and lift them a bit up in an attempt to twist the wrists outwards to place them on the FJ position when using a standard keyboard which, obviously, is bad for your wrists and posture, especially if you do this 40-50h/week
* there are other reasons which are more related to specific split keyboards but as I said I think kinesis adv360 is the best right now, pricey I know  at ~$500 but if this is your job and you value your health I'd definitely pull the trigger (I'd also pull the trigger on an ergonomic office chair and a comfortable mattress but that's off-topic).

I also have a gaming laptop running win10 LTSC IoT edition (the one without spyware and with extended support), I was frustrated with how slow WSL worked, so I chose to migrate to Linux permanently. Linux as a Workstation is still barely usable for the average Joe and  for me, an experienced developer, it's still very frustrating having to manage and learn all the completely different configuration files for every individual component none of which follow any semblance of coherent logic.

And if at any point you have files outside the linux subsystem, we prepared for loading times of death.

author: @atrus3823
text: I'm sure a million mac fan boys have already said this, but macs are not as expensive as they're made out to be. I used windows machines for 20+ years before finally making the switch, and while the up front cost is high, there are ways to mitigate that cost, and you end up with something of much greater value. I would argue that the lifetime cost of a mac is less than a windows machine (obviously depending on a million variables). If you go for official refurbs and get something a couple years old, it'll greatly reduce the price and probably still work better and last longer than a new windows machine. I bought my first MacBook 10 years ago and everything works like the day i got it (except the battery of course, though i haven't had to replace it). It's starting to show it's age for sure, but I've never been able to keep a windows laptop for more than 7 years without needing to replace it. Usually by the 7 year mark, it is unusably slow and at least a few things are completely broken. I bought an on paper much faster gaming laptop about 5 years ago for about 60% of the price of my MBP, and while it plays games decently, it is almost unusable for anything else. The bootup time alone is ridiculous! Final thing, resale value: look at even quite old MacBooks on eBay. It's insane how much they sell for. I'll never go back!

text:
The best operating system for programming depends on your specific needs and preferences. Here are some key points to consider:
- Windows is the most popular OS and has a large ecosystem of software and support. It also comes with Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) which allows running Linux distributions natively.
- Linux is highly customizable, has a large open-source ecosystem, and is lightweight and performant. It comes with many powerful programming tools pre-installed.
- macOS is Unix-based like Linux, has a polished user interface, and is popular among developers. However, it only runs on Apple hardware.
Ultimately, all three OSes are capable of running most programming languages and tools. The choice often comes down to personal preference and the specific requirements of your projects. As a beginner, it's best to stick with the OS you are most comfortable with.

text:
Here's my version of the differences. 

There's really just 2 different languages here, C/C++ and C#.
They are both high level programming languages, but C/C++ is lower level, C# is higher level.  

The lower level C/C++ is better for faster, efficient code, like video game engines, drivers, data analysis routines, operating system code, etc.  It is ancient, and the tried and true basic high level language out there in our culture.  It can be harder to learn as a first language, as you do direct memory manipulation, and you need to do more things yourself.  Think of it like playing an RPG where you need to make the ideal build for your character.  You can do awesome things, but be careful not to screw up the build!

C# is a real fully Object Oriented Programming Language that is very high level, and where most basic things are done for you.  This is basically Microsoft's version of Java, but with language Syntax matching C++ even more than Java already does.  This one is best if you are making Windows applications.  As a lot of stuff, like memory management is done for you, it is alot slower.  Think of this like playing an RPG where you are copying a build from the internet.  It will be great, you won't screw it up, but you don't have fine control over your abilities, as you follow the build exactly. 

Now, C++ is basically just C with Classes.  C is the basic, bare bones language, which is a Procedural language.  C++ adds classes to it, and some more Library functionality, and is now Object Oriented.  But almost every valid C program is also a valid C++ program.   So C++ is an expansion pack for C, while C# is a brand new game.  Just about everyone uses the C++ compiler nowadays, so the choice between C and C++ is whether you want the program to be Object Oriented or not.
C# was built from the ground up to be object Oriented, unlike C++ which just added it in, so if you really want Object Oriented all the way, go with C#.

author: @dovahsenbrom836
text:
Also, use C/C++ if you want high performance, properly structured code, not having to deal with 10 million classes, not having to create a class any time you want to do anything, learning operating systems, learning embedded systems, learning network systems, learning security systems, and even scripting if you're good enough - vim and fast fingers go a long, long way.

Don't learn C/C++ if you want to glue some code fragments together and hope it works. It'll suck your soul and joy like a Dementor. It'll make you want to rip pieces of your own flesh out just to balance out the psychological pain. It'll get inside your head and make your eyes bleed while spending hours parsing through those thousands of lines of code to find that shitty off by one that's generating your runtime error. It'll make you scream in agony when someone cracks your software open because you forgot to free a pointer or used a deprecated unsafe version of a string library. It'll fuck you up, heal you, and fuck you up again.

IMO these languages are the best languages. They provide both abstraction - you can implement OOP concepts in C if you're good enough to do it - and control - memory management, kernel calls, process execution, etc. You get fast speeds, you get proper syntax - so long having a line of code that fills up your whole screen - and you're pretty much forced to use best practices, principles and patterns - the other option is ripping your eyes out while figuring out why the hell 1 out of 3 runs generate a seemingly nonexistent segfault. These are not your standard find-a-lib-read-a-tutorial-glue-some-shit-together-there-you-go java-type languages. These are craft languages. They reward those that take the time to learn how stuff hows. To figure out how the compiler processes things. To understand how the linker manages resources. To deeply think about what's the best way to cut a corner and get that min-max optimization that will make your system 1ms faster on that particular function. On the other hand, they punish everyone who doesn't do that. Harshly. Terribly. They'll scream "WRONG!" in your face, and when you ask why the answer will be "STOOPID!". Very punitive. Very rewarding. Very fun.

And truth is, the world runs in C. Your OS runs in C. Your phone runs in C. Your browser, your server, your database, your router, your car, your toothbrush, your microwave. Everything. Even if it's not in C, you can code it in C. That's the beauty of it. That's why it's so hard. It's an art form in it's own right. Plus it'll make virtually any other language feel like pushing solids into shapes. It's wonderful - and highly addictive.

Then there's the culture. I've found that C coders are very ruthless, but very empathetic once they assert you're in it for the long run. The same person that gives a half backed sour answer will take their time to slowly guide you through the process if they feel you really want to learn, really want to master it. It's really a whole thing. Spiritual, even. Can't enter the Temple unless your heart is in the right place.

So yes. Access your goals, take your time, figure out how far down the rabbit hole you want to go, and if the answer is 1, you'll know.

author: @SkyyySi
text:
C is NOT functional, it's procedural. Functional means that functions have no side effects, which is definitely not the case for C. Functional also implies other things, like First-Class-Functions, meaning you can pass them around just like any other data type, ie:

def f(af):
    return af(5) + 3


def g(x):
    return x * x


print(f(g)) # --> 28


EDIT: Also, in functional programming, a function can be created anonymously. If you define an int, for example, you would use a syntax like this:

myint: int = 69420

In a functional language, functions can also be created like this:

myfunc = lambda x: x//2 if x % 2 == 0 else x*3+1

This comes in useful when, for example, a function A takes another function B as a parameter, but you don't want to bind B to any function name.

Chris, who’s been working with C++ for about 15 years, talks about how he got started and what beginners should focus on. He even found one of his first C++ files from 2008, which made him reflect on how people today often overthink which language to learn.

His main point is simple: don’t stress too much about picking the “perfect” language. Just start coding. You’ll learn way more by actually writing code, breaking things, and fixing errors than by trying to follow the “right” path from the beginning.

He also mentions that beginners shouldn’t be afraid of writing bad or messy code. Looking back, he feels he would’ve improved faster if he had just experimented more instead of worrying about doing everything correctly.

Overall, his advice is to open your IDE and start building something — there’s no perfect way to begin, and nothing terrible will happen if you make mistakes.

author: @gustavogallegos3661
text:
Summary of what he said (enjoy)

He saves almost all the code he writes (even tutorials and college assignments), out of paranoia that he might need it someday.
He sees a lot of content online that advises beginners not to learn C++: they say it's a problematic, outdated, frustrating language that makes people give up on programming.
He acknowledges that C++ has flaws (no language is perfect, especially one so general), but he believes that shouldn't matter when starting out.
The most important thing for a beginner is not to choose “the perfect language” or worry about whether they will still be using it in a year's time.
What really matters is: writing code now, making things appear on the screen, modifying files, making mistakes, debugging, banging your head against the wall, and learning in the process.
He himself regrets having spent too much time at the beginning obsessed with “learning the right way” or “not writing bad code,” imitating programmers he admired. That slowed him down and made him program less.
He believes that writing bad code and figuring out why it's bad is one of the fastest and most useful ways to learn.
Final message: There is no “end of the world” situation in learning. If you're interested or think you might like it, just open your IDE and start writing code. That's it.

author: @gersongodinez
text:
I currently work as a "Digital Transformation Consultant" (fancy words for someone who solves and implements SAAS products)

My journey through the tech industry has had its ups and downs: I started with Pascal and C++ in high school, tried Electronics at university, dropped everything to dedicate myself to audiovisual production (it didn't work out very well), spent some time in marketing and advertising, then technical support for companies like Apple and Boston Scientific, and finally my current position working as a partner and product consultant for Oracle, Salesforce, Adobe, etc., for companies.

I've never stopped working on coding, small projects, or just small challenges to keep my mind busy. What's been difficult for me is finding a solid anchor in the new development trends. I feel like there's something new every week, AI is becoming an increasingly prevalent requirement for processes that, in theory, don't need it to remain stable and scalable, thousands of new frameworks are being released each year, and the uncertainty of how economic factors are driving the industry's pace.

C++ gives me peace of mind. Everything makes sense and even feels obvious and necessary. It lifts my spirits and has recently made me want to create other projects. Feelings that other languages, more susceptible to trends, don't inspire in me.

C++ is a quiet valley where everything works because there's a reason for it to be there.

author: @distrologic2925
text:
C++ is the best way to start programming.

It is the largest ecosystem with the best compatibility, while being mostly low-level and true to the hardware.

Even if it is not the tool of choice for your task, it balances simplicity and expressive power well enough to learn the basics aswell as to venture into new territory and experiment.

With something like C you will get hung up with compiler settings and platform details and lack of convenience features.
With something like Java or Typescript you will miss out on most of the magic going on under the hood and will learn highly pragmatic and specialized styles of coding.

C++ seems right on the line between expressive power and runtime abstraction.

text:
27 years of software engineering here. My advice is basically the same: spend more time writing code, learning, and interacting with others' code as well. I started with C/C++ (Borland Turbo C, later C++ Builder), then Visual Basic 6 and C#. Now, Rust.

I also have a very interesting story to share about coding. At one point, we developed a web portal to monitor the robots in the warehouse. But, you know, staring at a screen for 8 to 10 hours a day just to see if things were going well sucked. So, I made a console app in C# to query an API every 500ms and check the status of each robot using the parallel library.

The code was horrible—something I'd be ashamed of today—but while everyone else kept staring at the screen, I was lying in bed most of the time. When a robot had a fault, the app just sounded an alarm. Later, I added different sounds for different fault statuses.

One day, I shared this with a coworker I trusted, and he said: "You know, man, many times, horrible code is what saves our lives." Not something to be proud of, but definitely something interesting to share.

author: @sekki2554
text:
One of the most important thing that actually opened my eyes, was to learn about what the code actually does and not, how to write it. I look up syntax all the time, but i know in advance what i want to achieve. I would never be able to enjoy coding without this mindset anymore and if i could go back, i would stop myself immediately when i was stuck in the overoptimization loop. I always thought i was learning to write code BECAUSE i realized that i wanted to optimize it all the time, but that‘s the famous pitfall in which probably most of us fell into at some point in their life. Don‘t be afraid to write unmanageable code. Refactor it as soon as you need to and only refactor as much as you need. Refactoring code that way makes you understand and remember informations way easier than going through all of this in a timespan of 1 - 2 years. I hope that my next 14 years of coding will look exactly like the last 14 years. Write code without thinking too much about the future (if you‘re allowed to). If you need to expand, expand only the parts that actually need to be expanded. If you look back at your projects in 10 years, you realize that you made fewer errors over time and that problems that seemed impossible to manage are just a few keystrokes away then. So if you can, write code without overthinking. If you work at a company, follow their coding style and adapt. If they have issues with your code, then the time has come to look over it and if a lot of these issues came up (i hope not at a company c:), then you got your perfect free coding lectures right there.

My english is bad, so a lot might be weird to read but i tried to explain as good as i can. Write bad code, refactor it if you need to, focus on your goal and keep typing. With every day i love to see those errors i make more and more. Making errors is the way to learn from them and if you do everything perfect from the get go, you‘ll have a hard time to fix them in the future.

This is for draughonc {see below}:

First, great idea. Its equally important to keep mentally sharp as well as physically fit as you get older.

So, I am a retired software engineer with over 40 years working (started before the internet was around). I taught myself Fortran and Assembly Language in high school. If you are a Windows user, Visual Studio is free and a great IDE.
C is a good language to start with. Check out the Brian Kernighan; Dennis Ritchie book or find whatever source help you.
Graduating to C++ is a natural progression. You can continue to write C code and gradually start with C++ extensions such as Classes and the concept of polymorphism. Classes are a great way to hide implementation and create what is called "loosely coup[led" software. This is a great concept and worth understanding and following. 
Don't get religious about polymorphism unless you fully understand how it works and when to use it. This is where the complexity level takes a jump.
Good advice: put debug code in your software such that:
1) Provide debug levels in your code and make it easy to turn on and off debug levels. These levels should mirror the levels of your application.
2) Make it so you can build your project with or without debug code.
Come back to these two points when you start writing larger, more sophisticated applications. Do a web search for help on implementing them.

I hope this helps and wish you much luck and success in your endeavor. If you ever get serious and like games, consider trying the Unity game development system. it is free for casual users.

author: @Thugblader92
text:
My highschool teacher for 3 years of C++ programming kept teaching everything in bite sizes on purpose so I was absolutely never satisfied with my own code.
Write a simple world clock program? - week 1.
Write a word processor that accepts typewriting modules? - week 2.
Go back to the world clock, make it accept modules for timezones. - week 3.
Go back to the word processor, make it able to read and edit different file formats. - week 4.
Go back to the world clock, make it able to accept API from different online world clocks - week 5.
Project/test time: write a PDF editor that automatically puts timestamps with your world clock code in the word processor... - 3 weeks.

In essence, every time I went back to edit the previous work I got more and more disgusted with what I had written before, because I never did anything outside the scope of the assignment.
Now I can't write a single code without thinking "What if I want this and that at a later point", and take it into account... Has helped a lot, but my old projects look like garbage and your retrospective from looking at old code is very foreign to me. Thanks for sharing!

author: @williamogilvie6909
text:
I have used C++ off and on since 1989.   There are too many ways of creating buggy code that can't be debugged with C++.    I have seen some very nice looking C++ code written by others that constantly hung up.   I prefer Python for structured code where speed and realtime performance is not needed.   Even worse than C++ is C#.   Instead of elaborate structures and inherited objects, etc programs need coherent states.   C++, C#, Python, Java, and all the other languages people learn at university today have no facility for synchronizing states.     If a program is not synchronous, any bug is possible.

Some people don't understand this concept.  Probably because they have been stuck doing the same thing over and over again.   I will elaborate:  There is a problem concurrent software has called the Mutual Exclusion problem.   It is very difficult to guarantee different processes get exclusive access to resources in the correct order.   I have seen that in large C++ programs.   Threads are queued with nothing that regulates in what order different threads get access to resources.   A similar case with multiprocessor systems.   About 20 years ago I developed an image testing system, for space telescope IR sensors.   It had a quad DSP board, that got sensor data over a DMA channel.  Concurrently a pixel row was clocked and digitized by an Analog to Digital converter board, the previous row of pixel data was being transferred by DMA to one of the DSPs, and the second previous row of pixel data was being co-added with earlier data.   At the end of each frame the image data was transferred to a desktop PC where it was saved to disk.    This concurrent operation went on 24/7.   The delicate nature of the image sensors (cooled to ~4.5 K)   meant the clocking, data acquisition, etc had to be very regular and constant.   Each process (4 DSPs, image array clock, user PC) had to operate in a state synchronous way.   They communicated by reading shared memory.   However if 2 processes tried to read or write to the same shared memory, the software would crash.    So the software was very deterministic.    In 5 years of operation the software never crashed and every test yielded good data.    This is an example of a state synchronous concurrent system.   The queued threaded systems (non realtime) software people consider to be standard fare today are not deterministic.   So there is no guarantee there are not any conflicts.
