Even worse than C++ is C#. Instead of elaborate structures and inherited objects, etc programs need coherent states. C++, C#, Python, Java, and all the other languages people learn at university today have no facility for synchronizing states. If a program is not synchronous, any bug is possible. Some people don't understand this concept. Probably because they have been stuck doing the same thing over and over again. I will elaborate: There is a problem concurrent software has called the Mutual Exclusion problem. It is very difficult to guarantee different processes get exclusive access to resources in the correct order. I have seen that in large C++ programs. Threads are queued with nothing that regulates in what order different threads get access to resources. A similar case with multiprocessor systems. About 20 years ago I developed an image testing system, for space telescope IR sensors. It had a quad DSP board, that got sensor data over a DMA channel. Concurrently a pixel row was clocked and digitized by an Analog to Digital converter board, the previous row of pixel data was being transferred by DMA to one of the DSPs, and the second previous row of pixel data was being co-added with earlier data. At the end of each frame the image data was transferred to a desktop PC where it was saved to disk. This concurrent operation went on 24/7. The delicate nature of the image sensors (cooled to ~4.5 K) meant the clocking, data acquisition, etc had to be very regular and constant. Each process (4 DSPs, image array clock, user PC) had to operate in a state synchronous way. They communicated by reading shared memory. However if 2 processes tried to read or write to the same shared memory, the software would crash. So the software was very deterministic. In 5 years of operation the software never crashed and every test yielded good data. This is an example of a state synchronous concurrent system. The queued threaded systems (non realtime) software people consider to be standard fare today are not deterministic. So there is no guarantee there are not any conflicts. Usually using overly fancy patterns and over-engineered early abstractions is a serious code smell. Code is read way, way, WAY more than it is written. Simplicity is the fucking king. Keep shit straight forward. And keep shit CONSISTENT. After you finish touching a file nobody should be able to tell that you bolted on new functionality. It should blend in as if it was always there.  Knowledge of weird C++ tricks doesn't really help you in the industry. What really matters in a professional setting is quick code navigation/comprehension and good communication skills. That's it.

author: @montpierce424
text:
Nice video. Enjoyed your down-to-earth attitude.  I've been a programmer for over 30 years ago.  

ALL programming languages have their Pros and Cons.  So I don't really understand people that put down one language over another.  I've always looked at any conceived shortcoming of any language as a challenge or opportunity to improve my skills.  

To me, learning the concepts of logical programming is way more important that any specific language.  In college I enjoyed learning Every Language available at the time at the college I attended: Basic, Fortran, RPG II, COBOL, PASCAL, and a brief intro to PR1ME Mainframe Assembly.  The coding syntax of many language overlap, even though some languages have quite different architectures.  I've enjoyed learning C/C++, C#, JAVA, etc. on my own for specific job opportunities, and, just for fun I've have messed around with a few Functional Languages like F#, Haskell, Elixir, ERLANG.   Lately I've been really enjoying Assembly on X86, ARM, AVR, RISCV, and others, to support my hobbies with SBCs and stand-alone Microcontrollers.


I dislike the Arduino platform myself, but I can see it has been a great tool for hobbyist learning to program for the first time.  Probably because of my career as Embedded Systems Programmer I like writing my own bare-metal libraries rather than relying on community supplied libraries.

Thanks again for a nice video.  And I'm looking forward to watching some of your others like "Escape 'Tutorial Hell'".   😯😀😀

author: @Leo3ABPgamingTV
text:
I strongly disagree with the notion that C++ should not be a first programming language. When there is nothing to compare to, then all the "hard" and "scary" parts about C++ are just normal everyday stuff to you. And being an adept at C++ makes it so much easier to learn and understand many other programming languages. author: @donaldwycoff4154
text:
My first professional C++ contributions happened in 1990.  I've been working in C++ ever since.  I got my first ahah! moment with template-metaprogramming several years later.  STL came a bit later, then boost.  The most interesting thing I wrote was a high-frequency algorithmic trading system, all the way from a book concentrator that was cache-coherent on x64, to an algorithmic language used by traders to define new algorithms, out to the risk analysis service that judged outbound orders before they hit the market.  For that particular project, "thinflow", I was fond of saying, "I wrote the first half million lines."  In my university days (in the 80's) I was already playing with C++, but the Dean (and other students) said I was wasting my time, that ADA was going to rule, and programs would be written entirely by computers in a few years.  So now its 2024.  The voices are from different people, but they say the same sort of thing...  "C++ is old, out of date;  RUST is the future", and, "AI will be writing all the programs in a few years".  Meanwhile, I have followed my love for C++ all the way, trying to keep up on boost, on the language standard; using conservative adoption of new language features and libraries.  I hated gitlab when it came in, but now I love it.  Anyway, I say all this because this video had a lot of truth to it.  I'd only add:  if you love C++, don't give up on it.  It has been in the top 4 in the TIOBE index from the start of TIOBE.  I get paid to work in C++, C, golang and Python, and I'll say this:  go for what you love, but don't skip opportunities that come along to work in other languages.  And don't believe the baloney about other languages being "better", or "destined to rule": that's been the claim year to year for decades, and C and C++ are still at the top.  And as you get beat up by new C++ experiences, think of this: good students are the champions of the C++ language.  If you want easy, and want to write easy stuff, there's always BASIC.

LEARN TEMPLATE METAPROGRAMMING.  You won't regret it.

text: I started programming on a VIC20 in 1982 at 13 years old. Turned into a, thus far, 35 year programming career where I go to work to play and they throw lotsa money at me. Pick Python, and learn those things while working with awesome AI tools.  Pick C#, and learn them while making a neat Blazor website or a Unity game.  Pick Java, and learn them while making an Android app that you can show to your impressed family and friends.

Pick C++, and stare at a black screen for the first 3 years of your programming life.  1990s simulator-- engage!

author: @puzzud
text:
My advice for newcomers:

Prioritize making (many) small functions.

Worry less about making efficient, proper, and even bugless code.

Make variable names meaningful--stay away from abbreviations.

Write comments as outlines for what you want to do; then as you implement them, remove each comment with a call to a well named function (usually some concise form of the comment). For me, comments are usually a sign that I need to extract a function or break up a function.

Following this advice should lay the foundation for code to be manageable and improvable.

author: @SuperVertraulich
text: As a programmer who has been programming C for about 25 years, 19 of them professionally (mainly embedded) and also a few of them with C++, I have to say that this is great advice for becoming a mediocre programmer. I also keep all my source codes and the oldest ones date back to 1997/98 and when I look at them I'm annoyed that I didn't do it right straight away. The old story that many paths lead to the goal ignores the fact that many of these paths are also bad. There are plenty of opportunities to make mistakes, but adopting a clean programming style from the start is certainly not one of them. I've spent a lot of time cleaning up code from other people who just wanted to get the job done and didn't care what their code or architecture looked like. At some point, the resulting problems piled up into a huge mountain and they could no longer solve them themselves, precisely because they never really developed software but only programmed it.

author: @Investigamer
text:
I hear you man, and I think I agree with your perspective on an optimistic day.

On a less optimistic day, my advice to people "considering" programming is this: if you are young and relatively keen when it comes to education, not easily distracted or dissuaded from a challenge etc, maybe starting with C++, C# or Java isn't such a bad idea. C++ especially is still the cornerstone of so many areas of software engineering, and learning C++ puts you in a really good position because it is more challenging than a lot of the other "job ready" alternatives, so if you can get your foot in the door with C++ you've probably got a solid hobby/career ahead of you.

On the other hand, if you are just an "average joe", as in average intelligence, didn't enjoy school, not easily persuaded to sit at a computer learning and practicing for hours, didn't remotely excel in math/discrete math or some other highly logic oriented discipline, or perhaps someone who's nearing their mid 20's and never wrote code in their life (entering the age where the brain becomes less plastic) -- my general advice is try out Python. Work with Python for awhile, learn the basics, work on a starter project or try to solve a problem that is interesting to you (such as webscraping to find the 50 best rated movies this year, or making a simple discord bot).

Why do I say this? Well here are my key reasons:
- 1) Python imo is the most approachable language on the planet for the average person, I don't think many will disagree with this point. The elegant syntax, idiot-proof package manager, huge wealth of easy on the eyes documentation and supporting modules.

- 2) Being as elegant and approachable as it is, if someone is still struggling with the essentials of Python after ~6 months of study... it's tough love time, they probably aren't the type of person who will enjoy a career in programming/software engineering. Maybe it could still be a neat hobby, but if basic Python is a serious challenge after a lot of time investment.. it just isn't a line of work you're likely to be suited for. Not making a value judgement, just saying more than likely they won't enjoy the work and I would consider what their other skills are and keep options open.

- 3) If all goes well, they can move onto something a little more challenging to cut their teeth on, BUT even if they DON'T -- Python still has great job opportunities, in the sciences, in machine learning, in backend web development or server applications, hell even in desktop applications! You've probably seen the occasional techbro say Python won't get you a job, because they are angling for those outrageous 175k React jobs (that probably won't be riding high forever), but the fact remains: Python has, what, the 2nd or 3rd most job postings of any programming language at the moment? Nothing to sneeze at.

- 4) Even if you decide against employment in software development... learning Python as a normie outside the tech field is still a fantastic skill! Anything in life that is data oriented, or organization oriented, or automation oriented, etc can take advantage of somebody knowing basic Python. There are so many tasks you come across, whether its accounting, or looking up information, or cataloging, or organizing, or mass downloading, where just knowing Python allowed me to write a script in 5 minutes that saved me an hour of busy work. IMO, Python should be REQUIRED learning in schools, because it shows you enough of what "programming is" to know if you'll enjoy it, and even if you decide against being a programmer by trade, it is an exceptionally powerful skill to have in the toolbox. No static typing, no fancy compiler setup, no obnoxiously complicated packaging/build systems. You write some simple instructions in the most elegant code you've ever seen, using human recognizable data types, and you hit a "green arrow" -- presto, you just downloaded every Pink Floyd album art known to man, named and sorted. You just generated a shortlist of the 5 big stock tips from each of your favorite trading websites. You just created a discord bot that can answer common questions asked around your discord server. So many super easy things you can do, with comparatively very little effort.

So yeah, the pessimist in me assumes the bar for "average tech intelligence level" is a lot lower than we sometimes think it is, so I always recommend Python, because if it turns out you ARE ACTUALLY that smart, you'll blow through Python in no time and have another tool in the toolkit, maybe even land a sick backend job or move onto something more ambitious. But if it turns out you're not as smart as you thought you were, you still learned a language that can actually help MOST people in their day-to-day life.

author: @sethbrown1763
text:
Not claiming to be a good programmer or any kind of programmer really (it's been a few years since I wrote anything) but I agree with the sentiment.

You can only learn programming by programming.

In a sense, the compiler (or interpreter or JVM or whatever) is your teacher, not books, not videos, not mentors, not gurus, just the compiler and its error messages.

Programming is a conversation between you, your mind and the compiler. You ask a question, usually "does this work?" and it tells you "yes" or "no". 

So, it guides your mind in the right direction.

One of the best books I've ever owned, is "Debugging C" by Robert Ward. Many books teach programming, this is the only one I've found, that teaches debugging. 
This is an old book; it referencs MS-DOS and CP/M, but its approach is timeless. 

But even that book for all its suggestions, did not teach me as much as struggling with the C compiler on a daily basis. 

There's a lot to be learned from programming in C. For example, the idea that every time you can a function, you should immediately test its return value, is now so ingrained in me that I shudder to see languages that do not enforce that. (NB: C does not enforce that, either :)

Also, from C, I learned to program using a debugger constantly. Never trust my own logic, always check to see that it's returning a sensible value. 

I'm not a great programmer, I just slog through it like everyone else but I think the hard way is the best way because in the end, the real computer is between your ears.

Thanks for sharing this video!

author: @ag1211x
text:
Some C++ is good, to the extent that it helps develop your overall programming skill and understanding of computer systems. Just as OP said, "you do not have to use the language you learnt after one year."

In the meanwhile, I am sick of the advice that people give by saying "just learn it". Of course, learning anything would be beneficial than spending your time watching Netflix. However people only have limited time and energy, and you absolutely need to prioritize.

I would say learn C deeply first, and use it to understand the operating system. Try to make a tiny shell application. After that, if you want, spend another 50 hours learning the object oriented side of  C++ is a good idea. But then PAUSE. Look around. 

As C++ is getting more and more powerful, the domain to which it is the first choice of language is getting narrower and narrower.  Moreover, there are a HUGE gap between these domains and their use of C++. There are almost no applications in real world that need you to use all aspects of C++.

If you are into embedded system, you will probably use C++ as mostly C but with class. You do not even have access to STL library in most embedded platforms. If you are into gaming, then you are mostly adopting a somewhat pure object-oriented paradigm. If you are into machine learning,  then you are probably living inside a few specialized libraries (opencv2, pytorch, etc.)

Even in the same domain, say server backend, the coding principal across different companies could be vastly different. In Google, you are not allowed to use Exceptions in C++. In Tencent and Microsoft, you are basically using their flavor of C++, with all kinds of in-house middleware. For e.g. Everyone is using their own string library instead of the standard library. This simply does not happen with other programming languages.

Be smart about where you spend your time. The bottom line is that you can spend 1,000 hours in C++ and you have only scratched the surface. The skill you have developed could be pretty non-portable across companies. Having said that, there are areas where C++ is irreplaceable (applications with significant desktop GUI components). I would say after an introductory course, stop and think what domain you want to go for, instead of trying to learn everything about C++.

You may like it to start but as soon as you are working with other people in these languages, you will learn to hate them, you will spend more time in a debugger trying to find what went wrong or sitting around for hours waiting for stupidly long compiles because there's no real module system. Just don't. And look for jobs which don't use it. If a manager with zero programming experience wants to use it, get out as soon as you can.

The reason you should be looking at strong statically typed languages is that the compiler will find errors for you much more quickly, compare that to this -> after 38 years (C++) and 51 years (C) they're still trying to make the compiler find errors on compile rather than relying on external tools; trust me it was a lot worse 20 years ago and it's still not great.

author: @nakatash1977
text:
I'm sorry but C++ is an outdated language. I've been using C++ since the early 2000s, and for many years it was the only game in town if you wanted a reasonably high-level and fast language, but in the last few years several languages have challenged its dominance, — most notably Rust. Rust is slowly taking over the dominant systems language...like it or not. It's happening. Why? Because it's a next generation language. The only reason to learn C++ in 2023 is if you have to. If you need to maintain a legacy codebase. But new, large-scale projects should not use C++. There are too many pitfalls and sharp edges. It's not a viable language anymore. Please don't use it.

Edit: C is a better language than C++. When I would write personal projects back in the early 2000s, I would often find myself switching from C++ to C, because C always ran faster, but was often faster to code with too.

author: @enitalp
text:
Practice is the key. 25+ years of C++ coding since 82. Gamedev also. 
I keep everything, and I'm always ashamed of myself when I read what I wrote 6 months ago.
Because I could have the same functionality in 1/3 of the code size and faster by a factor of many digits if I took the time to rewrite it. (I take it if I landed in that code during a profile session. 😁, else way I decide on the color of the "to do" post it )
Working in C# these days(20 years of experience there also), and while I have a lot of fun with some parts of the code because there is no way to have something approaching C# reflexion, or Roslyn, to name a few, in C++. But also,  I'm in total pain trying to reproduce features like a handle system, memory pool of classes, etc. 
Features that can be done in one hour in C++ but takes weeks to perfect in C#, with some black magic help.
But I'm there for the challenge. To boldly go where no man has gone before.

But on the other side, I'm also sick of those "languages wars." 
We don't choose a language because of X or Z when working!
We don't choose a language (and he doesn't choose us either), and those who are lucky are also a pain for those who arrive after him. 😁 
Example: Gamedev is C++ because we get all the APIs from the different hardware + software companies for C++, with all the tooling in Visual Studio. 
So no, we don't choose our language or tool. Your work does. When we make tools, we use C# because, at the start, a decision was made, not by all programmers but by a few. 
In that case, making tools in C# was good; the jury is still out on every GUI choice, lol.
Ok, more and more C# is used (still, some people are under the hood in C++, making the C# code work).
A good C# game is better than an average C++ game. 
You get what the company uses or the project. You could get a 20-year-old custom C++ engine, a C++ commercial engine with LUA, C# games or tvOS games locking you in Objective C and XCode. 🤣
Don't laugh until you get on hardware with only a C compiler. 

Just be curious, learn, "question" everything, learn your battle, and be an agent of change.
The time for the all-knowing entity/person is gone; teams rely on crowd work, r&d, knowledge, etc...
Teams act as a swarm for any problem or task. Because the solution is always the sum of the knowledge. Master one and be curious about the others.

text:
This video was really useful for me at this specific point in my life! I have been interested in learning c++ for years, and I have been kinda hopping in and out of learning it for years, and just last month I really started sinking my teeth into it again and something just clicked, and so much of it made more sense than it ever has. I understand that I am inexperienced, and that’s why I am looking for help. I don’t know how to ask the questions because of my lack of experience.

I’m not even trying to do this as a career it’s just for fun, so I shouldn’t stress so much about being an expert and making everything the “right” way.

author: @timkin4190
text:
I first started programming in C++ in the early 90s... (92 or 93 iirc)... but by then I'd already learned, used and put aside about 10 other languages ( started programming in 1981). I used it professionally for 25 years, studied it's inner workings and  taught it at University for many years (among other languages). About 5 years ago, when giving the welcome speech to the commencing 1st year computing students, I was asked how many languages an undergrad should learn... rather than give a definitive answer, I counted up the number of languages I had learned, used for at least 1 year professionally, then set aside... when I passed 35 I stopped counting (you can figure I must have used many languages concurrently)... several languages though I kept coming back to, as I could get most tasks done using one of 5 languages... C++ was in this set of 5.

My advice to anyone wanting a career that involves programming... keep learning new languages, even the ones that other people find hard to learn or try to dissuade you from learning. Don't take their word for it. Find out for yourself whether the language is useful to you (for the jobs you need/want to do and the way you think and work as a programmer)). The more languages you learn, the broader your understanding of programming will be and this will, in most cases, make you a better programmer.

author: @xcoder1122
text:
I've been programming out of passion since 4th grade, did it as a hobby throughout my school years, as a vacation job, as a side job to earn something during my college years and have been doing it full-time for over 20 years and here's my tip for new programmers: Hands off C++! 

No matter what the problem is, C++ is never the best solution for it. Don't do this language to yourselves. If it is low level and simple, then you can fall back to C, but as soon as C is not suitable for it anymore, C++ is even less. C++ has taken all of C's flaws, made some of them worse, and then thrown a bunch of incoherent concepts on top to create a complete mess of language features, none of which are really implemented correctly, coherent, or meaningfully in C++. 

There's a reason why the Linux kernel still doesn't contain a single line of C++ code, and why its developers are more willing to switch from C to Rust than to even consider C++. Where it is about readable, clean code that follows sensible language concepts, C++ is completely out of place and where it is only about raw performance, one falls back on C, GPU shader, OpenCL or even assembler.

"Actually I made up the term object-oriented, and I can tell you I did not have C++ in mind."
- Alan Kay

Quite often you read the advice: "There's absolutely nothing wrong with C++ if you use a small subset of it" but that's moronic. If a language is so bad, that you must restrict yourself to a subset of it to get a useful language, stop using that language immediately.

If you search online for "Why C++ Sucks", you find multiple good articles that all totally make sense as they present valid arguments how C++ messed up something that most other languages got right. Sure, every language may have its flaws but none of them tops C++. Also almost nobody uses even half of the language features in practice but that's again a bad sign as it means the language is completely overloaded with ideas of things that one may like to use one day. C++ is as far away from KISS most of the time as things can get.

I get one to three programmer job offers a week, guess how many of these are for C++? None! I've not seen a single one for C++ in maybe a year. C, Java, Go, Ruby, Python, C#, Rust, Swift, PHP, Objective-C, TypeScript/JS, Perl, Scala, even Kotlin, but no C++. Not saying that C++ programmers aren't needed in the industry but apparently there are more than enough of them to easily fill all open positions, as head hunters seem not to desperately look for those. So if you want to work as a C++ programmer, you will face lots of competition, not a good starting position for salary negotiations or getting your dream position. Mainly the game dev industry loves C++ and they are known to pay poorly.

author: @L1ghtOn3
text:
Well said.👍🏽

I see a lot of "stay away" from C/C++ on the internet, and my guess is that they are probably something web devs who don't really need it, but have tried it, then just thought, nope too much, I can just use JS/TS etc.

Personally I started at University 12 years ago doing Assembly/C/C++/Verilog/Matlab in my Electrical and Electronic Degree and it was a bit if a shock tbh, wasn't really expecting programming coming from a College Electrical Engineering course that I had no Electronics experience, especially Digital and what comes with that. 

Over the first couple of years I barely scraped the courses on Digital and Programming, because I felt the course was too broad and the Computer Science guys seemed to have a better gelled together course and more practical, like using the Unix/Linux suite for their extra labs and coursework and picking up a better understanding in extra programming classes we just never had, but had our own extra classes instead.

Looking back now I should have switched at the start to CS as it would have helped in the long run, but I guess I knew my Electrical Engineering from College and it helped me through a difficult 1st year but felt to Frankenstein a course, Jack of all trades, master of none.

During my time there, I thought when I would leave I would do microcontrollers using PIC Assembly, as I took to that more than C/C++/Verilog/Matlab, but after my 3rd year I started learning Java at home for Android as I took a couple of years out to help my family due to health issues and learning Java/Android I preferred that to what I was learning at Uni, things like FPGAs/ Robotics/ DSP/Control Systems/Embedded Systems etc., was far too dry for me abd Android was a breath of fresh air. I also didn't mind C++, but it was used less than the others unfortunately.

I then learned some HTML/CSS/ JS and quite liked that, I started to see I was more visual and liked animating things and that were interactive, this lead me to do a small game on Android in Java and that opened the door to looking at game Engines like Unity/Unreal etc., I got into C#, being similar to Java/C++ with Garbage Collection for the memory as most know and that suited me much better, as I always had a problem, especially at the start with *pointers.

I went bk to University not too interested in the course, but wanted to finish what I had started, I finally finished University with a hobble, but my focus was primarily on games now and Unity/C# doing 2D Android games, I also  tried Unreal with Blueprints/C++, but I found I took to C# better, although Unreal left a good impression for the future. 

I built a 2D space shooter, but that never went far, so decided to get a Google Daydream for VR development and go all in on that...oh what a mistake that was! Not only did Google stop selling the headset months after I bought it, but near the end of the app I was creating, they stopped people from selling/buying inside the headset and therefore the Daydream was finally dead and my heart sank after a ~year of Development. 
I had been doing some 3D learning for Android along the way mainly a 3P adventure game, but Unity was going through transistion after 2019.3 and there were problems going forward like no testing on the Remote5 using the ADB and new Input System which I had to change up and redo a lot of the UI/Player controls etc., so yeah my luck was at an all time low, I went bk to Unreal knowing 5 was coming soon, so statred a 3D FPS on that, spent a few months learning the SFX and more blueprints and a little more Unreal C++, then went bk to Unity once the Remote5 was working...~9 months later! I now find myself having had so many problems trying to finish my 3D android game and now wishing I had just finished the 3D FPS on Unreal!

So many lessons I've learned in 12 years and I feel I still have a ways to go before being really proficient in at least 1 language. I'm close with C#, but will probably have to do a .Net project to smooth the corners and feel "sure" I'm  up to par and If I choose another language it will be C++ for Unreal Engine 5 going forward, once my 3D Android game is finished this year...hopefully 😅

But overall to anyone starting out, what this guy says is correct, just open up your IDE/ Text Editor of choice and start plugging away, you might not know what you want to do right away, like myself going through half a dozen disciplines first before I found my calling. 
Just learn the basics first and then branch out, there is also nothing wrong with learning C or C++ first, if anything they will help you understand the machine better and with other languages moving forward if you choose to do so.

If I could start again, I would honestly start with HTML/CSS/JS, as it was visually pleasing, but that's my personal  preference, then try something like Java for Android, then C/C++ to understand the machine better. 
Some will say start with Python and that is also fine, it's just preference and then figuring out what you want to do moving forward. 
But if you want the best head start then start with Assembly/C/C++ and learn your Digital Logic and Design, Computer Architecture and CS topics, plus getting a firm grip on the Command Line/Shell, OS depending like cmd/Powershell for Windows or Terminal using Zsh/Bash for Mac/Linux. Nowadays Windows has their own "Terminal" that WSL2 can run a Linux distro like Ubuntu.

Happy programming to older and newer devs. All the best and good luck for the future. ✌🏽👍🏽

author: @keithnicholas
text: been doing C++ for 30+ years, while I still do some things in C or C++,  mostly do things in C# now ( for 20+ years).    C++ wouldn't be my recommendation for beginners, you can still learn it as a beginner, nearly every language trips new people up because of syntax, C++ syntax tends to trip people up more than others so it can be a bit more frustrating.    What I see the most is beginners often almost get things right, but syntax issues make them doubt themselves and they think they are completely wrong.    However, today with the likes of chatGPT, learning how to code is a LOT better.   One thing I see with people trying to make games is they often don't really understand the language too well, they get a working subset going, then they hit some problem, or foudn some code online, and they don't really understand how the language feature works, they often realize they don't properly understand but try to muddle through.  If you find yourself in this situation, stop trying to learn in your game, go spawn a new throwaway project ( just console/terminal) and work out how the language features works.    The other piece of advice is when finding resources to learn,  go to the official documentation for the language first, many languages have really good documentation (some don't).   If the documentation doesn't quite get you over the line, then go look for tutorials.  Then come back and read the documentation again.  Often I see this done backwards and people go to tutorials, and they only get spoon fed some of the information, then they have troubles when they try to use it themselves because they didn't quite get the full picture.  Books tend to be a lot better, more time and effort tend to get put into those.  But always go back to the official documentation and check your understanding with it.  Run little experiments in throwaway projects, then you should be better prepared to use it in your projects.   I've been programming 40+ years and I still run lots and lots of little throwaway experiments.

author: @johanngambolputty5351
text:
Ever since I found out you can do `for(auto item: items)` almost like `for item in items` like in python/rust, the language has felt so much lighter. And actually, the whole `Object object(args);` pattern for construction is quite neat. I actually think the syntax of the language itself is fine, there's a reason so many languages just copied most of it verbatim, its just (I think) a lot of c++ libraries can be quite boiler-platey, and don't necessarily come with some slimmer convenience functions. It doesn't have a package manager, and even though you can get libs from your OSs package manager, you may end up having to fiddle with header or shared object paths, which means you also have to start thinking about a compiler and linker, in the same time as getting to grips with everything else. But I guess as long as you focus on just making console applications with just standard libs to begin with, and keep all your code in a single file, it might be pretty painless.

For getting started at least, I still think an interactive interpreter/REPL with something like python, where you can perform live surgery on your code (without having to learn a separate debugger) is probably best. The main two challenges I see for beginners learning c++ are:

1. C++ is a failed abstraction. To drive a car you don’t need to have precise knowledge of how a combustion engine works. To program in c++, even at base level, you need to have an idea of how memory works, how the cpu works, and ideally knowledge of asm.

2. Many c++ programmers are in love with complexity for the sake of complexity. There is real elitism around some c++ programmers who want to be the next Carmak. The only thing they manage is to generate hyper complex code which only they can understand. Avoid them. Avoid for instance  all boost libs altogether as a beginner.

author: @caschque7242
text:
I would divide your argument into two main aspects, each with its own significance. The first aspect is the mindset of embracing mistakes as valuable learning opportunities, rather than striving for perfection. I strongly believe that writing code, reflecting on it, and learning from the process is far more effective than fixating on a single problem for hours on end. It's easy to become demotivated in such situations, which ultimately hinders progress and achievement. You could summarise this as the "Just do it" mindset/procrastinate less.

The second aspect is the importance of taking some time to make informed decisions, especially when it comes to selecting a programming language for a project. I've found that investing a little effort upfront, researching and gathering information, can save a great deal of trouble down the road. Choosing a language that aligns with the specific needs of real-world scenarios is crucial, as it can prevent unnecessary challenges and frustrations.

In summary, I would encourage individuals to strike a balance between research and action. Reading a few Reddit threads can provide valuable insights. However, it's also essential not to get too caught up in the pursuit of finding the "perfect" language. The initial research should guide you away from making glaringly incorrect decisions, allowing you to proceed with confidence and enthusiasm.

PS: If you would bring this in the context of todays standards, there are those that keep just trying to figure out what is the right tool, when in actuality you should focus more on the actual content and not the tool itself. This is a common problem not only in programming. I really understand what you mean but I would advise to differentiate a bit more.

author: @xybersurfer
text:
i disagree. the problem with C++ is not so much the language itself. the problem with C++ is the limited eco-system. you can't really do web development in C++, because all the new tooling and libraries are created in other more high level languages. there are plenty of other examples where the C++ eco-system is extremely lacking (Mobile App development?). web development and mobile apps alone are already such a huge part of the modern world. that's really where the problem lies and what makes C++ difficult.

but the other way around you do sometimes see more high level languages being used for more low level tasks (like embedded and game development). if you stick to C++, then you get limited exposure to the types of programming you do. i used to program in C++ myself, but i'm much happier with the exposure i'm now getting in C#, some JavaScript but also in Functional Programming languages. it makes me more useful outside of work. it's really interesting how the problems change and become clearer. not focusing too much on doing things the right way as you mentioned, is important. but there is more time to think about doing things the right way, with more high level languages because it really pays off in having to do less work and having fewer bugs because there is less code and memory safety.

i think it takes having been on both sides for a while to see this.

author: @floatoss
text:
I have learnt C in the first 2 semesters of my uni. We then were introduced to C++ in the OOP sense in our 4th semester this year, and dude I just happen to love C++. I initially just started out being frustrated knowing why we need to put the ‘std::’ and what even that meant for the input / output statements. What even the using namespace meant, and so on. I got very tired, mainly because I couldn’t find the right resources online. But after a while, finding the proper resources was very awarding, and I started to appreciate the language even more. 

Just yesterday, I got to know about ‘converting constructors’, and after having literally spent 1 hour to completely understand it, I was totally amazed. It takes a lot of effort, yes. But I think that is the only point of such low- level programming languages. I also am learning python currently, and yeah I hate it to say the least. I love that there is very little - no abstraction in terms of software for C++.

I would only ask people to learn cpp, it has the sense to in-still and embrace logical reasoning in my opinion. Use ChatGPT, learncpp.com, Bjarne’s books and I think anyone would be able to appreciate it. It’s just that it requires a lot of our time and efforts, and of course you need to be curious :) I just learn it, dig deep to satisfy my curiosity, and once I learn it, the feeling of knowing what every statement means, makes me just dig deeper haha.

text:
I'm writing C++ for roughly 6 years. 

If I have one advice to give to anyone  who wants to learn it : Don't use Intellisense , or any syntax checker... 
Write your code carefully without relying on automatic syntax checks, and discover your mistakes using the compiler . 
For two reasons : 
First : You need to learn how to read and interpret the compiler's errors and warnings (also , for warnings : enable everything ... your code shouldn't raise a compiler warning) 
It's easy to interpret what the compiler is telling you when it informs you that you have been using a double instead of an int as a function argument. 
But when you are using something more advanced , like templates , your compiler can become very verbose when you make a mistake and it fails a substitution. 

Second : Having intellisense mark your mistakes makes you too reliant on it , and sloppy ... you start writing code without paying much attention to what you are doing.

Unfortunately, you will need to learn about it eventually if you plan on joining the industry, but delay it for as long as possible.

text:
I agree. I dislike when people say, "Do not start with C or C++ because they are too difficult to learn." This statement is simply unfounded. Every programming language has been created for specific reasons and has its own appropriate areas of application. However, most modern languages overwhelm beginners with complex keywords and object-oriented programming (OOP) concepts that they may not yet be familiar with.

In my opinion, if you genuinely want to dive into coding, it is best to begin with C and gradually progress until you can write proficient procedural programming code. Afterward, you can transition to C++ and explore OOP concepts and its big advanced std.

Also I wanted to share, "Tell, don't ask". It's such a great principle both in OOP and in real life. It helps maintain encapsulation and abstraction in life as well, whether you're in charge of others or being driven around by superiors. Telling your current state, or variable, or expected Action to others is a great way to avoid issues like segfault when you ask someone to do something because you or they need to assume something that wasn't explicitly passed. You also prevent issues where you need to account for ALL different possible states for every person you talk to, ambiguous states, or not even getting what you expect because asking for something puts you at the mercy of what the other side returns, and you need to process it. If you tell, then they will do the necessary that they can do.

author: @itabiritomg
text:
nobody ever expected java to kill c++!
Java will never fully replace C++ because it operates at a higher level of abstraction, relying on the Java Virtual Machine, which isolates it from direct hardware access and low-level system control. In contrast, C++ allows developers to manage memory manually, interact directly with hardware, and build critical components like operating system kernels, device drivers, and high-performance engines such as Unreal Engine. These capabilities require deterministic performance and fine-grained control that Java, with its garbage collection and runtime overhead, cannot consistently provide, making C++ indispensable for systems programming and performance-critical applications.
And this is why nobody ever expected java to kill c++!

author: @fyu1945
text:
Ugh this comment section is painful to read.

First of all, I can't imagine how someone in the 90s could seriously think Java would kill C++. Even if it hadn't run on a VM it still didn't have any low level access or abilty to minupulate simple non-OOP data except for some basic typse like ints and floats. And this wasn't 2025 with our new and shiny CPUs and GPUs. This was 90s, where there were still games being written in assembly. Java was just completely not for the job, C++ was doing.

And this is important, when we talk about "killing a language" in order for it to become obsolete, there has to be a language that can do everything C++ can and bring enough new things to the table, that it will be cost-effective to actually replace it.

Rust, unlike Java, actually can do everything a C++ can. On top of it, it's a modern language, without decades of backwards compatibility bs baggage that C++ inevitably acquired. It's memory-safe by default, thanks to the borrow checker, but let's remember, this is actually just RAII stolen from C++ itself. Only in Rust, it's in every library and program by default.

The only thing that Rust doesn't have is OOP, but that's on purpose, cause over the years the industry realized that it's not as good as we previously thought. Instead, Rust keeps the good part - interfaces (called traits) with dynamic dispatch done slightly differently than C++ with it's own benefits and draw backs.

And most importanly, if you do need to dabble in memory directly, you can use the unsafe keyword to dereference a raw pointer and have every single superpower C++ has. As a bonus, if you do end up with a memory bug, you know exactly were to grep for, unlke in C++ where a memory bug can appear anywhere.

So, Rust can do everything a C++ can. It can do it much more safely. There aren't 5 different ways to do the same thing, of which 3 were declared deprecated by the community 20 years ago. And on top of it, it brings years many of industry's developments, like Algebraic Data Types, Errors as values (which contrary to some commenters is good, because not only can exceptions get unhandled, resulting in a runtime error, but also many code bases can't afford the additional performance cost that exceptions bring) and many more.

With that, is this enough to kill C++? No.

First of all, when people talk about "killing C++" it doesn't mean that no one will use C++. Legacy code bases exist everywhere, and people still program in Cobol, Fortran and PHP. There's no way, any language, even a divine hypothetical perfect one could make C++ just disapear.

When talking about killing a language, what most mean is to make the Rust, in this case, a better alternative to C++ when starting a new project. This is much easier, but still incredibely difficult task, especially with C++.

Those who doubt Rust and say things like "It's been ten years and I still don't see it" forget just how monumental C++ ecosystem is. For decades it was the only low-level language that provided some higher level ergonomics. Hundreds of thousands of libraries were made with this language and NO. Rust is not going to replace it in a fucking decade. Expecting that is just being incredibely dishonest.

However, Rust is steadily getting larger. Today it's ready for production and many giants from sillicon valley are already implementing it. Linux is implementing it. Startups are implementing it. It's ready NOW. It has the most enthusiastic community out of any language and it's good. The only reason the Rust doubters are so vocal about it is that they heard about it and that's only, because Rust community is ready for this discussion, unlike other alternatives.

Of course, it's important to ask, should we even kill C++? Can't it just stay? I believe yes, we should. Not because I hate it, in fact I respect this language immensly. But it is unsafe. Even with the newest safety features, it doesn't really matter, cause the ecosystem is already set in stone. And it is old. We as developers and language creators learned a lot about designing programming languages. One only has compare Kotlin code with Java code to see this. We know what works and what doesn't. And unfortunately C++ has a lot of bad things in it, that were piled up over the years. No ammount of versions will fix that. So perhaps, it's time to let it rest for legacy code and start writing with a language that's cleaner and safer. That's of course just my opinion.

Variables on the stack is not static memory. Static memory is for variables that are either global variables declared outside any function or variables inside functions declared as static (like "static int x"). Those aren't allocated on the stack but in a different memory area set aside for all the static and global variables. Technically there are two areas for static/global variables, the data segment for initialized variables and the bss segment (which is filled with zeros) for uninitialized ones. They are located towards the bottom of the memory map just above the text segment which contains all the code and is the lowest segment.

Variables on the stack are called automatic variables and there is actually a keyword "auto" you can use to declare them but auto is the default so "int x" actually means "auto int x" in contrast to "static int x" but you'll never see auto in any actual code.

Therefore it only becomes a pointer when you intend it to, even if it's not used, and even if it's pointing to an invalid address, because it's not a pointer at all, it's just a number, and the rest is you arbitrarily pretending otherwise.

Using something in an abstract fashion, meaning you pretend a thing is something beyond its physical state, and calling it accordingly, is solely based on your intent and imagination.

Anything beyond the on/off state of individual bits, like numbers or even calling the on/off state 1/0, is abstraction to some degree. Most functionality isn't really there before you intend it to, either directly or on behalf of the compiler, unless it exists as a distinct purpose-built function on the die; even then we define its output abstractly and use it as such, but the underlying physical function wouldn't be an abstraction.

author: @ako-d2m
text:
In the C language spec declaration is in this format: [type] [declarators list] where [declarators list] is a list of declarators. Valid declarators include are [identifier], ([declarator]), *[declarator], [declarator](), or [declarator][[constant expression]]. That is to say - the * is part of the declarator, NOT part of the type - BUT neither is it part of the identifier. Here's the important note: functions are also declared using declarators; using the format [[declarator]([parameter list]). That is to say; "int a()" is a valid function or variable declaration. A declarator means "when you see this construct, it will give the specified type".

So what's the confusion with *? Some people incorrectly attach it to the type. From a language perspective it is part of the declarator, not the type. This will cause issues in a few cases;
int (*foo)(); <- impossible to understand this if you have the mindset * is part of the type!
int* a, b; <- in this example a is a pointer, but b is an int!

Take your time to understand what "int *a" actually means; it means if you deference a you get an integer. "Customer *user" means if you dereference user you get a Customer. It does not mean the type of user is a pointer to Customer. 

Eg:
int a = 0; // a is an integer with value 0
int *pa = &a; // dereferencing pa yields an int, point it to the address of a
*pa = 1; // dereference pa (follow the address back to a) and set the value to 1

See the pattern? "*pa" = "dereference pa". Now you can see how simple it really is. Eg; int *(*(*pa)(int))[10]; = dereferencing pa yields a function that takes an int as an argument that returns a pointer to an array of 10 pointers to ints. int *(*pa())() = pa can be dereferenced to yield a function that takes no args and returns a pointer to a function that returns an int.

It says, "Milk not here. Go to 121 Main St." Program moves onto that address and finds the milk.

A pointer to a pointer, then, would be like getting to 121 Main St. and finding yet another card that says, "Milk not here. Go to 171 Main St."

Hope this helps. :)

author: @Muttisuri
text:
To be completely honest, I think I only started understanding pointers after playing with rust.
And I think I got it because the rust stuff is cleaver, they don't call it a pointer they use the word “reference” and somehow I think that made it easier for me. For usage, the fact that the pointer is “just a number” only makes it more confusing at the first approach (I know it's useful for incrementing, but that to me at the beginning is confusing questions).
And since &x is a “reference” to x I can then think of it at a more conceptual level. That added with the whole borrow checker thing of only one mutable reference allowed me to think in “references” not values without worrying about the technical details of hex numbers. Since I've seen people trying to learn C without having seen hex numbers before.

On the “incrementing issue” for me, it always caused some confusion due to the “assumption” that things can certainly be found by incrementing the pointer. I know that's true for arrays since they are defined by being contiguous in memory, but at the beginning you will likely think of them closer to lists.
Paradoxically, I think the more “complicated” and abstract language is better to teach. So you are first thinking of the logic of the program, and when you get that you can use it to anchor your newly acquired knowledge of the computer's internals.

EDIT: Also the usage of “reference” makes the term dereference be clearer, at least to me.


TL;DR I think we should stop using the word pointers and use the more descriptive word “reference”

text:
I've been programming UNIX C since i was 13 - I'm 39 - and I 'get got' still to this day especially when there's more than one dereference (e.g. void **, void ***, etc) or sometimes I ignore the compiler doing pointer arithmetic for me and am then rewarded with difficult to squash bugs. It was the third language I learned after BASIC and TCL, but was the first I tried to actually understand beyond syntax and best practices. Two things I recommend to help anyone looking to understand pointers:


1) Read the pointers chapter in the 1994 book "Expert C Programming: Deep C Secrets" by Solaris kernel *AND* compiler team member Peter van der Linden. Actually read the whole book. It's easily the most entertaining book on programming I've ever read. I return to it every few years. I wish he'd write a second edition!

2) Learn the basics of assembly language and the very essence of pointers and why they are what they are will become clear. The very basis and semantics of core operations in C are closer to Assembly than many realize. A basic understanding of how compilers work helps as well.


It may seem daunting at first but it's not just in the beginning. It's forever. C gives you not just enough rope to hang yourself but also to hang your family, the neighborhood, the town and more. But I still regularly program in C for many projects that aren't surface level apps because of the familiarity and the power I have. Then again most of my programming is at the kernel level or systems programming on *NIX (mostly Linux) but, hey. Understanding C and pointers will help you understand what is going on 'behind the scenes' when you write in higher level programming and scripting languages. After all the compiler or interpreter for your language of choice is probably written in C.

text:
I remember working with pointers around 40 odd years ago at college. At the time we were being taught on Motorola microcontroller evaluation boards using assembler, even down to working on with the machine code directly, i.e no use or access to highly abstracted languages like C etc;

The thing I remember from the time is that having a grasp how the memory in the device your working on helps visualise how pointing works in code and more importantly *WHY* pointers are used.

Simplifying the concept by abstracting it to an analogy helped me in the initial learning process. Visualising the devices memory as a street with houses as if boxes to which to deliver to and collect from is a good start. Then from there on visualising a delivery method (mail person) to go to and from from house numbers along the street is also useful. A knowledge of what a stack is and how it works is also useful at this stage.

Else, it's just a process of repeatedly practising not only the principle of pointers but also going over implementing them in code to achieve a task (purpose). Then build the experience by working with ever more complex problems/tasks on each iteration of learning.

That all said, although the person who presented this pointer concept is no doubt an accomplished programmer in his field, I felt this presentation didn't quite convey the principles of pointers as cleanly as I'd learnt it decades ago. However,.I thought the use of English to translate syntax an excellent approach to help less experienced students grasp syntax and semantics.

When you pass by value to a function: 
The changes done to the variables inside the function doesn't affect the real variable (unless we accept it back). 

When you pass by reference to a function: 
Since the parameter refers to the same variable being passed, any changes made inside the function will affect the real variable as well 

In modern languages like js, normal variables are passed by value and arrays etc are passed by reference. This is why we can edit the array in a function and the changes can be seen on the real array.

text_clean: Very good video. Th key points here are passing by value vs passing by reference. Passing a regular variable foo(x) copies the value of x, whereas foo(&x) passes x by reference by giving a memory address. & is simply used to get the address of a variable which essentially gives you a pointer. A pointer is just a memory address. If you need a reference you can pass a memory address of a variable using & or you can pass a pointer. A pointers value is a memory address. Using & on a pointer returns the memory address that the pointer (memory address) is stored at. So: Int *x = new int(5); Int address_of_address = &x; Address of address contains a memory address, whose value contains a pointer (which is a memory address), which contains the value 5. So address of address contains the memory location of that pointer on the stack. The visual of the table with the address on one side and the value on the other side is how you have to picture it. Just ask yourself are you accessing the right side or the left side?

author: @dr_jaymz
text:
I think the issue has always been squarely down to the way they are used in c.  You cannot intuitively infer what a * or & means if they used terms like addressof instead people wouldn't get so confused.  But its like that because only a few ascii symbols were available at the time and so that is the way that it is.  If you start by programming a simple micro controller using assembly its gets hard quickly, you basically need a higher level language to take care of branching and addressing memory - when you come at it from that angle it makes 100% sense to the point where you almost invent the need yourself - only to find c has your back. 
If you don't use c at least monthly you forget the syntax and thats when we get into the stabbing * or & in because we know its one of them of some form.
Efficient code uses pointers because its much faster to point  or reference  data than to keep moving it.  The downside is that since an address is just a number you can very easily point to memory that isn't what you intended.  Even the best programmers can easily get caught by an edge case - so there's a trade off between efficient and safe code - i.e. you can spend 20 instructions checking the bounds and 1 instruction copying data to be safe but thats inefficient, so it depends on what your doing.
By far the largest confusion for students are strings, char arrays, pointers to, const char arrays and when and which to use - discussion for another day.

The answer comes down to the context but my students don't have sufficient experience to be able to fully grasp the context yet.

# define addressOf(x) &x
# define valueAt(x) *x

hide the macros from the students, and then introduce these pointer concepts by using "the built-in functions addressOf and valueAt" at first before I reveal to them the ugly truth. Here's hoping it helps some. I also try and pass this video along to them in case hearing the same thing but in a different voice helps.

author: @BitwiseMobile
text: The way I explain it is that your house is a thing, and object, an instance of something.  Your street address tells people where to find that instance if they need to.  Pointers are the same as a street address.  Anyway, I taught myself x86 assembler when I was 13 using DOS Debug command (it allowed you to disassemble programs and even enter in your own assembly to execute).  In assembly everything is a pointer.  There isn't a concept of an "object" in assembly.  You have numbers and that's pretty much it in terms of data.  Those numbers are either immediate, or they have an address associated with them.  Later when I was in university they taught Pascal.  This was in the early 90s - Java was just in it's infancy, and Python wasn't being considered as a serious teaching language yet - so they taught Pascal and C in university.  Anyway, the entire class just fell on it's knees when it came to the section on pointers.  I breezed right through that stuff though.  It was intuitive to me because of my early exposure to assembly.  People still struggled in my C classes, but C is even more intuitive when it comes to pointers.  It's closer to assember (one of the original goals K&R hand in mind when porting B to C), so pointers in C/C++ just make sense if you have any experience with assembler.

Explaining the rest should be straight-forward. And, more importantly, the meaning of postbox number to computer address is understood. The postbox letter makes it clear how an address can be data as the address of any variable.

author: @ABaumstumpf
text:
3:45 - wait wait wait - "when an asterisk is placed next to a type it modifies the type" no.
That is wrong. The asterisk does not modify the preceding type but the following declaration. Yes, that makes a big difference:

int* a,b;
What you said would mean that we are declaring integer-pointers "a" and "b". 
But in reality what is going on is:
int *a, b;
A pointer "a" that points to integers and an integer "b". The asterisk binds to the name of the variable.

For your explanation of what "int *px = &x" - why so complicated?
it becomes much easier to understand if you split that into the 2 parts it is.
"int *px" - declare "px" to be a pointer to an integer.
"px = &x" - store the address of "x" in the variable "px".

with "int x = *px" it is the same - the '*' simply tells us that px is pointing towards something. We do not care what the value of "px" is - we want to know what it points towards.
So this is "the thing that px points to - take that and assign that value to y".

5:51 "by doing this we can pass around x by reference instead of value" and this is just flat out WRONG:
No, "px" is a pointer - those are something different from a reference. A Pointer is its own thing - it takes up memory and holds a value( the address of what it is pointing to), and you can modify it.
In Contrast to that a reference is nothing but a label - it does not have a place in memory, it does not have its own value. Instead it is a way to speak about another already existing object. It is basically a nickname - it allows you to refer to something that already exists.


A big problem for beginner programmers is that in C(++) many things have multiple meanings.
You see a '*' and it can be one of multiple things - multiplication, pointer-to-member, declaration of a pointer, derefrencing a pointer. 
The '&' also has multiple meanings: declare a reference to a variable, take the address of a variable, take an argument by reference, a bitwise operator, a boolean operator, forwarding reference, r-value reference.

it is best to just look at how they are named - "pointer" - obviously it is pointing to something. And in C(++) that something usually has a type (you want to know if you are dealing with a whole number, a letter, or a chessboard). And as you can describe the type of the pointing thing you can also point to that - so a pointer-to-a-pointer.
In general pointers have good descriptions in most introductory books, but horrible to outright false descriptions in Youtube "learn it in 1 hour" style crap videos.

author: @hiTocopter
text:
And if you don't get it, be aware that most languages out there do away with the concept of direct memory management for the exact reason that it's a really difficult thing to grasp, and more importantly, master. They create systems that handle memory for you. Even in C++ (Hello Unreal). These systems, called "garbage collectors", are becoming incredibly sophisticated and are in many cases just as efficient as manual memory management. If you are a beginner, chances are they're way better at wrangling memory than you are.

I.e. if you aren't struggling with pointers, you're doing something wrong.

I don't like how you didn't touch on "declaration reflects use" at all.
It says that the * in int * px is not "turn the type into a pointer type", but still a "dereference px", just like in a regular expression. Look how C considers "int (*px)" to be valid and equivalent to "int * px".

This way of thinking is backwards to many people but it is crucial to understand more complex type declarations such as function pointers (that also pass around function pointers, maybe). This one rule, combined with operator precedence rules, can be used instead of having to memorize dozens of special cases like the order of dimensions in multidimensional arrays or the spiral clockwise rule.

author: @SuperSmashDolls
text:
The fun thing about C is that it actually has three layers of "wtf, pointers" associated with it.

The first layer, which this video tackles, is just the basic syntax and concepts that C does a poor job of explaining.

The second layer is why Rust was invented - dealing with pointers overwriting things they shouldn't in unsafe operations. You need to manually track ownership and borrowing, or use a language

And the third layer is what happens why you do those unsafe operations - you break your compiler, because it turns out the C spec writers *don't know what pointers are, either*. Plenty of optimizations don't work together or break if you cast pointers, and then we learn something new about what pointers are or aren't by debugging infuriating miscompiles that will add new rules onto the second layer.

author: @jeffspaulding9834
text:
Back in the day when I was learning this concept, what helped me was the realization that function calls in C always copy the value of their arguments.

In other words, if you call do_something(x), it will copy the value of x into the function you're calling.  The function doesn't know about the variable x.

In a lot of cases we want to change the values of the variables we're passing into functions, so we pass pointers.  The value of the pointer is the address of the variable we want to change, so the function receives the pointer just fine and can use that to modify the value of the variable.

Arrays get a bit strange because of the "helpful" automatic pointer conversion.  If you have the the array y[] and you pass it to a function like so: do_something(y), it'll pass a pointer to the first element of the array.  There's all kinds of other weirdness regarding passing arrays, though, and I personally consider this a misfeature.

C++ muddies this up a bit with references - they're pointers under the hood, but the syntax makes them look like they're not.

C types reflect usage. That is why I think it is a bad mental model to think of `int* x` as an int-pointer named x. Instead, group it like this: `int *x`. That mental model also works nicely with function declarations. `int foo()` means that the expression `foo()` is an `int`.
But, C syntax is really gruesome, no wonder nobody wants to implement parsers for C. Luckily, most newer languages have learned from that. There is not excuse for having such a badly designed language anymore.

author: @BigIN0
text:
Pointers are not about code structure. Pointers are about memory usage. Do you really want for the passed data to a function to be copied to the memory allocated for that function? I hope you don't. That passed data can be a structure or an object. In that case it would be huge. Instead of passing the data around and be copied many time for that reason, we instead pass/share the information, where that data can be found.
You can compare that system to a library (not in programming sense). Not every library has to have every book in existence. A library can have some books and can request/borrow books from other libraries if the clients need them. This example translated to program: an object has some data and can request other data it has reference/pointer to.

text:
I need to start this comment with backstory. I learned programming for the first time back in 2008 when I was around 13, starting with HTML, a bit of PHP and Java. author: @telephrag
text:
Ok, I have couple gripes with this video.
1) Don't declare  "using namespace std;" globally. It can cause ambiguities. 
2) std::unique_ptr doesn't do what you say. Firstly, raw pointer is simply a variable that contains address to data of a certain type. int*, for example, points to date with type of int, char* to data with type of char, etc... std::unique_ptr is a wrapper over raw pointer that is deallocated on stack (at the end of {} block). When end of the {} block is reached destructor of class std::unique_ptr is being called which in turn calls destructor of an object the std::unique_ptr pointer was pointing at. When it comes to raw pointer only the variable that contains the address would be deallocated while data at said address would remain with no reference to access it (provided that data was created with "new" and assigned to pointer or created outside of this {} block).

Now think of ICopyable in C#. Now imagine that this property is explicitly deleted inside std::unique_ptr class. That means that the pointer can no longer be passed by copy into anything thus guaranteeing that one and only one reference to given piece of data exists. If you still want to pass it around you can use std::move but it will null the pointer at place where you passed it from.

Alternatively if you want to pass pointer to data around you can use std::shared_ptr which again is wrapper over raw pointer but it can be copied and atomically counts the amount of references to data across the program. Once the count reaches zero data is being deallocated.

Now think of ICopyable in C#. Now imagine that this property is explicitly deleted inside std::unique_ptr class. That means that the pointer can no longer be passed by copy into anything thus guaranteeing that one and only one reference to given piece of data exists. If you still want to pass it around you can use std::move but it will null the pointer at place where you passed it from. Alternatively if you want to pass pointer to data around you can use std::shared_ptr which again is wrapper over raw pointer but it can be copied and atomically counts the amount of references to data across the program. author: @kirdow
text:
I'd say there's 2 things that could be improved with this video.

First off, never do "using namespace std;" in the global scope, and especially not in a header. It will cause confusion for anyone unknowningly implementing it, and could also cause naming conflicts if other libraries or projects have similar names to types included in the std namespace.

Secondly, I think the last part with unique pointers should have mentioned the correct way of initializing a smart pointer.
For a Unique Ptr, you usually do this:
std::unique_ptr<Human> ptrJeff = std::make_unique<Human>();
And for Shared Ptr, you do this:
std::shared_ptr<Human> ptrJeff = std::make_shared<Human>();
While it probably won't make a huge difference for someone new to C++, doing it for Shared Ptr does mess with the reference table a fair bit, and could cause memory to become inconsistent with reality (correct me if I'm wrong).
similarly, if you want to assign a new pointer to an existing variable, you should try to do this, as it allows the previous stored pointer to correctly update the reference counter:
ptrJeff.reset(new Human);
This is also the only place where directly assigning it using a raw pointer is valid.

This is of course very easy to miss if you're new to C++, and a lot of resources do write it like you did, even if it's actually wrong to do so, or simply bad practice. So for a primarily Web based developer, this is quite good.

Either way, I'm surprised I got to see this C++ in 100 seconds video already, great work, and you honestly surprised me how much you can actually fit in 100 seconds, while still getting everything in that you should.

Java runs on a virtual machine meaning it is cross platform out of the box, it has garbage collection (no manual memory management), a package manager (no manual library configuration) and a lot of other features that make it an easier language compared to C++.

author: @Theraot
text:
C++ does not make it harder for you to shoot yourself in the foot.

The short and simple syntax (the one inherited from C) is almost always the unsafe one, while the safe versions are verbose and complicated. This is by design: the language has a lot of undefined behavior around the most common syntax (again, the one from C) allowing compilers to optimize it. So with C++ you get fast unsafe code out of the box, i.e. it will blows up very fast. While safe code is hard to master.

Part of the issue of mastering C++ is that after a long hiatus they rushed a lot of stuff into the standard, and so they had to deprecate it and unrecommend a lot of stuff fast too. Case in point: easy syntax: `*` (raw) pointers: unsafe and fast, safe syntax? Idk, one of these: `unique_ptr`, `shared_ptr`, `weak_ptr`, `auto_ptr`, each with guidelines of when to use and when not to (ask a beginner which one is deprecated).

Another consequence of this rushed standard is that they deplete the most reasonable names first. For the the C++ standard library is permanently soiled ground, and I don't want to remember more of the issues I've had with it.

If we are going to use C++, the only way is to carve a sane subset, but that is easier said than done. All in all, your advice of not using C++ features just because they are there is probably the best. Yet, I would not recommend C++. If there is no way around it, then so be it, but do not feel that you somehow SHOULD learn C++ as a general abstract thing. Far from it.

text: I would say learn a language appropriate to what you want to do. However, if you are one of those rare people that wants understand absolutely everything and are prepared to spend years, nea, decades doing it, then C++ is mandatory. One of the best things about C++ is that is does pretty much everything. In a language like Python, you typically rely on imported libraries. These libraries often can not be written in Python. They will be written in C++ (or C). So there will always be a limit to what you can do in Python before relying on a programmer of a different language to solve part of the problem for you. And this is fine for many professional areas. Interestingly if you never intend to write something that can't be written in Python, then you can write the same program in C++ just as easily and safely (if not safer). While C++ has many dangerous and complicated features, you only need to use them if you are doing something Python can not do. So a lot of work can be done in C++ easily and safely. The caveat here is that C++ is such a large language that you tend to need to become somewhat of an expert to discover that afore mentioned safe subset. I suspect how C++ is taught is a large barrier here. This is where I disagree with the video - I would NOT learn C before C++. I would find a modern book that teaches "modern C++" first, and ignore anything from the C language unless you need it. I regard everything in C as "advanced" and to be avoided unless or until you need advanced programming methods that allow you to employ low level techniques.

author: @kaisadilla_phd
text:
C++ is my favourite language, BUT I don't think C++ is a good language. I love it because it's just a _massive_ abstraction over assembly: you are directly manipulating memory and doing the CPU do what you want. BUT these are not features that make a good language, just features that make it a fun one. C++ is unsafe, absolutely terrible to decode and debug, and is probably the second worst designed language of all time (after PHP). And I don't mean it in a "haha don't like the syntax" way - but as in "some design choices make C++ extremely dangerous". C++ implicitly copies and moves memory with certain common statements by default, which is a massive safety hole where you can easily create dangling pointers and other undefined behavior without any indication that you are doing that. Many, many of the most damaging bugs in software history, bugs that have killed people and costed billions in damages, come from memory management bugs that C++ simply keeps adding to your code as soon as you make a little mistake.

C++ is utterly unfit for professional use. Any job that can afford a little bit of overhead should use Rust instead. Every job that needs to do manual memory manipulation broadly should instead use C, which is also unsafe, but doesn't have all the hidden booby traps C++ has. People can call me "hater" now if they want, I don't care. C++ is the language I've written the most code in, I speak from experience and I refuse to pretend that bugs introduced due to C++'s horrendous, unsafe syntax are the developer's fault.

author: @jeremygrice311
text:
Coming to this a year later to say that I disagree with the argument about "sugar". In the on-screen example, using iterators to step through a vector of numbers is obviously a silly way of just stepping through 0..3. But if you do have an iterable STL container that you want to iterate over, then you should use iterators. Comparing them to a for-loop that increments an integer doesn't do it justice.

Suppose you have a vector of 10 elements. You write a for loop that increments a value from 0 to 9 and uses that to index the vector and access each element. So far so good. But now imagine that your code-base has grown massively, and a shared pointer to that vector is passed to a function running on a different thread that changes the size of the vector. Now, your for-loop is either broken because the size of the vector has changed, or is slow because you rewrite it to check the value of the integer against the size of the vector with every iteration.

The clear solution here is an iterator. The loop will terminate when the iterator exceeds the memory owned by the vector, but no member functions need to be called to get a size value for comparison. By using iterators from the start, and always using them, your codebase is safe, consistent, easier to read (because you don't have two types of loops doing the same thing with STL containers) AND futureproofed.
