author: @StrikerTheHedgefox
text:
Honestly, I like C and C++, they are the primary languages used in my field. Learning those languages first will give you a better understanding of how a computer works, as it doesn't abstract important things like memory management behind black box nonsense (I'm looking at you, Java's garbage collector, you leaky POS) that can really make it difficult to tell what's really going wrong when something does. I also like the freedom it gives, you can do some amazing stuff with pointer math for example.
C++ might be capable of proverbially blowing your leg off, but at least you'll know it and why. Other higher-level languages might be slowly replacing your blood with pure poison without your knowledge until it's too late.

C and C++ aren't even hard to learn. I was able to get going with next to no programming experience, to writing my first programs in a very short amount of time. I have severe cognitive disabilities, never finished high school or college, I'm not mathematically inclined, and yet I was still able to teach myself the language and get going within a week. I've now got a commercial game under my belt, and multiple other projects on the go. Download Visual Studio Community, make sure to select C/C++ support, the Windows SDK, etc in the installer, then start a simple hello world project, there's no excuse. Go and look at the source code to an old game or program you love, tinker with it and compile it (there's plenty of projects that have building instructions), observe the results. It's a great way to learn the language.

author: @marcvanleeuwen5986
text:
I would not say that new users should first learn C when starting to learn C++. They should start with a very limited subset of the C++ language that suffices for small programming projects (which in the very beginning might be a subset of C as well), and then as they have need for more powerful or general stuff, they should learn the language features tof C++ hat suit those needs, and no more. Of coarse this does requires some guidance by people who know what C++ has to offer, to tell about the existence of features as they become more relevant.
It is however completely useless to start learning about the C idiosyncrasies like an array morphing into a pointer to its first element when used in certain ways; that is simply never the way things are done in C++. (Even in the rare cases where p designates a C-style array, use &p[0] rather than p if you need a pointer to its first element.) Don't learn about arrays at all at the start, use std::vector for everyday chores. And the day that you do need to use fixed-size arrays because of memory concerns, there is std::array. Using raw pointers into memory ranges, malloc and free, and such stuff can wait until the day you need to write low level memory management, if that day ever arrives.

author: @shapelessed
text:
If you're a beginner, do *not* start out with a low-level language. Start with a high level language that has an easy entry point, like JavaScript, the VM is already there, memory management is done for you, the devtools and debugging are super easy, you can easily create small UIs that feel more rewarding to finish and get working. Then, once you gain a bit of understanding how things work, start working with raw streams and data, then you'll have some basic knowledge that will make learning further things 10x easier, than if you were to start with C and only be able to create terminal apps. Terminal apps are boring, they don't excite anyone. Do things that excite you and you will WANT to learn.
Besides, you can start out with JS in Notepad++ or VSCode which have a super-low learning curve. C and C++ communities will immediately tell you to use an IDE. You do not want to learn a language and an IDE for it at the same time.

text: C++ is great for me when used in a reasonable way.   I often structure most of a program in a procedural way because it flows nicely like that.  It is a set of procedures to accomplish a goal. Sensors, databases of 'things', a representation of an overall interface that can be almost visualized as a thing with buttons and knobs to turn that do certain actions.  C is a nightmare for me with that but well designed C++ objects can make it VERY clear how to work with something.   It also lets me graft in new stuff that 'just works' in places the old stuff did.  I was writing some code for running a little robot and using built-in GPIO later added some I2C to it, then even later needed to work with an I2C GPIO expander.  I was able to make it so once that I2C I/O expander was initialized and ready to go it's GPIO pins could be substituted for any of the GPIO onboard and everything worked perfectly.  It was just another pin object that you could work with just the same as the others.  Sure it can all be done in other ways but for me C++'s 'The way' makes the most logical sense to me and I'm all that matters in what I create.

author: @TheOptimus1200
text:
C++ was my first programming language, but despite my bias, I think it is probably one of, if not, the best first programming language to learn because it is a good mix between higher-level and lower-level languages that, with PRACTICE, BECAUSE PROGRAMMING IS A SKILL, will give you an extra layer of programming skill that will make it easier to learn other languages. My only complaint with C++ is the lack of quality exception handling like Java has. Pointers are naturally going to be weird and confusing when first introduced, but when you PRACTICE with them to build your first custom dynamic array class, linked list class, binary tree class, etc, pointers become trivial. And if you don't want to learn pointers at first, you can still use the STL libraries that will automatically handle dynamic memory allocation and playing with pointers for you. When it comes to object oriented programming, I prefer C++ over Java because: 

(1) I like C++'s idea of a header (.h) file and implementation (.cpp) file. When someone wants to use your class, your header file acts like a dashboard with a quick layout of the buttons you can press without having to know all the electrical wiring behind the dashboard - whereas with Java, all your functions are defined in that class.

(2) Inheritance. In C++, I can have a class extend from all the parent classes I want and automatically inherit the data and functions without having to retype them in that class, whereas with Java, a class can only have one parent, forcing you to use interfaces if you want multiple inheritance, and I don't like that when you implement an interface, you have to retype and define all the abstract functions from the interface into your subclass. Why?

I'm really glad you brought up the classic Spider-Man quote "with great power comes great responsibility" because it is so true with C++.

author: @rockpadstudios
text: For low level embedded programming, C++ is overkill.  In the last 20 years I've come into many failing projects and the reason is C++ bloat.  With limited memory, C++ just bloats the code even when you use C+ and turn off RTTI, virtual classes, and exceptions.  I recently had to redo a product and the old one was all C++, factory patterns, singletons, etc. and it was nearly impossible to figure out where the code was at any instant in time.  With message queues and pointer passing, even when you hit a breakpoint you only get a pointer or function pointer and it's really hard to find out where the message came from since the messages typically don't have a sender in the object.  In embedded systems you will typically only have one of every major object (screen, keypad, etc.) so you don't really need classes.  I create a base class struct so each object can have a common interface and register an error callback etc. and it works great.  It would be nice if C pointers to functions could have more type checking but pointers to functions is all you really need.  I love C++ but C++11 and C++14 is a whole new language and most companies don't need that power.  Most use Java/C# for GUI's anyway now.  C++ is still the best for server based backend code that need efficient code execution when grid power is the limiting factor.  Spinning up C# or Java apps is not cost effective.  I recently worked with a C++ SDK for a BLE SOC from Microchip that was C++ and what a nightmare (so glad we didn't pick that chip).  Like all designs there was a "god class" with hundreds of small classes in it so the call tree just to blink an LED was 5 calls deep.  What a mess and the RTOS was non-standard and hard to compile out.

C++ is great and rather simple in nature but a lot of the C++ community just make it their job to make the most unreadable and complex code for performance reasons.

C++ was my first language in 2015 when I started a physics degree: as part of an *introduction to programming*. It was tough. To this day I don't know if the teaching methods were disadvantageous or if the language is genuinely a poor choice for baby's first programs. Because we started with basic control flow and then structs that could have just as well been C, I think they just didn't want to introduce us using another language once the time came for abstractions and other OOP concepts.

I've since ditched that degree and just last year restarted uni with a bachelor's in IT. Our first language there was Java. For all the hate and memes, it's an easy language to learn (with lots of often unexplained boiler plate). Now we're doing C for the operating systems module and it's... fun. I'm just at the start of my low-level programming but I'm looking forward to where it takes me, and to the things I can build on it - including C++.

author: @baphomet8958
text:
Who am i ?
=========
Im a former Software Engineer and currently working in the video game industry as Unreal Developer with over 17 Years of C++ experience in total.


Should you even learn C++ ? 
=======================
Sure if you need very fast and performant code you should learn it.


Is it easy to learn ? 
===============
Not even close... 
It will be very frustrating to get your head around the whole "Pointerstuff" and learning to write useful class orientated C++ code even with the "best tips and tricks"
is a very challenging experience.


Why are so much people struggling with C++ ?
======================================
Most people coming from modern scripting languages like Python and using these languages compared to C++ is like driving a car with automatic gear shifting.
You simply dont need to fully understand how a Computer works internally to get some decent results. 
Compared to this in C++ you will reach a point pretty soon where you will realize that something like "automatic gear shifting" for a PC doesnt realy exist. 
At this point you will have to learn "IT Basics" and try to understand how your PC is performing tasks and why you need things like float, int, char , shift operators and so on...

Pretty much people were telling me "You dont need to know everything just the stuff you realy need because its to complicated bla bla bla...", trust me you will need a strong knowledge base to become a decent C++ programmer ! 
Honestly spoken i have never met a real passionated C++ programmer who didnt knew the "IT Basics" but i met alot of "perma-googling Stackoverflow fulltime users" which where searching for answers 5 - 6h on a 10-hours workday .... 


Where to start ?
=============
At first you should learn the C++ language and get the necessary Keywords, data types, get comfortable with the C++ Syntax and write some simple code.
There is a very good course from learnprogramming.academy called "Beginning C++ Programming - From Beginner to Beyond" which seems to be an excellent entrypoint these days.
After that you should get your hands on sites like Codewars and start practicing C++ coding. Just because you took an onlinecourse dont make you a good C++ programmer, constant programming and problem solving will do that ! I highly recommend to take a look at the github repos called "awesome-for-beginners" and "build-your-own-x" (last one is more advanced) to take the next steps forward.


And after that ?
=============
Depends on what you wanna do 🤷‍♂

You wanna become a Gamedev in Unreal ? Do it you have everything you need because to become a Gamedev you dont need a Bachelor or any kind of Computer Science Degree.
Everything you need is a strong Portfolio with good and advanced Projects which are showing your knowledge 👍

You wanna beome a Software Engineer ? Go to a University because noone hires "unofficial educated Software Engineers".
To get a Job as Software Engineer without a degree you have to be very VERY lucky.

Just take the next necessary step to reach your goal, its pretty simple 👌

author: @Spiderboydk
text:
I switched from C++ to C a few years ago and never regretted it.

The main reason is C++ is so endlessly complex that takes a big cognitive toll in your head while developing.

There is no such thing as not paying for features you don't use, because even if you don't use them, you still have to know about them and deal with them. You can't just ignore knowing about exceptions, move semantics, overload resolution, etc.

C++ also likes to hide a lot of code from you in constructors, destructors, operator overloads, etc. so seemingly innocent statements like x = y + z; might execute all sorts of code from all over the code base. You really have to have a good knowledge of the code base to understand what's going on. It makes it hard to ballpark how fast or slow code might be.

Switching to C freed up a lot of mental capacity I can now spend on actual problem solving.

author: @XiremaXesirin
text:
I think it's worth talking about why, precisely, C++ programmers don't like certain C-style conventions.

To use malloc/pointers as an example, the main reason we don't like malloc is because on its own, it doesn't express ownership―a concept that is really important to memory management and preventing memory leaks, but which isn't enforced by the language at all in C, or is automagically managed in garbage-collected languages like Java or python. When you write something like int* value_ptr = malloc(4); in C, there's no enforcement at the language level that the memory you allocated will later be cleaned up. The only way to ensure that is for the programmer to be a good girl and remember to clean it up.

But in C++, we express the same concept as auto value_ptr = std::make_unique<int>(); which does nearly the same thing as the C code (it also initializes the memory to a default value, which the C code doesn't do; this can be good or bad depending on whether you actually needed the memory initialized) but also has the extremely valuable benefit of preventing memory leaks. The programmer doesn't have to remember to write value_ptr.reset() at the end of its use; the language automatically calls the destructor when value_ptr falls out of scope, freeing the memory at the exact moment it is no longer being used.

Of course, there are occasionally situations where malloc and manual memory management (or memory management by an external library) are what you need, and C++ offers that stuff for compatibility, which makes the language more complex (and potentially dangerous), but also more flexible.

There's other examples I could cite which have their own debates (C-style unions vs std::variant, C-style arrays vs std::vector or std::array) but a lot of the same points apply to those cases.

author: @sw33t.angela
text:
So, the reason for not wanting to use raw strings in C++ is due to raw C strings being actually unsafe. Null termination relies on the string having it, and, if it's missing, some copy mechanisms break due to buffer overflow. These are why there are so many strcpy functions because the checks that you get what you expect and never overflow is needed. It also relies on single byte ASCII characters and can't accommodate multibyte UTF-8 charsets.

Std::string and by proxy Rust strings include the string length in bytes inside the structure so it can be safely dealt with without relying on external functions and dealing with memory management directly.

Not to say that c strings are all bad. If you have a stream of characters that there's no expected length and needs an end character, then null terminated strings are good.

author: @recarsion
text:
I worked in C for about 2 years in total and about 1 year in C++, and while both languages can be pains in the ass in their own ways, C++ was way more convoluted, unintuitive and tedious to work with in my experience. High-level, near-zero cost abstractions sound good but unless you can somehow solve memory safety without GC, you're building on sand. C++ couldn't quite achieve that, though many of its features and libraries are undeniably an improvement over C. Rust managed to do decades later what C++ couldn't back then.

In conclusion, I wouldn't use C++ for any new project anymore unless I had no choice, like an Unreal game or a Qt application, though I wouldn't be surprised if both already have viable bindings in other languages.

author: @the-programing
text:
From doing a personal projects (around 100,000 lines+ of code) using C++, C, Java, TypeScript/Javascript, and ObjectiveC, I truly think c++, Java, or ObjectiveC are the best languages simply because they all offer near zero cost for abstractions. For example, when I was writing TS in ReactNative I wrote a lot of classes and abstractions, but the performance gets worse and worse to the point a cold start takes more than 10 seconds, which I just recently found out TS doesn’t “compile” to js but simply translates to js. I was expecting TS can “unroll” the classes to js. This causes the project to get extremely bloated since you have to write as much logic into the same file as possible to preserve performance. I am not very experienced with javascript, but this property alone makes me dread writing any js.

In C++, you can write pure C style, zero class projects; or, you can write completely object oriented project. Both styles will give you the same performance (some times the oop style will give you a better performance due to the -O2 level optimization the compiler can re-reference the class structures to decrease binary size, but C style code doesn’t have that information). I personally think oop offers clearer abstractions while writing code, and in the long run make the project scale a lot easier. That’s why I personally prefer it. 

However, I think anyone who can proficiently write C style code should NOT switch to C++. If you can write scalable C code, C++ definitely offers little value for you. Even so, I recommend anyone who is starting programming to start with C++ or Java, because these languages helps you to learn about structuring a project that can be scaled from the start. And you can switch to C style languages at a later date without any trouble.

C++ is indeed inferior to Rust : 

- It is more complicated
- It is less readable, syntax can go terrible
- It is very not safe to use. at least half of all security vulnerabilities are due to these old languages
- It does not force you to handle errors, C++ programs cannot be as robust as Rust
- C++ exceptions are so bad
- It is not easy to use, no provided dependency management system, no provided linter/formatter. CMake is garbage and no one likes it. Visual Studio is so terrible i don't even want to say a word about it.
- The STL is clusterfucked because of interoperability with C types
-  Even modern C++ does not look modern when compared to Rust
- It is a pain to make portable code or real apps
- No official package registry, you either write everything or use gigantic libraries.
- Multithreading is just scary to use

It only takes a few weeks to learn Rust and it's just a relief : 

- Just as fast as C/C++
- Memory safe and you don't even have to deal with allocation by yourself, safe multithreading is also enforced by the compiler.
- Official package registry and dependency management system
- Suitable for anything, even embedded devices
- Very nice standard library.
- FFI with other languages such as C, because we still live in a C world
- Modern syntax and features, just as powerful as C++, but so much simpler (generics, traits, macros...).
- Easy to use, test, benchmark and everything, it's all included in the box
- Does not even have the concept of a null pointer.
- If you really want to do whatever you want (like using C-like pointers), you can also use unsafe Rust. But you are never actually required to do it in most cases.
- No garbage collector, no reference-counting pointers unless you ask for it.
- Will never have any breaking change for the language itself
- Huge community and almost 100.000 packages already available
- Ready for the web and even for frontend programming, using webasm

The only caveat is that Rust is pretty slow to compile, but maybe it will improve in the future.

Everything in Rust beats C++. 

There can be no denial about that. 

It is just a matter of time before Rust replaces C++.

For beginners it's a challenge to soak up and distinguish so much legacy knowledge together with the new knowledge. But I'm having a lot of fun in my journey.

Just a little correction, structs and classes in C++ are basically the same thing, except in classes it's possible to define the usual qualifiers for its members (private, protected, public...). That means you can define functions, constructors and destructors on structs as well (unlike C), but since all members are public, it's recommended to be used when dealing with a "pure data" object.
Also, one interesting fact that surprised me: Classes in C++ can be instanced at the stack, you don't need to use "new" or create/allocate a smart pointer.

Approaching the language like it's C with extra features means that you're not taking advantage of what C++ offers you.  Most real world C++ codebases look a lot more like Java with the stick removed from its ass.

There's exceptions, of course - Arduino being one of them.  If you're in a resource-constrained environment then there's an argument for making your C++ look like C.  If you're working on larger microcontrollers or doing application programming, C will only hold you back.

author: @metal571
text:
Learning C first will tend to lead a developer towards a C-like C++ style. This tends to defeat the purpose of C++; See Kate Gregory's talk "Stop Teaching C".

Avoiding sugar is also not the best approach, and in fact the range for loop over a std::vector generates less assembly instructions than using a traditional loop variable. You can prove this in Compiler Explorer with -O3 and is mentioned in Bjarne's book A Tour of C++ 3rd Edition. This makes some sugar in C++ what Jason Turner calls a "negative cost abstraction".

Also "near zero cost" is not quite right. The language design involves what they call the Zero Overhead Principle, which is often misunderstood. This means not that there is actually zero overhead in using an abstraction, but that if you implemented it manually by hand using only C or assembly, you wouldn't be able to do better. At least, that's the goal...I won't go into how exceptions allocating and Run Time Type Identification are clearly in violation of this.

c++ has it's advantages, but it introduces a bunch of headaches if you don't know every little detail, and it has a lot of stuff to it, so it can be overwhelming to learn, but if you have the patience/time to learn it all, I would rather suggest you try rust instead, because that way you avoid the memory management headaches you get with c++, and the compiler helps you avoid a lot of mistakes. author: @FuzzhyFoo
text:
I don't think people have to learn C first. As a starting language, I think C++ contains a much simpler language trying to break free, chained down by legacy. I feel we scare away people from it by spooking them with scary concepts like pointers, references and memory safety. As though that is something exclusive to C/C++.

If I were to introduce someone to programming through C++, I wouldn't teach them about raw memory allocation. No pointers, pointers to pointers, or even references. Reduce the friction between them and their code until it becomes relevant to understand the more core concepts. Let them pass variables by copy while they're learning. Move semantics have reduced the overhead of that dramatically. Let them return copies, they don't have to understand copy elision or NRVO. You don't teach someone java or C# by telling them how to appease the garbage collector. 

It's naive, yes. But even basic things in C can appear arcane. Take the supposedly safe "sprintf" - lovely name. 
You need to understand stack vs heap allocation, when to alloc/free. null terminators, the caveats of the sprintf family of functions, the 'safe' versions of them, what that strange 'restrict' keyword means, etc. 

Of course, there are nice, basic, declarative examples like adding strings together, which while basic, lets beginners appreciate how that happens under the hood.

author: @gabrielb.2886
text:
Very nice check up, even for seasoned programmers! Let's grow the list ;) (it ended up longer than I initially thought)

32: Using pointers instead of references for function parameters when the pointers are expected to never be null.

33: Using references and constant member variables which disable copy and move assignment for no good reason (there might be other good reasons to do so, though).

34: Not marking move constructor and move assignment operators noexcept. This makes many STL algorithms introduce costly intermediate copies to preserve exception guaranties, especially std::vector.

35: Using too many levels of nested control structures (especially loops). Extra functions or just local lambdas with good names help greatly decompose the work in self explanatory steps. Control structures body should remain as short as possible.

36: Thinking comments can make up for bad variable/function/type naming. Comments are reserved for complex *things*. Complex *code* that addresses simple things must be written better so that it does not need comments.

37: Not using assertions to check invariants in debug builds without sacrificing performance in release builds.

38: Not using sanitizers as they are really simple to use and catch many "nooby" broken constructs

39: Not using iterators in many places where they should.

40: Using getters and setters for everything inside classes. If a class is just a bundle of data, it should be a struct with public member variables.

41: Using dynamic_cast when virtual functions would do the job.

42: Calling constructors with parenthesis instead of curly brackets. Parenthesis allow narrowing implicit conversions. Beware of classe with an std::initializer_list constructor like std::vector though ;)

43: Using exceptions for flow control or like a secondary return path. Functions that throw under normal conditions make code difficult to understand as they might act as a "goto next catch clause" every time they are called. Plus they are computationnaly expensive. Exceptions are for abnormal situations... When they are not just completely forbidden by coding rules like at Google.

44: Thinking signed integer types wrap when overflowing. It is undefined behaviour and *the compiler will assume it does not happen* when enabling optimisation, breaking code in pretty subtle ways. In particular, signed integer overflow detection tests like "if(i+1<i)" are not valid.

45: Using global variable dynamic initialization. Non constant global variables are terrible anyway. But dynamically initialized globals are bad in all cases. They look fine util the order of initialization starts acting funny.

46: Not testing code. Testing code catches bugs at the time of writting code but also catches bugs introduced by later modifications of the code. Also, testing requires to write code that can be tested, which is often a sign of higher quality code.


47: Using std::list instead of std::vector. std::list should be reserved to non-movable types. std::vector is superior in almost all other aspects.

48: Not going through the effort of making classes movable whenever possible (it's actually often trivial). This results in the best case in smart pointers flying all over the place (complexity) to compensate for the inhability of the object to move itself. In the worst case, it results in no ownership management at all, thus late object destruction, and thus wasted memory. 

Regarding output function parameters, they have a use case, even for single returned value: they let the caller manage the allocation of the output object. It is pretty common to have "to_string" functions that let the user provide the std::string object they want the output to be stored in to let the caller reuse the same string over multiple calls, potentially saving large amounts of costly heap allocations.

std::array is great but leads to a different function template instance for every size of the array passed as an argument. Fine for tiny functions that get inlined anyway. Not so fine for larger functions that lead to binary size increase and worse instruction cache locality (performance degradation). Iterators usually are the right interface for functions expecting a range of some sort.

About the constexpr example: adding constexpr to the function will likely not bias the compiler into evaluating the function at compile time to initiallize a non-constexpr variable (it might equally do it with a constexpr or non constexpr function if the definition is available). Adding constexpr to the variable as well is required to ensure compile time evaluation.

Marking the destructor virtual is only required for polymorphic classes but discouraged otherwise (none of the STL classes I can think of have a virtual destructor). Virtual destructors can especially have a significant impact on the cost of object destruction when the destructor is empty but virtual: STL containers will optimize out the destruction phase when the destructor of the stored objects is so called "trivial", which is not the case for virtual destructors.

Regarding const_cast, there is one legitimate and safe use case I can think of: when a member function has a non-const and a const version that happen to be implemented identically but just differ by the constness of the return type (e.g., int& foo();    VS    int const& foo() const;). One method consists in casting this to const in the non-const function to call the const version and cast const away from the returned value. Templates can help with this as well but it is cumbersome for such a simple task. Only C++23 with the explicit this parameter really addresses that issue.

text: Great video! I have a couple critiques. #10: Even if the string literal outlives its scope, I wouldn't generally recommend writing an interface that implies returning a pointer to a local. As a consumer of this function, its interface alone is enough to make me at least suspicious about whether it invokes undefined behavior. Coupled with your points on RAII, I might also wonder who owns the character array, given that this function is returning a raw ("non-owning") pointer. If you find yourself writing a function that returns a constant expression, just define the constant expression directly---their lifetimes are not dependent on some blackbox implementation, and the ownership is clearly global and not my problem. #12: You don't need to define a dedicated structure type just to group some data. This is exactly what std::pair and std::tuple are for. As #11 discusses, they can also be used with structured bindings. If you want it to have a nicer name, use a typedef.

author: @markwiering
text:
1. using namespace std;

I always do this and I have never encountered any problem with it. Without "using namespace std;", the source code becomes too verbose. I prefer writing "cout << "Text" << endl;" over having to write "std::cout << "Text" << std::endl;"

I use "using namespace std;" globally, but only in CPP files; not in header files.

2. Using endl a lot - also in loops.

Yes, I do this 100%. I was not aware of the performance impact. I can switch to using "\n", though.

3. Using a for-loop by index instead of range-based for-loop.

I always use for-loop by index. Then I can peek at the next and previous index, depending on the index. It's really handy. You limit yourself greatly by not doing it this way.

Also, I HATE the "auto" keyword. Just type out the type. I always want to know what each type is, so seeing "auto" everywhere annoys me.

4. Writing a loop when a standard algorithm already does this.

I do that, too. First, I want to know what exactly the algorithm does and why it does it this way. The best way to understand this, is by writing that algorithm myself. I have a header file full of commonly used subroutines on for example strings. Moreover, many "standard" features that C++ programmers use, like "stoi()", do not exist in C++99: a version I regularly program in on my older Fujitsu Siemens computer. To maintain cross-compatibility, I "re-invent the wheel", so to say.

5. Using C-style array instead of std::array.

I do this, too. The C-style array is much easier to use and easier to read than the std::array.
Moreover, I don't use the C-style array when programming casually. The C-style arrays are only used "under the hood" in a self-written dynamic array class, that I always call when I want an array where the program does all the automatic expansion and boundary checking for me.

6. I don't do this. Never done this.

7. Using at() instead of [].

I disagree. I always use []. It's easier to use and easier to read. To avoid reading and writing violations, use a built-in boundary checking mechanism. That is easy to implement in a class.

8. Not knowing that the [] inserts the element into the map if it doesn't already exist.

Indeed. I did not know this. But, it's not important for me, either. I don't use std::map. I use my own map class for that, that does not do this. It is precisely for this reason that I made my own map class: because I don't want to face unpleasant surprises due to C++ doing weird stuff like this without my knowing.

9. Ignoring const correctness.

I don't do this. I mark references as "const" in functions where I do not plan on modifying them.

10. I knew this.
11. Not using structured bindings.

I never did this. I didn't even know this was possible. Judging from my own programming style, doing this would be unnecessary for me, so I won't do much with this discovery.

12. Interesting. I knew this, but I did not know that the syntax you showed me was valid. I did this the more old-fashioned way.
13. I knew this, and I use this, but not in the form of making a function a constexpr. Instead, I do it simpler. I just use constexpr for variables, without resorting on needlessly difficult function structures.
14. Interesting. I did not know this - and I do neither of these. I never make my destructor virtual, because I don't make use of class inheritance. I just create a class and use it. Sometimes, I have a class in a class, but never an inherited class.
15. I did not know this, but I also never exploited this.
16. I knew this.
17. I do this, too, albeit I prefer the #define PI 3.141592653 method over the contexpr method.
18. I have stumbled upon that problem before: removing an element of a list while looping through that list, followed by malfunction. I have learned from that. Now I don't make that mistake any more.
19. I agree. I never do this, either.
20. I didn't know this. I have never used the move()-function anyway.
21. I have never used the .replace() function on strings. I do know that in if-statements, the evaluation goes from left-to-right. I have experimented with that.
22. I almost always use stack allocations. I didn't know they were faster, too. I just found the cose of stack allocations more concise.
23. I never use unique_ptr or shared_ptr.
24. I never use make_unique or make_shared either.
25. Yes, I use new and delete instead of unique pointers.
26. Yes, I do my resource management manually. However, I have written classes to lighten the burden. For example, a dynamic array class.
27. I agree with you here, though the last "struct FreeDeleter" is the most useless class I have ever seen. All it does is calling free(). Why not call free() directly? Why coming up with an artificial extra layer for the same exact thing?
28. Well, again, I never use unique or shared pointers.
29. Never thought of this, since I don't use unique nor shared pointers.
30. I didn't even know that "int *const ptr3 = &x;" was valid. I only use const at the leftmost or rightmost part (functions); never in the middle.
31. I never ignore compiler warnings. Instead of turning them off, I always use a compilation tag -Wall to give me more compiler warnings.

My noob count: 
p1 + p2 + p3 + p4 + p5 + p7 + p8 + p11 + p12 + p14 + p25 + p26 = 12
12/31 nooby points.

But, that is because I omitted the points 20, 23, 24, 28 and 29. If I include those, the noob counter is 17/31.

author: @SkyerSSK
text:
Some things are only valuable if your code base can use the latest standard. For example, structured binding was introduced in C++17, and if your code can't use C++17 - it's a mess. 
Same rule for other things like std::byte (C++ 17). 
Meanwhile, the rule 25 and 27 are conflict "nooby habits". If you think using new and delete is bad, that implicitly means you can't use raw pointers - remember, shared_ptr is contagious. Same for the C array vs. std::array. If you don't use a C array, why use C-styled function arguments like func(void *a, size_t b) when you only have to use func(std::array<T> a) and use a.size()?
If you leak a RAW pointer from shared_ptr or unique_ptr, it's very dangerous behavior. Avoid any use of shared_ptr<T>::get() (same for unique_ptr<T>::get()), because that pointer returned is raw, and it will NOT go away when the unique_ptr or shared_ptr deletes their internal pointer. You may get a dangling pointer later on. But this video seems to imply you do that?
Now, reinterpret_cast<T> is handy when you want to serialize a POD structure back & forth: for example, if you're writing a structure called "PositionStruct" into a binary file, which contains two floats, you only need to do this: fstream.write((char*)&position_instance, sizeof(PositionStruct));. Which is basically fstream.write(reinterpret_cast<char*>&position_instance, sizeof(PositionStruct));. This saves you time from copying the struct (especially if the struct is large or you're using an embedded device and memory is limited). Not to mention std::bit_cast is a C++20 function. 
So, I usually call such kind of "video" misleading and confusing. It does not provide proper guidance to tell you the proper way to do things; it only scares you with some rumor habits that "seem" correct. 
Now, based on the fact that you made so many "nooby x language habits you need to ditch", are YOU, the video maker, a nooby, or intended to confuse people watching this video, is my question. You see, your video has conflict items that will easily confuse beginners. Is that what you really want to do?
Noobies, please go and read something more useful, like a real, offline tutorial, not such a messy video.

author: @nerdastics3987
text:
I’ve been programming with both c and c++ for a long time, and I can say that while most of the points you make in this video are true, there are some things that aren’t really good:

1. Sometimes writing your own algorithm can be faster, especially if you’re doing it for something specific in mind. The standard library, while definitely useful, was written for general purpose, and most likely not your specific project and/or task in mind. Also, most of the time, the standard library is going to be much slower than a custom implementation, because the standard library is a general purpose library, not a specialized chunk of software. So even if an algorithm in the standard library may exist, it will almost all the time be slower and likely be even harder to debug (especially the gnu g++ library, that stuff's a mess).

2. The issue with the pointers and arrays thing isn’t really an issue unless you are a complete moron with pointers, but if you are using c++/c to do the job, you should already have a firm grasp on how pointers work (and should not be afraid to use them)….

3. Reinterpret casting can be quite useful, thats literally what a sugarcoated dynamic_cast is. However, it can be used incorrectly, I do agree with most of it. And also, you can do so much more with a reinterpret cast than just casting it back to the original type. Also keep in mind that reinterpret_cast is just a glorified static_cast. When you look at the assembly generated from a static_cast or a reinterpret_cast, it's the exact same as a c-style cast.

4. Structured bindings, the one thing I would say is don’t use them unless you wan’t to restrict compilation from c++17 (or maybe 20) or higher. It reduces portability.

5. For loop by index, sometimes it is better to use it, especially if you don’t just want to go from 0 to [length of the array].

6. Manual memory allocation. Smart pointers are slow…. So slow. Also, sometimes the complexity and the overhead of a shared or unique pointer is far too much of a cost instead of just using a simple pointer.

7. Manual resource management. C++ is high risk high reward, it's not garbage collected for a reason. People use it to have almost complete control over when and where a resource is allocated and deallocated, so saying that people should never manage this stuff themselves is kind of against the design of the language. If you don't want to manage resources yourself, use C# or something higher level.

author: @fenril6685
text:
reinterpret_cast is very useful for specific circumstances. Not everything that is technically undefined behavior is bad in all circumstances. Undefined behavior just means that in general doing this thing is generically unpredictable. In very specific circumstances you can adequately predict what will happen if you reinterpret cast say an array of bytes (char) into a different type of array, because you know by design what that array is supposed to be.

You might ask, but when would you need to reinterpret_cast an array of bytes to an array of doubles? When you're working with some legacy code base or C and you're doing something very low level like uploading raw data to a GPU to use mass parallel processing frameworks on that data, and then you want to get that data sent back to the CPU side.

Ok, but why not just use C++20 std::bit_cast in that instance? If only you could use the latest version of C++, and if only every project you will ever work on will be a new project from the ground up. This is like the most naive question that is readily apparent to anyone who has worked with a variety of companies as a software engineer which deal in codebases or products with specific requirements. Many companies have projects which require interacting with code bases which are stuck with C++11 or C++14 and can not be easily migrated, or they specifically can't be migrated because the target systems run on some old linux kernel.

Nothing in C++ is "useless" or a "mistake" in all instances, and this idea that there are somehow steadfast rules for things that you must never ever do under any circumstances is brain dead and a huge part of the problem with teaching low level languages to new software developers.

C/C++ is foremost a low level language about versatility and customization. There are best practices that are distributed for the general use case of a feature, and then there are many specific use cases in which such features might be appropriately used in a completely different way.

In my opinion, any of these generalized statements about "mistakes" to warn newbies of the dangers of things like using reinterpret_cast should also be accompanied by, this is because in most instances there is a better way to get the effect you are looking for and using it without knowing what you are doing can be dangerous. It should never be just "here is this language feature, now never touch it, because it has no real purpose other than being dangerous". This is just idiotic and also misleading to new developers.

text:
Good video. But for someone who's so strict about wrong and right ways of coding, I noticed one of the most newbie mistakes in your on-screen code. And that is the placement of the * and & symbols when declaring, assigning or otherwise using pointers and references and addresses.

When you declare a variable "int number = 5;" then "number" is a label for a memory container. At declaration time, the compiler takes note of where in memory the container is, and (by being declared as int) how many bytes of coherent memory it has assigned, and also how these bytes should be interpreted. (Think signed/unsigned bit use, or float/double splitting of sign/exponent/fraction bits.)

So when you use it in your code as e.g. "std::cout << number;" then the compiler sees your use of the label "number", goes looking where in memory it points to, how many bytes of memory to read from there, and in what way it should interpret the bits/bytes there. In the end, it will substitute the label "number" with the collected and converted int representation of what was stored in the memory container.

This means that the label "number" is, effectively - in code, equivalent to an integer with the bits arranged to represent the value 5. So the data type of the label "number" is an integer. As simple as that.

Now, when you take the address of that integer variable, e.g. like "&number", then the & is in a way a modifier for the "number" label, like a sort-of "number.getAddress()" call. The & is applied to the label "number" in order to tell the compiler "I don't want the contained int value itself, I want the address in memory where the int value is located".

And if you have an address stored somewhere, you can de-reference it by using the * modifier. So say you have your "&number" result (i.e. the memory address) stored in a variable with the label "address", then you apply the * modifier to the "address" label to tell the compiler "I don't care about the address, I want the value it's storing", like a quasi "address.getContent()" call. And as a result, such a * modifier call will return the integer value hiding behind the de-referenced address.

So when de-referencing, the * symbol is not part of a data type, but a modifier to what the "address" label stands for, i.e. a modifier for the address it stores. And the data type of the "return value" of the memory-address-getter "&" is not an int, but a pointer to a memory address. These are two very important sentence for my case. The * and & symbols are MODIFIERS to the LABELS, they are NOT DATA TYPES of the returned VALUE.

Let's consider declaring a variable that will contain the memory address of an integer container somewhere in memory. Even if the integer type is just a tiny 8-bit int8_t, the memory addressing in 64-bit systems requires 64 bits of memory to store memory addresses. So storing the address of an 8-bit integer will require 64 bits of memory, which means the pointer can not be an 8-bit int8_t i.e. you would - or rather could - NOT declare it as "int8_t address = &number;" because the 8 bits of the int8_t would not suffice to store the 64-bit memory address returned from the & modifier.

In other words: the int8_t before the label "address" has nothing to do with the address itself, but it's a hint to what the data AT the stored address will be interpreted as, and how many Bytes of memory it actually has covered. But ... since the address we're storing is not the int8_t value in "number" itself, but the address to it, and the & modifier returns the data type "pointer to int8_t", the only sensible way of notation is to add the * symbol in the declaration to the int8_t mention - because it's part of the data type of the "address" label.

The "address" label is a  "pointer to an int8_t  container", so the only rationally sensible way to declare it is "int8_t* address = &number;". Because, as explained earlier on, writing the * symbol immediately before the label suggests it's the de-referencing modifier. If you declare your variable "int8_t *address = &number;" it would suggest that you think the * modifies the "address" label, which is not the case. So it would be irrational and unsensible to use it there.

And if you pass an argument into a function by reference, the & is NOT a modifier to the label of the variable, but again - like the * in a pointer variable - part of the data type of the variable/label. Adding an argument as "std::vector<double> &numbers" would suggest that the & symbol is applied to the "numbers" label as a modifier, which obviously isn't the case. The & should go where it belongs, and that is left to the data type, as in "std::vector<double>& numbers", because that's the only rationally sensible place to put it. The label "numbers" will contain a reference to a double-vector. The argument label "numbers" is not modified by the & symbol at all, so why suggest it should be.

double number = 8.0;
double* address = &number;
double alsoNumber = *address;
void useNum (const double& NumReference, double* NumPointer) 
{ std::cout << "Reference: " << NumReference << ", Pointer: " << *NumPointer << -std::endl- '\n';}

That's the only sensible way to place those symbols. Anything else would be ludicrous and completely illogical. Even if we all know how to interpret them correctly, it takes extra time to make this *gong* newbie habits.

Writing things like "for (const auto pair.getAddress() : colors)" wouldn't make a lot of sense now, would it? So why write it that way? If you want the pair to be of a referenced data type, the PUT THE & WHERE THE DATA TYPE IS, i.e. "for (const auto& pair : colors)", because that's the only way it makes sense. :)

Thank your for your attention. If you all implement my reasoning in your code, you will all make the world a better place.

text:
For 25, there is one case where you would want to use new instead of unique ptr. When you have a long lived singleton type object, you can run into static destructor cataclysms where an object is destroyed but it was depended on by a separate static object. Static destructor memory issues are horrible to debug as there's no usable stack, just _exit.
Now, the concept of a singleton is quite nasty but when you truly have global state like a logger or multithreaded exception handler it's not super great to pass it 12 layers deep into your implementations... So keeping in mind that for certain cases, when leaky singletons are required... New has its use. Bonus: Valgrind and address sanitizer fully support this pattern and won't flag the leak.

There are quite a few things listed here that are simply just NOT "Nooby Habits". Why does nobody ever care about performance? How quickly your code does it's job, usually does matter. Okay, that's not a license to write unreadable/unmaintainable code, but performance is an important metric. Using a std::algorithm does leave you at the mercy of its implementation. Usually, they're pretty good, but not always. I've come across some shocking std::algorithm implementations. It's convenient and it's syntax is reasonable, but it's not always a safe bet.

Then there's using std::array over a C style array. I guess this is a bit more nuanced and down to personal choice. std::array in my opinion has lousy syntax, although it can be useful having some helper methods sometimes. My main gripe is that it doesn't really give you anything more than a C style array does, as you have to declare its size at instantiation time, so that renders things like .size() sort of redundant. Also it can't deal with things where the array size is defined by its assignment or initialization.

text: So not to kneckbeard too hard, but I would disagree with "never use new / delete" slightly. Some times you actually need to flush the buffer, e.g. for debug printing so that you know it will print e.g. when the breakpoint hit. But I could be wrong here.

In the std::find_if() case, you get an iterator instead of an index, so you need to use something like std::distance() to get the index which may make your code more convoluted. In my job we have a namespace called stlutils where we have wrappers for std::begin(c) to std::end(c) -cases but also sibling functions like stlutils::find_if_idx(). So, as the STL API becomes more versatile, we then might simplify our stlutils implementations and maybe in the future be able to remove the whole stlutils library which would be the most ideal situation of course.

author: @ABaumstumpf
text:
for "std::endl" i would say it is the exact opposite.
Printing like this is done usually for one of 2 reasons:
1 - user interactions. You tell the user what is going on and ask him for an input
2 - tracing - you wanna see what the program did.
In the first case the performance is a complete non-issue, in the second case NOT using "std::endl" would be moronic cause in the case of an error you have no idea when it happend as you did not flush the buffer, not even considering yet that your claim about it taking extra time is actually not really that correct.
Often saw people try to be "clever" and avoid the supposed performance-impact of flushing that later get frustrated cause they can not find out what went wrong cause their logging is not showing them what is really going on.

People think/claim this makes such a large difference yet don't even know that 'sync_with_stdio' is a thing - by default the I/O-buffer used by std::cout is synchronised  with the buffer of the old c-streams. This alone has far bigger of an impact than std::endl vs \n. If flushign the buffer makes ANY relevant performance difference then you are well beyond newbie-territory and at that point you really should know a lot more about the standard behaviour of streams and their buffers.


Structured binding - that is still relatively knew and very often simply not available. Nearly no business-software created before 2018 will even use C++17, often still c++11. Upgrading your entire platform on an existing codebase is rather laborious.
Right now i am glad that we can use C++17 in most of our current projects, but in some i am still restricted to 14 or 11, really looking forward to C++20 with the easier string-formatting.

author: @sheeftz
text:
1. Using std::string, using std::cout ect. has the same drawback as using namespace std. You are make a choice for someone that 'string' will refer to 'std::string' and cout will refer to std::cout. You are substituting one evil with another, instead of solving it.
If it's domestic code, don't be afraid of using namespace std. If you'll use 'using std::something;' instead, you'll end up using all of the most populare std names in your headers anyway, and all your header files will begin with a screen of text telling "using std::this; using std::that; using std::those_two; using std::half_of_the_rest_library". This is not what you want.
If it's a public library code than use a library namespace, otherwise you are doomed to use std qualifier before every single std name.
3. Don't use 'auto' keyword without a purpose. The 'auto' keyword was designed to solve certain kind of problems. The given example is not in the list. Using 'auto' without a purpose makes your code hard to read. Use auto in general code (templates) or when type referencing is tedious (i.e. typename std::unordered_map<std::string, std:int32_t>::const_iterator).
5. There is nothing wrong in using C arrays. Using a core part of a language can not be wrong. There is std::span to solve the problem with function parameters.
6. Regarding the famouse Quake 3 code. Note that C style casting converts one type of pointer to another type of pointer. This is not UB. UB is dereferencing it because it violates type aliasing rules.
12. If you want to return multiple parameters, use std::tuple instead. It helps to avoid unnecessary struct declaration.

Overall good tips.

author: @pitri_hub
text:
Great video. After over 10 years of C++ usage, my score is 3

I still do:
• use std::endl, although mainly because it's an abstraction for plattform dependent newline symbols. "\n" or "\r\n"? So far I haven't found anything that just behaves like std::endl without std::flush... :/
• occasionally rewrite std algorithms. The common ones I use, but once in a while I still stumble upon a lesser known one that makes me facepalm, because I just implemented that a few days/weeks ago (std::partial_sort_copy has been one of them, for instance).
• forget virtual destructors. The amount of dynamic object oriented code I write is basically zero. I'd rather utilize the strengths of static polymorphism with templates.

Interesting additions:
• const_cast can also be used to add const, for instance to ensure that an unknown callback/lambda function can not modify the local variable you're passing in: callback(const_cast<const type &>(obj));
• Removing const is still legit in rare circumstances, if the library in use did not mark a pointer/reference parameter const, even though the function guarantees that the parameter won't get modified. Happened to me once somewhere in the Windows WIC library.

author: @LarryRuane
text:
Thank you, great video! Especially enlightening for me was the description of structured bindings; I see `first` and `second` used all over the place in bitcoin core. I knew item 30 (const ptr versus ptr to const) from many years of C programming; the mental model I used is: if the `const` is to the left of the `*`, then the thing pointed to is const; if it's to the right, then the pointer itself is const. And it can make sense to have both! `const S * const p` means that what p points to can't change, nor can p itself. Or even `const S * const * const p` (p is a pointer to a pointer to S; none of these 3 things can change). 

Another thing people often don't realize is: don't write `int * const p` in a declaration (header file), just write `int *p`, even if the function definition (implementation) is `int * const p`. This is because p being immutable is an implementation detail of the function, not part of its interface.

text:
Will you do one of these for JavaScript? Here are some ideas off the top of my head:

- End each line with a semicolon. VSCode has an option to insert semicolons automatically on file save.
- Ditch == and !=. If you want to compare a string and a number, cast one to the type of the other and compare them with === or !==.
- Declare your variables with `const` and `let`. Ditch `var`.
- Use `const` rather than `let` if you're never going to reassign the variable.
- Prefer template literals over string concatenation.
- Don't define all your functions in one file; use modules.
- Don't pollute the global scope. Prefer local variables.
- Avoid if-else hell; use switches when you can.
- Avoid if-else hell; use early returns.
- Avoid callback hell; use async/await.
- Simple callbacks should be written as arrow functions. `array.every(num => num % 2 === 0)` reads better than `array.every(function(num) { return num % 2 === 0; })`. I'd argue it's better to write all callbacks as arrow functions but that's just my opinion.
- Destructure arrays and objects when needed. Write `const { username } = req.body;` rather than `const username = req.body.username;`.
- When a function has many parameters, replace them with a destructured object so you can pass in arguments in any order.

author: @rassman48
text:
It started with nonsense, Can't call yourself professional with only one4 language? 
I am sure we all know that we only tried each language as it came out to see if it added something or if it made the developer's life easier. It rarely did either of those.

Starting with assembler, you built up massive libraries of macros and procedures, so when the first decent looking C came along, I could still knock together software with my assembler/macros faster than I could using early C, and I knew there was no hidden code.

Pascal was always too much typing. 
Ada was wonderful, had to use it for most military stuff, but still out side the military I could still knock together an assembler prog quicker.

However, when C6 happened that changed everything, I know C6 was an environment rather than a language in it's own right, but it was the only thing that tempted me away from assembler, for a lot of years I was still a heavy mix of assembler and C, but you learn to trust the C part in time, so that took over. 

And frankly I would not have moved on from there if the contract work didn't insist on using the latest thing that their IT department had bought. Don't tell anyone, but when I had to do some freaky OOPs work, I used my own lib files to do most of the work and pretty much ignored as much of the oops as I possibly could.

One other thing came along, C#. I thought from the start that it was the direction C was always meant to go. Ok so the early years you kept crashing into stack size problems. But it isn't like that now, I don't know off the top of my head what it's current limits are, but I know I haven't bumped into any of them.

author: @sertunc-k5o
text:
To those who are just beginning their journey in software development, I’d like to offer a humble suggestion; Programming languages are ultimately just tools — not the goal itself. The language you choose should depend on the problem you're trying to solve. You select the appropriate tool, study its documentation, learn it, and apply it as needed.

But more important than mastering a specific language is developing strong problem-solving skills and learning how to approach problems methodically. For this reason, I recommend that you first build a solid understanding of algorithms and programming logic before diving deep into any particular language.

And by “algorithms,” I don't just mean sorting or searching algorithms — I mean the ability to think through and design the logical flow of tasks in any given software. Writing code is a result; without proper planning and a thoughtful approach, creating efficient and maintainable solutions becomes quite difficult.
Start your software journey with strong foundations.
With respect and best wishes

author: @pouris
text:
TL;DR
All in all, it's all about performance and it's tradeoffs. Python is a simple language thats easy to get something up and running fast but not efficiently. C++ is a harder language that creates something robust and fast (if used properly). This is a plea to every short creator that constantly compares the two. Please, stop.

-- 

First of, in C++ std::vector should be contiguous meaning that each of the vectors elements come one after the other in memory. In order to achieve this, you'd want to know the type of the content of the vector beforehand. To illustrate why this is the case I'll provide an example.

If a vector (vector<char> vec = {'a', 'b', 'c'}) has a type of char, which has a size of 1byte, the vector will occupy 1byte * vec.size() of memory in RAM. If for example the starting position of the vector in RAM is 0x0 and it's size is 3 the compiler knows to pre allocate enough bytes in memory to host it's content so the ending position would be 0x3 (ignoring overhead like capacity management). Not only that, but the lookup of an index in the vector becomes trivial as you just need to offset the beginning of the vector (i.e 0x0) with the index * sizeof(char). However, if your vector was to contain multiple different types, it would drastically decrease performance as preallocation and fast index accessing would cease to be trivial. 

Take for example a python list:
lst = [1, Chicken(), 4.0, 'eggs'] # Chicken is a class

This is a valid python list but, the python runtime needs to work overtime in order to make this happen. Every type in python is an object and python lists are implemented as contiguous arrays of pointers to python objects and each object is allocated in different locations in the heap.

1 -> type int -> size around 28 bytes
Chicken() -> type Chicken -> size is ambiguous 
4.0 -> type float (c doubles) -> size 8 bytes
'eggs' -> type str -> size is 1 bytes per char so 5 bytes

Python needs to keep track of all the elements positions and sizes and dynamically allocate memory to host the lists contents which is way more inefficient than the vector implementation.

author: @oconnor663
text:
> mutable values...are stored in the heap

This is incorrect, and it's a pretty fundamental point. Rust is happy to have mutable values on the stack. The stack vs heap distinction in Rust is similar to the same in C++: objects need to live on the heap if their size is unknown at compile time (as the video mentions) or if their lifetime isn't limited to any particular scope. In Rust this is often done with Vec, Box, or Arc, much like C++ would use vector, unique_ptr, or shared_ptr.

Rust's unique approach to mutability is unrelated to the stack/heap distinction. The rule in Rust is that a mutable object can't be aliased; there can only be a single, unique reference to it while it's being mutated. This dovetails very closely with the ownership and borrowing rules that keep track of object lifetimes and prevent use-after-free bugs. These are the parts of Rust that make it really unique.

text:
I'm really not sure why so many people like rust. I despise the syntactical sugar sprinkled around the language all in the name of memory safety. It completely sacrifices readability and writing speed for that functionally negligible performance increase (I say functionally negligible because, while rust IS faster than many languages, the speed difference won't be relevant unless the author is writing the code for a real time system (no, NOT your game engine -- think microcontrollers in ECUs, where nanoseconds are essential). A good example of this in practice is the simple fact that C# game engines exist. C# is a MUCH slower language than rust in many ways AND is garbage collected, but can still perform well enough to power AAA games.

Those reasons alone are enough for me to far prefer something like go over rust -- golang being a language that is "minified" while managing to be extremely capable, performant, easy to write with, AND garbage collected (the GC is extremely efficient and can be configured or even turned off in special cases). I would much rather write code in another language than fight the rust compiler over memory management, wacky syntax, and an arbitrage of single-use keywords for functionality that simply does not need to be included in the base library of a language.

TLDR; IMHO rust is the wrong language unless you're writing a kernel or embedded code and don't want to use C. I dislike it very much.

author: @tenv
text:
Sorry, I have to be that guy.

1. The example C++ code is very contrived, you rarely use malloc and free in C++ (like you would in C) because...
2. C++ uses RAII. Necessary heap memory is allocated when the object is created, and freed when the object falls out of scope. The same system is used in Rust.
3. Just because something is variable, does not mean it is stored on the heap. If it's size does not change over the program's lifetime, there is no reason to allocate it on the heap. For example: a mutable u32 is initialized to 0, and later changed to 5. This u32 does not need to be on the heap, because no matter what it's value is, it will always have a size of 32 bits.

author: @scheimong
text:
Normally I like every video you make but I'll make an exception to this one. The few errors you made here can be very misleading to someone just starting out.

First, `let mut` does not put a variable on the heap; `Box::new` (or other smart pointers) does. Someone else already explained it so I'll pass.
Second, "mut" is not pronounced with a flat "u" (as in "mud"), instead say it the same way you would say the full word "mutable". This is a minor issue but nonetheless.
Finally, for most use cases you *really* shouldn't be using rustc directly. Instead use `cargo build --release` and `cargo run --release`, which is not only easier but also compiles your dependencies.

Granted Rust is particularly complex and 100 seconds is a short time. But I feel like this video could use some more research and is not up to your usual standards in the current state.

author: @PROgrm_JARvis
text:
Great and long-expected video!

Just some notes which may make it better:
Except for the already mentioned /mut not requiring heap/ error. It is also worth mentioning that the type inference is smart enough to make it not needed to place explicit type annotations (as on 1:43) in most cases. The reason why it has to be used in this particular example is that `collect()` works on arbitrary *target* types and thus it need a type hint into what to collect the data.
Also, to be fair, the screenshot at 1:27 has not got much to do with borrowing checker (there may be better examples, I guess).
Also, the preferred way to build binaries is `cargo build` instead of `rustc`.
So I guess (just my personal opinion) that it may be reasonable to have the video updated/reuploaded with these patches so that it gives a better image of the language in general (and not get used in holywars as an argument, haha).

author: @Speykious
text:
Despite Rust being my favorite programming language, it has 2 major problems:
- its ecosystem of external libraries is quite immature, and there is still a lot of improvement on the line.
- it *statically* links its standard library by default, which is a huge issue for the disk space that your executable will take. This way, every program, _even one that just has an empty main function,_ will take at least 3 megabytes of disk space.
Now of course there is the `-C prefer-dynamic` flag on rustc to compile the program with dynamic linking, but now at least you know that it's not the default.

author: @gogobram
text:
Every programming has a natural lifecycle.

How languages respond to innovation depends on the size of the community. If the community is small, they will redesign to make it blend in the way it should, keeping it compact. If the community is large, they will add a backwards compatible extension, making the language bigger.

The result is that old languages become feature-rich but ugly. While young languages stay slim and accessible.

And then at some stage, the community reaches its maximum size because it becomes easier to rewrite, then to learn it. It gets harder to recruit employees, but there's money to spend. So, then a rewrite happens, or it gets split in multiple applications in different languages.

A nice example is how XML and SOAP got replaced by JSON and REST. Even though XML and SOAP are way more powerful, they are also way more complicated. It just got too difficult to learn.

author: @skilz8098
text:
It is a leading language in many fields but that is determined by the environment you are working in. It's based on context. In other words, in some trade areas it is the goto language, but it's not the leading language for every scenario. It depends on the type of job or project you are working with. If you're writing a compiler, drivers or operating systems code, game engine development, hardware emulation, avionics, navigational systems, audio and signal processing then yes languages like C and C++ are probably the better fit. A lot of your lower end boilerplate code for servers and databases again C and C++, not always but is still a good choice. If you're doing basic and simple desktop applications it still has its place as does many other languages. Now once you get to the more abstracted areas such as web development, user interfaces, etc... then other languages like C#, F#, Java, JavaScript, Python, Pearl, Ruby, Rust, etc... are probably more practical. It depends on the requirements of the application's primary tasks and goals. If it is data driven crunching through a lot of data performing high volumes of calculations with efficiency and little overhead in mind as well as wanting it to be portable, generic, modular, and maintainable code such as libraries or interfaces then C / C++ are very good choices. If the code is user event or I/O driven and there are many calls back across the bus where there is going to be known delays, then other languages like C#, Java, JavaScript and Python are probably better. If it is task driven with repeatable tasks then shell languages would be a good fit. If you're doing A.I. or Machine Learning then C/C++ Python and a few others are all good choices. It all depends on the requirements and specification of the job as well as the already existing infrastructures. In many cases it is a leading language and in many other cases it is not. Knowing what the appropriate language is for the task at hand is more important than C++ being the #1 or #5 language of choice. One thing that does make C++ so powerful today isn't just its speed and efficiency, it's also the plethora of libraries that are already out there for you to integrate into your existing code base pending on licenses and permissions. 

I'm 100% self taught in C++ since around 2003-05. I started with C++ when I taught myself how to use DirectX and OpenGL, and these days I started to pick up a little bit of Vulkan. I've never worked in the field as I have done this as a hobby, yet I have very decent to a very good understanding of how the business and industry standards are. When a company invest millions into a specific platform and language and they're offering you work you will have to adapt to their environment. They're not going to switch from one format to another on the drop of a dime just because you're better at one language than another or because another language might be better for the job than the one they're using. Now in some cases if a language becomes "dead" or if the entire original code base is so old that no one knows that language and there's no one left around who originally wrote it to explain it, then they might consider updating their systems to a new format. A good rule of thumb would be to know programming concepts more than a language as that is your trade and from there to know maybe 3-5 of the most commonly used languages as tools in your tool kits. 

What do you think is more important? Your ability to read and write C syntax, SQL syntax, Lisp syntax? Or is it your ability to understand containers, algorithms (sort, search, find and replace, etc...), space and time complexities, object lifetime and memory management, thread safety, compression and decompression algorithms, encryption and decryption, file parsing, version control, project management, etc? Again which of the two do you think is more important? A language can easily be picked up and learned switching it out for another. The ability to derive well structured algorithms through Pseudocode is much more valuable. If you're not sure what the Pseudocode is meant or is going to do what makes you think you're going to be able to instruct the computer to properly do it for you in an efficient and precise manner? 

When you start to excel beyond that is when you'll begin to start making your own tools!  Here's an example, there's a game developer who left the mainstream or AAA developer studios that used C++ as a primary language and there were some things he liked about it but there was a lot that he didn't. On his own time, he decided to write his own programming language that is slightly similar to C++ in some ways but far different as it was geared to be a language specific to game programming. He removed a lot of the overhead from various components, added in capabilities the language didn't have to offer, etc... and from that he started to make his own games. One of the latest games that I'm aware of that he written and designed is called The Witness. Understand the Hardware and how it works to better know how to get it what you want it to do! In your spare time, trying writing a few novel programs in Assembly, or try to write a program in the language of your choice that will act as a CPU with its registers, cache, instructions, etc. and design your own ISA and your own Assembler. That'll truly strengthen your skills more than any one language can! And I'm just a Hobbyist!
