author: @DysoniaMultiverseNews
text:
I agree a lot with the key message of this video. It really doesn't matter which languages to learn so much. Sure, there are jobs listing the languages they are looking for job applicants to have. Your wage or salary is not so much about what languages you know but your education, knowledge, experience and ability. So it's that experience and ability to deliver. The languages they point to is for what they (employers) are working with and using and sometimes they just aren't ready to re-do what they had already invested in.... the issues of 'legacy' software. 

Now, when I began programming, I was working with BASIC and Assembly/Machine Language for various CPUs and computer hardware platforms such as 6502 based systems (including 65c816 CPUs and microcontrollers, etc.), TMS9900 from Texas Instruments (used in TI-99/4 and 4A), 68K series, 8080/z80, 8086 through  286 and some additional stuff with 386/486 and Pentium but these later x86 systems to present, I would use languages such as C and C++ and other languages that often have compilers to produce decent performant code. For performance, back in the earlier days, programming in machine language was the best with highly tuned programming. Back then, C++ didn't yet exist in the public commercial tools in the microcomputers era. Around mid-80s, we started to see C. Then C++ was emerging around 1990. C++ was not very beneficial for 8 bit systems and it was in the 16/32 bit era that we saw the emergence of C and C++. There was a few C compilers for C but it's code was only okay but machine language code can be more performant. 6502 machine language wasn't that hard to learn. However, modern CPUs have much more complex instruction set so it was easier to program in C and C++ and other high level languages that would compile. As C/C++ compilers evolved with optimization features, the code would be performant and as computers also got faster, the time and effort to code in machine code on the newer and faster computers was quickly becoming a waste of time for highly advanced code. Over the years, I have learned the myriad of languages including QuickBASIC/QBasic, Visual Basic, Java, various web-oriented scripting/programming/etc. languages such as HTML, CSS, XML, DHTML, XHTML, PHP, PERL, Javascript,  and newer stuff like Dart (with Flutter), Typescript, AssemblyScript / WebAssembly, more modern C++, etc. The languages are a long list, so it's matters to understand the software engineering principles and applying them regardless of the languages. The point of using the right tool for the work at hand that meets the requirements and that you can adequately deliver with less work because that is what employers are going to look for... time is money after all. 

If you can do the job in a language that meets the requirements that you know well enough to do it in 6 months but you would have to spend 12+ months in another adequate language that meets requirements, its fairly clear what language to use.... under most employment situations, the one that requires less time is what you would be expected to use. There's real world practical considerations. 

In my experience, a lot of the languages I have experience in are now obsolete in any work situations but I can tell you C/C++ is one of those languages that have stood the test of time. 

Stefan, good job with the video.

author: @reneb86
text:
I don't know why this video keeps popping up, but after ignoring it the first two times, I can't ignore it a third time.

I understand that the "Experienced C++ Developers" mentioned in the title is not a reference to Mr Mischook himself, but rather the commentors he's reading off of Quora. Nevertheless, since he does give a summary at the end, I think the direction of my comments is not too far off target. A quick online search does not reveal any obvious hints of Mr Mischook's experience with C++ in a professional capacity. In addition to his focus on webdesign, and a self admitted Java background, all my red flags are raised. The phenomenon of Java-enthusiasts that know everything about C++ without having written a single thing in it is worthy of its own Netflix show.

Here is something people without extensive C++ backgrounds always forget to mention: Your favorite software is most likely written in C++. If there is a piece of software you admire, be it an operating system, a videogame, a creative suite of applications, a scientific tool, an IDE, a new cryptocurrency, a consumer product with digital components, etc. it is written in C or C++. If it works well enough to the point to be admired, it is almost always C++. The facebook back-end is 99% C++. Every app on your Mac is C++. Try wrapping your head around that. Javaneers like to make you think that C++ is rarely used. Trust me, most consumer machines do not run a JVM, nor do they have python installed. The software running on consumer machines is plain and simple written in C or C++.

The question you need to ask yourself is this: Why do you want to write software? Do you just want a job as a programmer and it doesn't really matter what you make? if yes, then go study something hip and recent. You'll be fine. But if you want to drive a rover on mars, work on the latest iPhone, contribute to GTA6, or start an elite software development project of your own; you'd better bite the bullet and start learning C++. It forces you to think deeper about software, information systems, data structures, and how machines work in general. 
Having to manage your own memory forces you think about who should truly own an object in OO. And once you can address those thoughts throughout your entire architecture are you a professional. 
Writing OS-independent code forces you to think about what a filesystem really is and why a file and a socket are both read through the same mechanisms. 
I am not a webdeveloper nor do I aspire to be one, but when I was forced to set my mind to it, my webwork was vastly superior to those of other specialized webdevelopers in my team because having to work in C++/OpenGL/GLSL gave me the best position to shift into javascript/WebGL. 
Writing excellent software is about being obsessive. And where other languages often very quickly reveal their design constraints and intended purposes, C++ is a nearly inextinguishable source for learning that seems to have no heads or tails, but is somehow "Turing completer" than the rest combined (in spite of there not being such a thing).

In my line of work I am responsible for the technology stacks of integrated but distributed systems that operate in embedded/baremetal, web, mobile, cloud, and desktop environments. My biggest takeaway from years of headache is: keep your technology stack the same as much as possible in an integrated system. Good luck doing that with any other language.

I will get a lot of shit for saying this, but it is the closest statement to the truth, and the truth is worth being said; learn C++(20) and you really only need the other languages if you happen to join a project that is written in one of those other languages. And even in those cases; you're better off having learned C++ first. That said; 17 years of daily C++ work, and I still learn new things about C++ on a regular basis. But I wouldn't have it any other way.

Languages are just tools, although the first languages were invented to be "general purposes", modern languages are invented for a specific solution rather than to be used generally.
Also the one must admit that all general purpose languages such as ( c, c++, java, c# and python and more) all focused on a specific domain over time. Moreover, all the languages eventually converted to the single language (assembly) to be executed on a machine.

---> ios | android | desktop | web based | game - front end and application developer (communication with backend occurs via web protocols)
---> server part development - backend developer  (communication with front end occurs via web protocols)
       --> (note that, embedded systems can be considered as servers with low computational power)
---> application library development(may require low level development for the speed and specialization to the device. can be combined with system level development)
---> system level development (developments on the devices of both frontend and backend, any operating systems development and kernel developments are included here)

short time before i moved to deeper levels such as application library and system level development since i am interested in HPC and parallel programming. To do that i changed my sand box to c/c++ and verious libraries(openmp, openmpi, cuda) and computer organization.

as i am concluding my words i must say that " you must learn the languages and libraries which are used in the sandbox that you're in".

Rather this sort of legacy code base exists because it is already using the best tools for the job and very highly optimized.

author: @haroldmcbroom7807
text:
You can't always trust the "industry", as the "industry" is somewhat of a tight knit group, when one corporation has a "good ideal" others are quick to jump on the bandwagon.   They lack passion, and care only for $$$.    They set the standards by which everyone else is dumbed down, and they control the industry, so that no individual person can create something that makes them look STUPID.  I'm 51 years old, and I've grown with the gaming industry since the mid-80's, and I can say that today, the gaming industry feels DEAD, because of "cross-platform" programming, or "migration" as I like to call it, "Early Access" development which allows developers to get paid before the game reaches completion, while not being under and obligation to complete the games, small 1 to 2 or more member development teams which lack the experience to optimize their own games.   And this is just the software side of things, next comes the hardware side, where companies are making computers using cheap components that break down; it's as though the industry is being intentionally sabotaged by those who want to control "technology and information".

I was told that it was a bad ideal for new developers to create their own "game engines" from the start, and that they should learn existing game engines, how they work, and to become proficient, once they have gained experience in creating games,  and have the money and expertise, only then should they consider creating their own "gaming engines".  Another reason, is because it takes a lot of money to create a game engine, an top of that, the high cost of developing the actual game which utilizes the game engine.

To be honest, I have two years in Business Programming, where I was taught C++, COBOL, Pascal, and BASIC, but I was *NOT* taught the CORRECT way to program as is found in the REAL WORLD, when you examine professional C programs such as those by the popular YouTuber "Bisqwit", who is a sheer genius.   I was only taught the basic syntax of the languages, and introduced to "hello world" type programs.   I had no ideal before I attended Interactive Learning Systems, that "no one is going to hire an entry level programmer", and to be further honest, I wouldn't have even hired myself.  When you want to create the best game in the world, no one wants to hire entry level programmer, but someone who knows their stuff.

My education wasn't a total waste.  It's true, that if you know one language you can easily learn others, with a few exceptions.  No matter how good you are in COBOL will never prepare you for Assembly Language.  My knowledge of BASIC, allowed me to quickly learn Excel VBA, in which I was able to take a job being performed by 3 different people, sometimes had help from others, working 8 hours a day, write a program that did the job in 3 to 4 minutes.   It was the difference between hiring a data entry person, and hiring a data entry person with programming knowledge.

If you're new to programming, and want to be a developer, or even somewhat experienced, but do not have a premium license, then you'll go through "toolchain hell", trying to find a free compiler with IDE, along with third-party graphics libraries.   Back in the day when I was learning, we were given everything we needed, including graphics libraries.   You'll run into so many problems now days, from "free compilers" that are no longer being worked on, or that have migrated under new names, to issues installing them, once you install them, then you have to fight over getting the third-party IDE to work with said compiler, and once you've banged your head on your desk with THAT, then comes that point that you press F1 for help, and there are no help files installed.   It almost feels as though they do not want us to learn anything for free on the internet.

It wasn't my vocational school that taught me anything, but the books I bought from Herbert Schildt of Mcgraw Hill who wrote books such as "Teach Yourself C++", etc.   First off I owe GOD for giving me the ability to understand these things, and I appreciate Herbert for all of his wonderful books.

author: @razterizer
text:
I've been coding C++ since college and I'm coding in C++ professionally (for 16 years). I've programmed in other languages as well, but I will always love C++ no matter what. 

It has great performance but another feature I really love is that you can choose your layer of abstraction. Do you want to be as agile as possible then learn and use the newest features, and if you feel the need to do really low level stuff then you can do that too and there is a range in between. Just choose a subset of language features that work best for you. I don't know any other language that has this amazing range of features and layers of abstraction. 

There are platforms for using C++ to make GUIs and such but for that I rather use a language that has great tools for that such as C# albeit a bit slow. I occasionally code Swift and I love that too, but I'm married to C++ for life!

text: At my job I code Linux systems apps (automation) and I use C++ because it's the right tool for the job.  Could I do it in perl or python or <your language here>, sure. Programming should be taught this way because then my Nagios XI memory graphs wouldn't look like a reverse saw while running java code under tomcat.  (Garbage collection happens at out of scope not when memory is full, small reclaims not long pause for the big ones)  I get asked all the time, why C++?  My answer is always why try to pound a nail with the Eiffel Tower?

text:
C++ is a bad language. It does not offer memory protection and lets any contributor to a big project to crash it entirely. It has very complicated syntax with many many many hidden traps you gradually discover as you try to design more complex things.
It carries stone-age legacy of C.
Standard C library within C++ is ancient. Standard Template Library also carries 90s legacy and gives subpar performance. Fortunately, some of this is fixed in C++20 with ranges.
C/C++ are designed to support many more CPUs than you care about and as result define no fixed length and no standard representation for, say, signed integers. If you rely on ints being 32 bits, or on 2-complement representation,  a compiler may punish you severely, often without a warning. C/C++ standards are full of Implementation-Defined and Undefined Behavior.
With C++ you spend more time fighting the language, deciphering cryptic errors, making workarounds for specific compilers, than solving actual problems.

Language is irrelevant in programming. All you need to know is how computer works and how lines of code are translated into machine code. No matter what language you're using it will lead to the same CPU instructions in the end.
If someone says that learning one language is better than other, then he's not a skilled programmer. If you know how programming works, then you'll need a week to adapt for any new language to create highly efficient code and just within few hours you'll be able to work with that language.

This is why C/C++ are so important. They're really close to the hardware, while still being high-level languages. Learning C/C++ might seem hard at first, but in the end it will pay off with very advance stuff that makes code very stable, fast and resource efficient.

Programmer should be good at problem solving and he should know to pick right tool for the job. C/C++ isn't the best choice most of the time. Other languages generate cleaner and easier to maintain code, while requiring less effort to make code stable and reliable.
In general C/C++ should be used for stuff where raw performance is most important. If you need to call something thousands times per second, it should be written in C/C++ or other efficient language. If you call something only few times per second, you can use C#, Java etc.

Using multiple languages in single projects is the way to go most of the time.

This means you don't get nasty suprises with sudden memory allocations, garbage collection, etc. in the middle of time critical routine execution.

text:
That was actually a very reasonable video. I like that you are not strident. 

Yes, it's important to be exposed to several languages, not just in a classroom settings, but in an actual work environment.

I remember the Java craze when everybody said it would take over the world. I have precisely one Java program that I keep around on my machine - one, after thirty years in IT.

I'm sure C++ has its use cases but I've also heard that it can be difficult to debug because of all the class libraries. I suppose that can be true of any object oriented programming language.

Javascript is now all the rage but it suffers from depending on things other people somewhere else on the net may have written. 

I remember a case where a programmer pulled his code from a repo and an amazing amount of Javascript applications crashed because one obscure function in his code disappeared. That's a vulnerability no one expected.

I liked the Fortan example. I've never written any Fortran myself but I do appreciate that older languages have had more time to mature and become highly optimized.

I kinda like PHP. It's certainly easy to use. I've used it as a scripting language for applications that have nothing to do with the web.

But something I find that programmers, in general, overlook, is programming for maintainability.

 Good programs can last for decades. And the first thing that happens to a good program, is that it constantly gets modified. 

People always want customisation, reports, changes to screens, workflow, new features, etc.

There's a big difference between programs designed to be maintained over a long period of time versus something written quickly to solve an immediate problem. 

C++ was developed because of the problem of maintaining huge programs over long periods of time. 

PHP was not. It has always been a quick-and-dirty-fix-it-now kind of language. Though it has improved over time. And despite its warts, it is used in a lot of websites, including Facebook.

The syntax is often ugly and hard to read, meta programming is full of nasty traps and it can be cryptic; surprising semantics, often involving surprising implicit casting. author: @meatgoat4084
text:
Still so much misinformation here.

C++ was my first and forever love.  My life with it began in college in 1989 with cfront.  My first paying C++ job was in 1993 with AT&T C++ in the telecom industry.  My most recent C++ job was less than a year ago in the enterprise storage industry.  I've worked closely with C++ over the course of many jobs (including within the game industry) through all of its generations over a span of 31 years and I consider it my most marketable skill.  But throughout that time I've also had years of experience with C, C#, Java, Scala, and Python, and I'm currently having to become proficient with Go.  None of those have been by my personal choice but were required of the jobs that I've chosen to accept.

The bottom line is there is no "choosing a language" if you want to be a professional software developer.  That is a phoney meme promulgated by non-practitioners.  In the end you'll be expected to do whatever the job you've accepted demands from you.  So people entering the career should be more concerned with "choosing the right job in the right industry".  Developers who are happy in one industry may be completely miserable in others.

I know that the hiring process for developers is badly broken.  Believe me, I've been battling this condition for many years.  There is some truth to the accusation that resumes and CVs are screened for certain magic phrases, again by non-practitioners.

But, when you get past those levels of idiocy you will at some point have to impress actual practitioners.  That's when you will find your "choice of language" is not very important.  More important will be your proficiency and competency within the technology ecosystem that surrounds particular languages.  For example, I can easily determine your proficiency with Java by probing your knowledge of JVM performance, how you engineer your build and test environments, and how you engineer integrations with the outside world, without asking you a single question about Java syntax.  If you can't provide satisfactory answers to those concerns then your knowledge of language specifics is not going to impress me.  The same goes for C++, Python, C#, and anything else.  Each language is surrounded by an even more important ecosystem of supporting packages and libraries, tools, patterns and practices, and cultures.

So, how do you spot the practitioner poser?  When they confidently reply to the question "what language should I learn?" by actually naming a language.

author: @zvxcvxcz
text:
Everyone should learn C/C++, probably starting with roughly a C subset and then building up.  This introduces them to and gives them practice with all the low level concepts that will inform their later choices even when using more abstracted languages.  Understanding what is going on under the hood informs the choices we make.  I don't think it was discussed here, but aside from raw speed, C/C++ allow you to have real-time guarantees on execution that you don't get with Python or Java.  You also learn about the advantages of compiled languages, both for error checking and for the compiler to optimize things for you (loops in a language like R are sloooow, if there were a compiled version of R they could be optimized and fast in almost all cases, there are other way you can write that code in R to be decently quick, but the nice thing in C/C++ is that often the straightforward way to do something is a reasonably fast way).  

Even if you don't want to use C/C++ every day, you should know about memory management, there are scenarios in Java where the Garbage collector doesn't clean things up as early as it should and I have needed to manually trigger garbage collection.  If you assume garbage collection is always good, then you would be there searching forever for a bug in your code that doesn't exist.  

Knowing C/C++ makes learning most other languages pretty straightforward, but the converse is not always true, many other languages really won't prepare you to jump into C/C++.

author: @agugyin
text: According to the creator of C++, it is a "language design language". Just keep that in mind. C++ is BIG and layered. Probably bigger than anything one would need for solving a particular problem, but that also means it's universal, most versatile and definitely not dead. However thinking big as Stroustrup is insane for anyone without at least 5 years of C coding experience IMO. C is the best systems programming language (enough for a lot of structuring and organizing a system - an automation tool, industrial control/monitor equipment, embedded computer, instrument/controller device, inter-device device, so, many things - from a hardware perspective) for nearly any "living" hardware out there, regardless of infrastructure, yet with the "roll your own" driver feel that of Unix/Linux systems, which other OSes hide and outsource from the developer. C++ stems from that and takes it to a very high level, yet, the use of C++ is rarely reaching this proposed level of abstraction. C++ tries to maintain the reach to the underlying system while being more application-friendly with advanced safety and security considerations, but that won't stop beginner programmers to break the rules unknowingly (it shouldn't be a surprise that most operating systems come with tons of non-standard versions and language extensions as hardware development is very out of sync with the development of the C++ standard and yes, this breeds legacy bloatware as adaptation of new tech is faster than standardization and spread of its concepts and uses). In a way, the option of bringing computer language closer to say, technical English is already available with the C preprocessor and its standard library. C++ on the other hand is for modeling and designing much less hardware-dependent software on top of already present OS/network infrastructure. That goes with a lot of extra work and newer languages with their dependencies already carried out by newer technologies (virtual machines, containers, advanced internet protocols and lots of processes hardly relatable for non-engineering disciplines) make using C++ seem obsolete - yet it's still almost everywhere. I think (rather believe :)) C++ is for the highly literate who are ready for never coming out of the rabbit hole but keep in mind that some *customers* write *specifications* in C (that's direct experience, don't ask, why :D).

author: @Songfugel
text:
Oh damn, this video warms my cold dead programmer heart, such words of wisdom and sense.

I have personally been getting more and more frustrated by the narrow minded language diss and boost propaganda some other programming youtubers (won't be naming names) spread as gospel about their own chosen language, giving horrible short-sighted advice to people based on merits completely subjective to their own use scenario.

Even worse, is when they make "performance and usability" tests and demos with only partial knowledge of the other languages, using only the most basic features of those languages, and not the best practices for such a problem. Not to mention when they are comparing them on task parameters that the language is not meant for at all

Only one small thing I'd like to add for anyone new in the scene and watching this video for insight on future plans. DO NOT start by learning all the languages, just take one that is most suited to your or your company's needs and feels comfortable/enjoyable for you to use. And only AFTER you have gotten proficient in that language and the software engineering skills, should you move in to absorb more languages into your toolkit

Big problem I see all the time, is that people try to learn several different languages, always jumping on to the trendiest language, without ever mastering any and ignoring all the really important software development skills, since they are too busy learning to write "Hello World" in 7 different languages

And as a personal opinion, I would advice against starting with C, assembly, Perl or even with C++ for that matter, since those require more initial investment just to get started than the others. But at some point, you should absorb the C/C++ knowledge, since it will give you a more fundamental knowledge about programming

author: @ruffianeo3418
text:
Does 25-ish years of C++ programming count as experienced? Well - I mostly used it in embedded programming as a less error prone and more productive alternative to C (and the C fanboys never liked it). On the desktop, my embedded software also ran in test beds (software in the loop) as one step towards running it on the embedded targets (which varied frequently in terms of OS and hardware platform). 
For Tooling on the PC (stuff like generating code or configuration apps or test systems), we opted for the highest level language which also worked fine for GUI programming (was C# back then, nowadays, I would go with F# or Common Lisp).
At that point I started screening for alternatives (did not like C++11 and what came after (C++17 was more to my taste, eventually)) and I did a language tour, including the hyped functional languages (like Haskell). And to my surprise, what I now use for my explorative, prototyping, proof of concept and tooling language is none of the fancy new languages but Common Lisp. Why? High Level AND fast (if you aim for fast). 

For embedded (and probably server side programming), Rust looks like an alternative if people can accept the slow tool chain (it also does a lot a C compiler does not... but still) and really want applications which have higher prospect of being reliable.

The one language I never used and probably never will (unless you pay me triple :)) is Python. The syntax makes my eyes sore and it is slow. So why would I use it if instead I can use Lisp which is closer to C speed and once you got used to it, the syntax makes sense. Python is still in the uncanny valley, performance wise - comparable to interpreted lisps of the era between 1958 and 1990 (after, Common Lisp was more a compiled language than an interpreted one).

If there was more financial and support power behind OCAML, it very well could be the high level language of choice. But sometimes it feels as if it is maintained by just 3 dudes in a basement... And when I benchmarked ocamlopt compiled ocaml, it was slower than F# on .NET core. So I moved on.

author: @lionkor98
text:
My take as a pretty experienced C++ dev is this;

- The guy that wrote that article writes that C++ is "no longer a leading language". Hot take; JavaScript isn't a "leading language" in embedded systems, Python isn't a leading language in high reliability scenarios or low latency trading, etc. My point being that taking any language and ranking it regardless of which domain it's used in against other languages from different domains is not a valid way of comparing languages. Yes, Ada/SPARK isn't a "top 10 popular coding languages 2020" contender (not even close), but near irreplaceable in high reliability systems like aircraft, missile controls, etc. 

- Should you learn C++? If you have to ask, probably not. Writing C++ is engineering, its not "coding" in the same way that beginner level Js is. Yes it can be a pain, but a lot of my fellow C++ engineers agree that it's absolutely worth the trouble, because of the extreme amount of control and freedom you get. I would say, instead: Learn C. Does it inspire you to make things? If so, you're the right kind of person for C++. I would say anyone who likes to dive really deep and make intricate, fast and complex machines should look into C++. It's very fun! And after C++, almost all common other languages are a breeze to pick up.

- No clue what the author is saying about 2000-2011 C++, but recent C++ is C++20 (from 2020) and its getting close to the point where there is absolutely nothing it can't do. This is why its so strong, why games use it, why it's so fun for the people that spend the time to get into it. You can write in any style, use any paradigm, write code that looks like JS or write code that looks absolutely unreadable - you can do all these things, and it gives you the ability to use it for anything from low-level up to high level scripting.

- You cannot measure a language by "speed". It all depends on the programmer. The slowest code you can possibly write on a modern machine is likely C++ code, because you can fuck it up so damn bad if you don't know what you're doing. Missed a `&`? Surprise, now your entire dataset is copied each time you do an operation on it. C++ has the ability to be very fast, but it itself is as slow as the programmer who writes it is bad.

However, "better" depends on your goals—safer code, easier concurrency, modularity, or even AI-assisted development in the future. 

C's Weaknesses: 
Manual Memory Management, Lack of Type Safety and Bounds Checking, Concurrency Issues, Undefined Behavior (UB), Portability Pitfalls, Error-Prone Macros and Preprocessor, Security Risks.

Existing Alternatives to C for OS Development:
 Rust, Zig, Ada/SPARK, Go, C++.

Experimental/Future-Oriented: Languages like Vale (with region-based memory) or Carbon (Google's C++ successor) could evolve for OS work. In the 2030s+, we might see languages with built-in AI verification or quantum-safe features.

text: The inheritance example is just bad and gay OOP design. And you can't magically "propagate exceptions beyond project" unless you explicitly design such a way to exchange error data, and Google likely has it. author: @PedroOliveira-sl6nw
text:
Regarding Tabs vs Spaces, Yesterday I saw a video about Larry Osteramn's opinion on Tabs vs Spaces - and of course, he works for Microsoft so maybe his opinion is different. I like Tabs but as long as the project contains a clang-format file, I'm okay with any style, regardless of my preferences.

Regarding, "auto uFoo = myWidgetFactor()" is just a bad example of poor naming; has nothing to do with auto. "auto myUniqueFactory = make_unique<Factory>();" is a good example. "auto uFoo = MyWidgetFactor::CreateFoo();" is a good example. Naming functions the proper way is what you need here.
I'm not saying to use auto everywhere. "auto pi = 3.14F;" is a bit too much for me unless the surrounding lines already use auto.

C is not C++ but I'll tackle that as well. Memory Allocation is extremely important in large codebases that need to run fast. Only highly skilled engineers should touch that code. Everyone else, should use smart pointers to the best of their knowledge. There are reasons to use new/delete, reasons to use malloc/free, etc. It depends on the underlying memory layout/structure for the program.

Regarding exceptions, there are a lot of talks about how exceptions are not that bad. But I will give them a fair point there. However, handling errors is as hard as handling exceptions; you do it wrong, and you will still crash the system #crowdstrike.

Regarding inheritance and the diamond problem, bad example. Inheritance represents an is-a relationship but it does not correspond with our (human) idea of "is a". Like the shape example, mathematically speaking, we say a Square is a Rectangle but in programming, that would break the invariants, pre-conditions and post-conditions of that object - in the end, I think inheritance is on an expert level problem but a junior should think about its design first. For example, I like to use the Strategy Pattern and that requires some sort of inheritance sometimes.
Also, if you are going to show Composition over Inheritance, please use the same classes. Don't change the example to fit your needs.

author: @cruz1ale
text:
The example with Child inheriting from Mother and Father makes no sense. A class defines an object's identity, and inheritance is just a way to inherit parts of an identity from a different class. It doesn't have anything to do with objects inheriting from other objects. A Child cannot inherit both from a Father and a Mother, since a Child cannot _be_ both a Father and Mother.

A better example would've been to say that Child inherits from Person, but since a Mother is also someone's Child, the multiple inheritance scenario would be Mother inheriting both from Person and Child. But that's easily solved... there's no need to inherit from Person, since Child already inherits from Person.

author: @ov3rcl0cked
text:
I follow this inheritance rule in pretty much every language. Unless it's a clear cut case where inheritance makes the most sense, in terms of sharing a lot of code,  I'll opt for interfaces. I'll also prevent multiple layers of inheritance. I feel like the further you come from the base class then more confusing and implicit things can become. You end up not really knowing what the class is composed of. I instead will often look to encapsulation, and usually dependency injecting these encapsulated pieces, because it's also astonishingly easier to test. I have no strict rule around this, but I feel like if you're 5 layers of inheritance deep you're usually shooting yourself in the foot. I feel like many developers stray away from encapsulation when they can use inheritance, like one is somehow intrinsically better than the other.

A trick I've come to like when things start to get complicated with inheritance is to create an interface that defines all common methods, in C++ this would be a purely abstract class, and then have a base class for any common pieces to inherit. So in the case of a mother, father, and child, the parents might have their own base class which implements the interface, and child would just implement the interface, and maybe child could encapsulate a reference to the parents. This way any similarities in implementation the child shares with either parent is also specific to the instance of their parents. Child could even have it's own base class and you could create daughter and son, where maybe they each emphasize the characteristics of the parent who has the same sex as them, given this isn't how it actually works but serves the analogy.

I really see inheritance as mechanism to not repeat yourself, but I often see people trying to think of it too literally. Like the example mother, father, child, the child obviously literally inherits the mother and father, but you're kind of abusing the programming term "inheritance" to mean something it really doesn't. The child CLASS doesn't inherit traits from the parent CLASSES, it inherits PROPERTIES from a given INSTANCE of it's parents. Java doesn't allow multiple inheritance, and I honestly feel like that's prevented a lot of mishaps. On the other hand, I've dealt with inheritance nightmares in Pythons. I've seen a lot of people who abuse inheritance. We had a network protocol that had a major change between version 1 and 2, and the original developer implemented a base class to handle all the lower level networking pieces, many of which were common among version 1 and 2, and then inherited that into the v1 client. That's all well and good, but the real mind bender is the fact that they inherited the v1 client into the v2 client. Wild. It was so hard figuring out what happened where, and why these 2 major versions had overlapping code bases. It was a nightmare to pull that apart. This guy actually now works at Google, though I'm sure they've taught him a few lessons.

from my point of view if they don't have enough context to reason about auto widget = myWidgetFactory(), replacing auto with a type still shouldn't give enough information to reason about that line

so that last part is to follow SOLID design.  Each class holds unique concerns, and use composition over inheritance, so that functions and responsibilities stay separated.  Inheritance has its place, but is not engineered correctly.  With classes that mainly hold data and handle some transformations inheritance is not well suited.  For objects that build upon each other like window systems, then behavioral design there says that inheritance is good.  

With all of this said it is impossible to write debt free code.  We are developers.  The use of tabs should be encouraged.  Set your editors as a preference.  We engineer differently and have unique styles.  Some solutions are only found when people can be themselves.  All of this will lead to debt though in the sees of style.  

The issue here of debt free code is not the style of coding that one uses.  The issue is how to engineer properly.  This video touched on using interfaces.  Interfaces are really important and needed in all projects.  We should be designing for interfaces as that allows for modularity.  Need a new way to access data?  Not an issue as along as the data access returns all of the correct data sets.  Which data sets are there well that is where an interface comes in, as the functions should be set based on the business logic necessary to run the front end.  In this way we can reduce debt as we are only changing one concern at a time.  Debt is not style, but failings in logic. 

I also disagree with the non-use of exceptions.  Exceptions are not just program breaks, but are failures in design, and should be looked into.  Without the exception we have no idea why the program just crashed.  What is needed is a better way to handle logging.  They will need a standard library for logging exceptions.  It is now each concerns responsibility to report the error to the logging and then handle the exception per the concern.  In the example in the video the function g handles no exceptions from H or more likely handles errors in H by raising the exception again, which passes it up to F. I've always heard terrible explanations as to why "inheritance is bad", and yours is... well it's better than the rest, but you still make the mistake in the diamond problem of extending two classes where it doesn't make sense to, i.e. a child is not both their father and mother, they have a father and mother, thus this is a bad example and composition would be clearly used. These bad examples were one of the reasons I never took these "arguments" seriously.

A better example is when modularity is involved. Say you want to create an object that is both a Sprite (has x and y coordinates and can be drawn), and is a Damagable (has hp and stats). Perhaps you may even want to change stats based on position and so interactions between both are necessary; changing one should change the other. Both of these make sense to have internal state to potentially inherit from. However, the diamond problem occurs here too.

There are still drawbacks to composition, like desynced state between child members. I always say to use what makes sense, don't pick something because you always did it that way.

text:
You never inherit something like Child from Father and Mother. Or Car from Engine. Those are clear compositions. Think "has-a" vs. "is-a", which have distinct semantics. A child is not a father, or a mother. Neither is a car an engine. Sorry to be pedantic about this, but using better examples would lead to better informed learners.

If you want to compare inheritance vs. composition, you need to introduce the notion of preferring abstractions or interfaces and dependency injection. Parent can be the interface that can "hasChild: Child". Similarly, MotorVehicle can be the interface that can "hasEngine: Engine". Instead of Person > Parent > Father | Mother and MotorVehicle > Car.

author: @haxney
text:
Great video!

A few things, from a Google engineer (not speaking for the whole company, of course).

1. We absolutely have tech debt. These things help reduce certain kinds of tech debt, but it still exists all over the place. We're not magical; we make bad choices which we're then stuck with.

2. The lexical code style goes beyond just tabs vs spaces. Our code review system will yell at you if the code isn't formatted according to whatever clang-format would produce. Our style guide for indentation, line breaks, etc, is just "run clang-format and use that". I don't always like the choices which clang-format makes, but it's infinitely better for everyone to use the same standard than for me to use a standard I like more, but for diffs to be larger due to whitespace changes.

3. An important part of the style guide boils down to "don't get clever with template metaprogramming." I've been writing C++ for about 3 years now, and as soon as things get beyond the most basic template usage, I'm lost. If you're relying on SFINAE, you should probably reach for a different solution. Same thing once you start dealing with rvalues and lvalues. There are some places where those features really do make sense, but for things like "call this service. If foo is greater than 25, set bar to true", you probably don't need that stuff.

author: @triularity
text:
If C++ developers just assume exceptions could be thrown by almost everything, and defensively code for that, then dealing with them generally isn't a problem. Of course, this is easier when done in a language which has them from the start (e.g. java), rather than after the fact. To help mitigate the problems, there is always the noexcept declaration (but only if using C++11 or later).. and even its design is broken since it doesn't prevent them indirectly bubbling up and pulling the rug out from the function. I think it would have been better for the compiler to require the function dealt with any potential exception to guarantee nothing (like you would with checked exceptions in java).

[For the record, I avoid using C++, unless I have too -- it's basically a dumpster fire of things piled on top of things, piled on top of things, over the decades and many revisions. With a new spec seemingly every year now, it's only getting worse (no mature language should be changing that often)]

author: @dabbinchap
text: Not using exceptions is not viable with containers using dynamic memory. Constructors, copy constructors and copy assignment operators MUST be able to throw if they cannot allocate enough memory. And since they must throw, you must catch the exception. Sure, you could ban allocating memory in constructors, and force use of separate reserve methods. Sure, you could ban the use of copy constructors/assignment, but how the hell would you make a copy of an object that owns dynamic memory? Maybe use a obj.copy(T& to) function, which makes a copy from object to argument reference and returns true or false depending on whether the copy succeeded. That only works as long as programmers remember to explicitly delete copy constructor and assignment methods for a type; if they don't some other programmers will certainly do an implicit copy and then all hell breaks loose. Deleting copy methods plus overloading some global copy function (with boolean return value) is messy. Using such semantics is messy. In these cases just using exceptions works best.

text:
I definitely don't agree with indenting code with spaces. My rule is simple: at the start of line, only tabs are allowed as the whitespace and after first non-tab character, no tabs are allowed at all.

This allows every engineer to set their tab width just like they want it and the code still has identical *logical* indention for every engineer. If a line must be indented two levels, it has two tabs. And if the engineer wants to see it as 4, 6, 8, or 16 character wide indentation, they can adjust their editor as they like it.

author: @cameronmyron5776
text:
Using C/C++ in a professional setting (large code base that has been worked on for over a decade, many contributors of varying backgrounds, not strict coding standards, etc.) is why I’m looking into Rust.

Bad code is inevitable and will not always be caught in code review (not only does it require reviewers to be very thorough, which is diametrically opposed to getting work done fast, but the reviewers also need to collectively know everything to look for, which is unlikely). C/C++ will let you write provably (but maybe not obvious at the time) bad code, only giving a warning if you are lucky. While strict, I feel like Rust’s approach of assuring the lack of common bugs at compile time and requiring explicit marking when something can be unsafe (opposed to in C/C++ where it is up to the programmer add an unenforced comment to mark it) is ultimately the more future proof approach since it prevents people from unintentionally writing bad code.

author: @Tapajara
text: I started to outgrow C in the mid 1980's. Most new programming languages grew in the wrong directions. They threw out things I wanted to keep (e.g. pointers) and adopted things I didn't want (e.g. garbage collection). So Rust is immediately disqualified. None of them adopted Unicode as their base character set, although Python did a mediocre job in this area. You'd never want to write an operating system with that crippled interpretive scripting language. In 1988 I started developing what I now call ϕPPL. The 'ϕ' in its name emphasizes that its base character set is Unicode. PPL stands for "Parallel Programming Language". ϕ is the mathematical phi (rhymes with pie) that was brought into Unicode with the ANSI extensions. There is another φ that is part of the Greek Alphabet and you can pronounce it like "fee" if you want to say it that way. My entire tool chain is written in C and assembly. That speaks for itself.

author: @christianm4906
text: It's been about 12 years since we first heard of Rust, and despite the extensive marketing campaign it has received, it is still considered a niche programming language. Don't get me wrong, I'm not saying Rust is a bad programming language. In fact, it might be better than C/C++ in many aspects, but its approach forces developers to either write everything from scratch or deal with the pitfalls of the 'extern-function approach' for integration with the outside world. The industry has invariably proven that this approach is a failure from day one. A very good example of this is the Dart programming language. It was originally intended to replace JavaScript, and despite being better than JavaScript in many ways, it miserably failed to do so. Similarly, Rust is unlikely to succeed in replacing C or C++. Rust and C++ are fundamentally incompatible. I see more future in replacing C/C++ with other approaches such as CPP2 or Carbon if the first production-ready versions of those languages are released, which seems very likely to happen soon. Once that happens, there will be even less chance for Rust to replace C or C++. Also, note that C++ and TypeScript are very successful languages in terms of adoption because their approach doesn't require rewriting everything from scratch. You just change the extension from .js to .ts in your JavaScript programs and start seeing results in terms of migration right away. Similarly, with C++ and C; you compile a C program with a C++ compiler and start seeing results. That's why industries are reluctant to migrate to Rust. This approach is in opposition to code reusability, which is too important to give up.

author: @Diablokiller999
text:
When people ask me, how they should learn programming, I ALWAYS say - buy an Arduino learn kit for $20, do some projects with it, remove the Arduino Bootloader, do the same projects again without Arduino header and alter this code to use pointers.
After that, you've got a pretty good understand on how C works, how compiler work, how RAM and storage devices work and how processors work.
Next step would be to grab a Raspberry Pi and program a driver or two for the ICs from your Arduino kit and you know basically everything there is to know for a starting programmer.
You know C (and can switch to C++), you know hardware, you know drivers, you know how to extend the most used operating system in the world.
Taking interpreter languages like Python or going wild with web development could be your next step, easy to learn an master if you've got the basics from C.
All the code you will ever write, runs on computers so its one of the most valuable things to know how they work, either for optimization, portability and to know in general what the heck you are even doing.
Also it's getting hard to find embedded programmers these days, since it seems (to me) that no one wants to go through all the hustle with computer knowledge.

author: @madezra64
text:
Just gained a new respect for you. Many Rust tubers try to shit all over C, that you should avoid C like it's Aids, that C is useless, etc, denying the fundamentals of systems programming and understanding of programming as a whole in general. C is an incredible language, BUT so is Rust. It's very refreshing to see a Rust advocate step up and be honest about it. I tried learning programming from Python, C++, C#, and a few other languages first and it was a literal nightmare. Without any logical understanding of what was happening behind the scenes I was basically at the mercy of whatever tutorial or teacher I had. You know print("Hello, World!") displays "Hello, World!", but you don't know why or how. You just ASSUME the computer sees print and displays your sentence. Now some tutorials are better than others and give you some insight into abstraction, but the reality is most don't, and with that lack of fundamental understanding most beginners are confused from the beginning to the very end. It's like okay I see what these things I typed potentially can do, but I have no way of manipulating into my own will and desires because I know fuck all about the basics beneath it... It was when I finally decided to learn some basic assembly (cause why not at this point of my confusion) did I FINALLY understand what I was learning at the higher level. It was the epiphany that all beginner programmers stride for. That moment where shit just "clicks" and you now KNOW the path you must take to get better and know what to look for and learn. Did I understand how to do anything specific? Fuck no! But I understand the path I needed to take. I understood I needed to learn a, so I could learn b, then approach c, for approaching d, and so on and so on. I didn't learn assembly, but I learned what a programming language actually was. That's when I jumped right into C and began accelerating and actually learning finally!

I really don't believe Python is a good beginners language for this very reason among other languages.

You no longer have freedom to experience of how it is to go beyond/or close to boundaries. 
Boundaries are set for you because you are "stupid" and "irresponsible".
Don't get me wrong I still think Rust can offer a lot especially with web assembly, cargo etc., but this obsession for safety and control is just staggering and overwhelming.

author: @bushrat0118
text:
Ok I understand the "You should learn C first because it teaches you how a computer works" argument is really common, and I used to believe it as well. But now I actually think this is a bad take. Despite what everyone thinks their start in programming was, nobody started writing in C.

My grandfather's generation learnt by writing ladder diagrams, a trivial language with arbitrary rules and little bearing on the fundamental hardware.

My dad's generation learnt by writing in BASIC, a trivial language with arbitrary rules and little bearing on the fundamental hardware.

My generation learnt with JavaScript, a trivial language with arbitrary rules and little bearing on the fundamental hardware.

Sure, in a computer science course at the university level you'll learn something like C right now, but does C really teach you how a computer "works"? It completely obfuscates how registers, caching, context switching, etc. work. C only feels bare metal because you already know how a computer works and you're projecting over the gaps.

By the logic of "learning how a computer really works", you could make the argument that people should be writing assembly as their first language, and some schools still believe that. The problem is, assembly is awful for teaching how to think algorithmically. 

This is why most schools would teach maths and assembly: something high level for algorithms, and something low level for implementation.

Now, we're in a world where languages are expressive enough, and computers are fast enough, that you can write complex algorithms in a very expressive language and compile them down to fundamental instructions.

The C memory model is no less arbitrary than the Rust model. 

After all of that, I still think you should learn C, but not because you need it to understand a computer. You should learn C for the same reason you should learn Zig, Rust, TypeScript, BASIC, etc., Because knowledge is transferrable, and learning anything helps with understanding everything.

author: @Veinnie-the-Pooh
text:
Rust’s async model is known for its complexity, especially when compared to other languages like JavaScript, Python, or C#. The complexity mainly comes from how Rust handles memory safety, concurrency, and ownership, which is at the core of the language itself. Here’s how it compares:

1. Ownership and Borrowing in Rust
	•	In Rust, memory safety is enforced through its ownership system. This affects asynchronous code, as you can’t just freely share data between tasks like you can in languages with garbage collection (e.g., Python or JavaScript).
	•	In asynchronous Rust, the compiler ensures that data is either mutable or owned by a single task at a time. This can lead to more work upfront for developers, as you need to carefully manage lifetimes and ownership when dealing with async tasks.

2. Futures and the Polling Model
	•	Rust’s async model is based on futures and uses a polling system to check if a task is complete. This is lower-level compared to how async works in languages like JavaScript, where the event loop abstracts most of the complexity.
	•	In Rust, you must often deal with the Poll enum, which can make asynchronous code harder to understand, especially for beginners. You also need to explicitly use the .await syntax and be mindful of when and how tasks are polled by the runtime.

3. Async Runtime (Tokio vs. async-std)
	•	Rust’s async ecosystem relies on external libraries like Tokio or async-std, which provide the necessary runtime to execute async tasks. This adds another layer of complexity because you need to choose the right runtime for your project and understand its features and limitations.
	•	In contrast, languages like Python and JavaScript have built-in runtimes (like asyncio and the event loop), which abstract away much of the complexity.

4. Lack of Garbage Collection
	•	Rust doesn’t have garbage collection, so memory management is done manually by the compiler. This provides more control but also more complexity in managing the lifetimes of objects between asynchronous tasks.
	•	Other languages like JavaScript or Python handle memory management automatically, which simplifies async programming but comes at the cost of performance and predictability.

5. Error Handling
	•	Error handling in Rust async is more explicit. You need to propagate errors through the Result or Option types, even in async functions. This requires more boilerplate and explicit handling compared to languages like JavaScript, where you can rely on promises and try/catch blocks.

6. Concurrency vs. Parallelism
	•	Rust encourages you to think about concurrency (multiple tasks happening at once) and parallelism (tasks running in parallel across multiple processors) explicitly. You can’t just spawn threads like in some other languages; instead, you have to use async/await or spawn tasks with specific considerations.
	•	In contrast, languages like Python (via asyncio or threading) or JavaScript (with its event loop) abstract away a lot of this complexity, allowing for simpler concurrency models.

Summary

Rust’s async model is more complicated and requires a deeper understanding of memory safety, lifetimes, and task management. It is designed for performance and safety, which means more upfront complexity compared to languages like JavaScript or Python. However, once you grasp these concepts, Rust offers more control over concurrency, parallelism, and memory usage, which can lead to highly efficient and safe async code.

author: @1over137
text:
Go low enough level and enter into "digital electronics" and you (a software person) will hit some pretty funky realities.
First off, there are not 2 states.  Digital electronics are NOT binary.  They are usually "tri-state".  HIGH, LOW, or the third or "tri-state" is who-cares, invalid, floating, do-not-use.  Basically when outputs of gates as disabled and there remains no device "driving" the bus line, it is considered "floating" or "tri-stated".  It is also considered "random" by the laws of Maxwell.  You can get some pretty funky entropy using a floating shift register.  WARNING, it will also destroy most 74 series inputs if you leave them floating, the oscilate and overdrive themselves burning the chip out.
Second you realise that all electronics are analogue.  Not only that, but "square edge" pulses are formidable on wires and traces and come with a whole bunch of "analogue" domain complications as they get longer or your clocks get faster.
There are real situations where a "whoopsy" in hardware design can leave open the potential for a line of software to release blue smoke and physically destroy components.

text:
I think this is bad advice for a new programmer. I often see a lot of people experienced in their respective field advocate for learning their discipline "ground up". But while going ground up leaves no hole unfilled and covers all the bases, its usually hard to convey larger motivating ideas that drive these low level techniques in the first place. In the same way you wouldn't teach a grade schooler peano axioms before their first math class, you shouldn't teach pointers to a new programmer without teaching them why something like pointers would be useful. 

I think its easy to forget that programming has almost a century of history at this point and covers a very diverse set of paradigms, each with a very deep rabbit hole to go down. I think this advice is more appropriate for experienced programmers on entry to a new language. IF your language lets you interface with memory, then you should probably learn what you can do with pointers in that language.

author: @cipherlens
text:
What you said is 100% true. If you are a C programmer, understanding how Assembly code is generated and the instructions of the Architecture on which your program runs gives you a lot of insight into the code that you write. Likewise, when you write Python code, how most of these python features are implemented in the interpreter is by calling a native (C/C++) library behind the hood. 

If you know C and then think about how some feature like string concatenation using just a '+' symbol is possible in Python you'll get what goes on behind the scenes, which is nothing but multiple malloc, free, memcpy for each and every operation. This will give you some idea of the the performance hit by doing a simple '+' operation on strings in Python, which will eventually help you reduce the number of such calls and give you ideas of optimizing a badly performing code.

The ultimate truth is that every CPU runs on instructions that were mostly cast in stone decades ago. All these languages are abstractions over abstractions (several layers), which is a luxury.

author: @mth32871
text: I've taken various programming classes (Fortran, Pascal, C) and learned Python on my own, which is what I ended up using the most.  While I didn't really program for my job (although I used Python a lot for scripting), my job task changed in the last few years when I had to write test procedures for an 8051 based PCB, and the code was written in assembly.  I had not seen assembly very much before that, but I had a certain fear of it.  As I learned the details of reading (but not writing) it, my understanding of how computers worked increased tremendously (I also happened to be reading a book called "But How Do It Know?" which also helped a great deal).  I've always loved details, and knowing how things work, and learning 8051 assembly, an extremely easy to understand form of assembly, I now have that understanding.  Even though I had a pretty good feel for pointers in C before all of this, seeing how memory works on the 8051, in particular indirect memory, it became all that much clearer.  I know there are people who don't care about the details but only the high-level, but I would encourage every programmer to at least take a look at how computers and programming works at a low-level, at least for a cursory understanding.

author: @SidewaysCytlan
text:
No no no. I learned how to program in Actionscript (yes, you can laugh), but what *really* kickstarted my programming career was when I learned 6502 assembly. To this date, I think learning 6502 assembly (or a similar 70-80s microprocessor) is *the* best way to learn how computers *really* work. It puts you into this small little sandbox, but gives you the tools you need from grown-up architectures. 6502 assembly has pointers. And it can dereference pointers. And it gives you that in a memory space that's only 64K. Even if you mess up, you can still debug and follow along where your pointer went and how it got there. C isn't "low level", 6502 assembly is low level and an amazing tool for when you get around to actually learning C and modern computing.
Mind you, I'm not a greybeard. The 6502 was outdated and obsolete before I even was born. It's still an amazing low-level architecture that you can expand on when you dive into x86(/-64) or ARM, or any other architecture that's still at the forefront of computing technology today.

author: @grkuntzmd
text:
Good recommendations! I started programming almost 50 years ago. The second language I taught myself was RCA 1802 assembly language. I learned C in 1983 and never looked back. I was disappointed to find out that college computer science programs no longer require an assembly language course. Even though I've rarely used my assembly language knowledge (I worked at Bell Labs as part of the C compiler group and wrote some there), I think my background knowledge has helped in subtle ways throughout my career. I still recommend that anyone who wants to become a master programmer learn assembly language for at least one architecture. Even if you never program in assembler, it will change the way you write in higher-level languages.
BTW, hypothetically, of course, when I was in college, I bought a copy of the Sargon chess program for my Radio Shack TRS-80 computer. It came on a copy-protected floppy disk. I wanted to make a backup in case something happened to the original. I called the authors of the program and asked how to do that. Their answer was that it was impossible; they had paid a lot of money for the copy protection scheme they were using. Oh ho! That was all the challenge I needed. I disassembled their loader code and in a couple of days, rewrote it (in assembly, of course), and made several copies of the disk. Hypothetically.

Excellent tips, and that's a good objective you have.
The first computer programs I ever wrote were in IBM 360/370 Macro Assembly Language. Thinking back, that was a relatively high-level Assembly Language with macros like PRINT that abstracted away the details of text output, also macros to simplify access to the SORT/MERGE utility and disk access.
This was 1981 and we were keying in the programs on punchcards. There were still jobs in the paper for keypunch operators.
In my systems analysis class, I had an epiphany about how the actual binary opcodes actually trigger the CPU to do things and set or clear status flags. I rushed home and dove headfirst into 6502 Assembly Language on my new Atari 800.
C is something of a hybrid. Designed to be higher-level than assembly, which itself was designed to be higher-level than binary machine language. I've seen code to actually do object-oriented programming with it using pointers to structures of pointers and such, but that just hurts my head. It can also work right down on the very lowest level for bit-twiddling and such. It's been called the "portable assembler" because it first allowed the movement of the fledgling Unix operating system from one computer architecture to a completely different one.
I really prefer coding "directly on the iron." "But Momma, that's where the fun is…"
Sure, modern C compilers can generate machine code much more tightly than anything we can do by hand, but it's still good to know how to do it.
Rust looks to me like doing Swift the hard way. They are both good languages that work close to the iron and provide safer coding methods than C does while producing code that often can run even faster.
I was dismayed to find that X86_64 Assembly still looked a lot like the 6502 code I used to write.
After learning Motorola 680X0 Assembly, this was quite a shock. 
Now I'm learning ARM Aarch64 on my M1 MacBook Air. 
But I have the time for that now because I'm retired. I don't really know how much longer I'll be doing this.
I appreciate your carrying on the flame.

author: @TonyTigerTonyTiger
text:
This may not be the case universally, but in general, the stack is, in a sense, hanging upside down.  It “levitates” a little way up in memory and grows downward, from its bottom.  Pushing items onto the stack makes it jut down farther and farther into memory; popping items off of the stack results in the bottom of the stack receding upwards.  Why is this technicality “important”?  Because a phrase often times heard when dealing with exceptions would not make sense otherwise; it is said that unhandled exceptions “bubble up the stack”.   
 
Suppose there are three functions, funcA, funcB, and funcC, and that while executing, funcA made a call to funcB, and before funcB completed, it called funcC.  Functions are nested three levels deep, with funcC currently running.  If an exception occurs during the execution of a line of code in funcC, and no code is setup in that function to handle it, the exception will bubble up the stack one level to funcB.  And if funcB does not handle it, the exception will bubble up the stack one more level to funcA.  Unless one understands that the stack is inverted, the terminology of exceptions ‘bubbling up the stack’ may seem to be upside down.

text:
void pointers dont should be casted in C pure.

It is unnecessary, as void * is automatically and safely promoted to any other pointer type in this case.
It can hide an error, if you forgot to include <stdlib.h>. This can cause crashes, in the worst case.
It adds clutter to the code, casts are not very easy to read (especially if the pointer type is long).
It makes you repeat yourself, which is generally bad.

Hi Kundan, 
Here, we were talking about c/c++ only. In Java we have concept of reference variables. Primitive types like int and char go into stack. All the objects go into heap and their name is actually a reference sitting in the stack. Implementation of reference is almost like pointers, but that is internal to how java works. The heap is managed and garbage collection (cleaning up memory that's not referenced) happens automatically. So, there is no memory leak in pure java application.

a stack memory is fixed. If too many variables are created there will be a stack overflow. (no space available for the variables)

You have to remember to delete the object on the heap when you are done with it
The heap = dynamic memory = large free pool of memory
Pointers pointing to heap memory is saved on the stack
if there are no space on the heap the result of the call will be null
